title: Note-literal patterns in `match` never match a Note scrutinee (wrong arm / silent Void)
finding: A note literal in match-arm position is parsed as `LiteralPattern(location, PreviousToken.Text, ...)` where PreviousToken.Text is the raw string "C4" (Parser.cs:2033). MatchLiteral then does `Value.From(lit.Value)` which produces a STRING value, and compares via Utils.LooseEquals against the scrutinee. The scrutinee is a Note value (Data="C4", Type=NoteType). LooseEquals(Note,String): types differ, neither is numeric, so it returns false unconditionally (Utils.cs:66-83). Result: a note pattern can never match a note. Repro: `Note n = C4` then `(match n | C4 => "is C4" | _ => "other")` returns "other"; with no wildcard `(match n | C4 => "x")` falls through to a non-exhaustive Void. String patterns (String vs String) and chord patterns (dedicated MatchChordQuality) work, so this is specific to Note literals. A composer writing `match note | C4 => transpose... | D4 => ...` silently gets the default/Void for every note, i.e. wrong audio.
rootCause: A bare note literal in match-arm position is parsed at Parser.cs:2028-2034 as a plain LiteralPattern carrying PreviousToken.Text, the raw string "C4". PatternMatcher.MatchLiteral (PatternMatcher.cs:86-94) wraps that payload via Value.From(lit.Value), and Value.From (Value.cs:184-197, line 192: `string s => String(s)`) produces a String-typed Value. It then compares via Utils.LooseEquals(scrutinee, lhs). The scrutinee is a Note value: Value.Note(text) stores Data="C4" with Type=NoteType (Value.cs:32). In LooseEquals (Utils.cs:63-84) the types differ (line 66 fails the same-type StrictEquals path), neither operand is numeric (lines 70-76 fail), neither is Void (line 79 fails), so it returns false unconditionally at line 83. A note pattern therefore can NEVER match a note scrutinee. Verified by running the repro: `(match C4 | C4 => "is C4" | _ => "other")` prints "other"; with no wildcard `(match C4 | C4 => "x")` emits the non-exhaustive advisory and evaluates to () (Void). The String-vs-String control (`match "C4" | "C4" => ...`) correctly prints "is C4", confirming the defect is specific to Note (and any other reference/special-typed) literal patterns where LooseEquals' cross-type fallthrough is false. This is not charitable-by-design: charity here HIDES a real defect — a composer writing `match note | C4 => transposeUp | D4 => ... | _ => keep` silently routes every note to the wildcard/Void arm, producing wrong audio with no error.
repro: dotnet run --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'Note n = C4\n(print (match n | C4 => "is C4" | _ => "other"))'  # prints "other", should print "is C4"
suggestedFix: In MatchLiteral (PatternMatcher.cs:86-94), when the scrutinee is Note-typed (scrutinee.Type is NoteType) and lit.Value is a string, build the comparison value as Value.Note((string)lit.Value) instead of Value.From(lit.Value) so LooseEquals takes the same-type StrictEquals branch (Utils.cs:66 -> 109-110 string compare on the stored note text). Since both the scrutinee (Value.Note(text) at ExpressionEvaluator.cs:87) and the pattern (PreviousToken.Text) store the verbatim note text, a direct StrictEquals on the text fires correctly for the common case. Cleaner alternative: have the parser emit a Note-discriminated literal pattern for TokenType.NoteLiteral (mirroring the IsChordLiteral/IsArticulationSymbol ConstructorPattern flags) and route it through a dedicated MatchNote helper. Either way, consider normalizing enharmonic/octave forms (e.g. C#4 vs Db4) to match the rest of the language's note semantics, though that is an enhancement beyond the core fix.

title: Negative numeric literal in argument position after a value-end token fails to lex as a signed literal
finding: TryLexSignedNumber only treats `-N` as a single signed literal when _lastEmittedType is in a fixed expression-start set that includes LParen/Comma/Arrow/Assign/Pipe/Semicolon/Identifier/Match/When but EXCLUDES IntLiteral, FloatLiteral, all music-literal-end tokens (NoteLiteral, etc.), and At. So in a space-separated arg list `(add 5 -3)` the `-3` follows IntLiteral(5), lexes as Minus then 3, and the parser throws 'Unexpected token Minus'. The same forms after a variable or `(` succeed (Identifier/LParen are in the set), creating a confusing asymmetry: `(mul n -1)` works, `(mul 5 -1)` errors. Phase 26 removed infix arithmetic entirely (the parser already errors on stray `-` between values), so there is no infix-subtraction ambiguity to protect against. Affected ubiquitous forms: `(add 5 -3)`, `(mul 5 -1)`, `(max 5 -3)`, `(add -3 -4)` (second negative after the first literal), `(transpose C4 -2)` (after a NoteLiteral). The documented negative array index `xs@-1` also fails because At is not in the set (Parser.cs:1360 comment claims '-' is supported; EvaluateArrayIndex at ExpressionEvaluator.cs:510 implements negative indexing, but the literal syntax is unreachable — only xs@(neg 1) / a variable index reach it).
rootCause: TryLexSignedNumber (SimpleLexer.cs:498) only folds `-N`/`+N` into a single signed numeric literal when _lastEmittedType is in a fixed expression-start set (lines 506-532: null, LParen, Comma, LBracket, Arrow, Assign, Pipe, Semicolon, Identifier, Match, When). That set EXCLUDES every value-end token: IntLiteral, FloatLiteral, all music-literal-end tokens (NoteLiteral/SemitoneLiteral/CentLiteral/TimeLiteral/DecibelLiteral/HertzLiteral/BeatLiteral/ChordLiteral), At, and RParen. So in a space-separated arg list the `-N` following any literal lexes as a standalone Minus then a digit, and ParsePrimary (Parser.cs:1379) has no leading-Minus path, throwing 'Unexpected token Minus'. Verified by repro: `(add 5 -3)`, `(mul 5 -1)`, `(max 5 -3)`, `(add -3 -4)` (second negative), `(transpose C4 -2)` (after NoteLiteral), and `(transpose (| C4 D4 |) -2)` (after RParen) all error, while `(mul n -1)` (after Identifier) works — the asymmetry the claim describes. Phase 26 removed infix arithmetic (ParseFlowExpression at Parser.cs:1252 only matches Arrow/TildeArrow, never Minus), so there is no infix-subtraction ambiguity the narrow set protects against. Separately, `xs@-1` is unreachable: ParseUnaryShorthand (Parser.cs:1339) only lowers `-` to (neg X) when the next token is an Identifier, never a digit; the negative-index logic at ExpressionEvaluator.cs:510 (arr.Count + indexValue) IS implemented and reachable only via `xs@(neg 1)` (verified: returns 3 for [1 2 3]) — the Parser.cs:1360 comment 'supports unary minus for negative indices' overstates what the literal syntax can express.
repro: dotnet run --project flow-interpreter -- -e '(print (str (add 5 -3)))'  # error: Unexpected token Minus. Also: '(print (str xs@-1))' on an array errors.
suggestedFix: Add the value-end token types to the TryLexSignedNumber expression-start set (lines 506-532): IntLiteral, FloatLiteral, NoteLiteral, SemitoneLiteral, CentLiteral, TimeLiteral, DecibelLiteral, HertzLiteral, BeatLiteral, ChordLiteral, RParen, and At. This makes `-N`/`+N` after another argument (or after `@`) lex as a single signed literal, which ParsePrimary already consumes cleanly via its IntLiteral/FloatLiteral match arms (Parser.cs:1397-1401). No regression risk for the music-context sign paths (tempo/swing/pan/gain/reverbTime) because those `-N` tokens follow the keyword token (Tempo/Swing/...), not a value-end token, so they still reach their dedicated Match(TokenType.Minus) parsers. The `-IDENT` shorthand is unaffected (it is a Parser-level concern in ParseUnaryShorthand, not the lexer). After the change, re-run the negative-literal lex Facts and add coverage for `(add 5 -3)`, `(transpose C4 -2)`, and `xs@-1`.

title: A tuple literal cannot start a statement — `<<a,b>> ~> f` (the headline `~>` form) parse-errors
finding: ParseStatement dispatches `if (Check(TokenType.LessLess)) return ParseTupleDestructureStatement();` unconditionally, so ANY statement beginning with `<<` is parsed as a `<<Type? name, ...>> = expr` destructure target. A tuple literal used as the LHS of `~>` (or as a bare expression statement) therefore fails: `<<3, 4>> ~> add` and bare `<<1, 2>>` both report 'Expected identifier in destructure pattern'. This breaks the primary documented use of the `~>` tuple-unpack operator (CLAUDE.md: '~> tuple-unpack flow op'). Workarounds (parenthesize as `(<<3, 4>>) ~> add`, or bind to a variable first) are non-obvious. Confirmed valid destructure `<<Int a, Int b>> = t` still parses, so the fix is a disambiguation, not a removal.
rootCause: ParseStatement (Parser.cs:304-307) dispatches `if (Check(TokenType.LessLess)) return ParseTupleDestructureStatement();` unconditionally. So ANY statement whose first token is `<<` is committed to the destructure-target grammar (`<<Type? name, ...>> = expr`). When the `<<...>>` is actually a tuple LITERAL (elements are values/expressions, not `Type? identifier` slots), ParseTupleDestructureStatement hits a non-identifier first element and throws "Expected identifier in destructure pattern at ...:1:3" (Parser.cs:525-527). Confirmed by running the repro: `<<3, 4>> ~> add -> print` and bare `<<1, 2>>` both error at col 3; `(<<3, 4>>) ~> add -> print` works (prints 7) because parenthesizing forces ParsePrimary, which already builds a TupleLiteralExpression at Parser.cs:1502-1515. The defect is a missing statement-level disambiguation, not a missing feature — ParsePrimary already supports the literal.
repro: dotnet run --project flow-interpreter -- -e '<<3, 4>> ~> add -> print'  # error: Expected identifier in destructure pattern at 1:3
suggestedFix: Before committing to ParseTupleDestructureStatement, do a non-consuming lookahead from the `<<` to the matching `>>` (depth-counting LessLess/GreaterGreater) and only treat it as a destructure when the token immediately AFTER the matching `>>` is TokenType.Assign. Otherwise fall through to the expression-statement path so `<<...>>` is parsed by ParsePrimary (Parser.cs:1502) as a TupleLiteralExpression — which then composes normally with `~>`/`->`. This preserves the existing valid form `<<Int a, Int b>> = t` (followed by `=`) and unblocks bare `<<a, b>>` and `<<a, b>> ~> f`. Alternatively, lighter touch: peek that the first post-`<<` token is a type keyword or an identifier-followed-by-`,`/`>>` before dispatching; the `>>`-then-`=` lookahead is more robust against ambiguous cases like single-element tuples.

title: Multi-statement lambda body only parses when its first statement is a type declaration
finding: ParseLambdaExpression decides between a multi-statement body `( stmt1 stmt2 ... )` and a single parenthesized-expression body using `if (Check(TokenType.LParen) && IsTypeKeyword(_tokens[_current + 1].Type))`. The multi-statement branch fires ONLY when the first token after `=>` is `(` followed by a type keyword (i.e. a variable declaration). A multi-statement body whose first statement is an expression — e.g. `fn Int x => ((print "side") x)` — is mis-parsed as a single parenthesized expression `(print "side")`, leaving the trailing `x` as an unexpected token. Confirmed: `fn Int x => (Int y = (mul x 2); (print "side"); y)` parses and works, but `fn Int x => ((print "side") x)` errors. This silently blocks the natural form of side-effect-first lambda bodies (common when passing lambdas to each/map/forEach).
rootCause: In ParseLambdaExpression (Parser.cs:1738-1759), the choice between a multi-statement lambda body `( stmt1 stmt2 ... )` and a single parenthesized-expression body is decided solely by `if (Check(TokenType.LParen) && _current + 1 < _tokens.Count && IsTypeKeyword(_tokens[_current + 1].Type))`. The multi-statement branch fires ONLY when the first token after `=>` is `(` immediately followed by a type keyword — i.e. when the first statement is a variable declaration. A multi-statement body whose first statement is an expression (e.g. a leading `(print ...)`) does NOT match this heuristic, so it falls into the single-expression branch (line 1757). That branch parses only the first inner expression `(print "side")` and then hits the trailing token with `Expect(TokenType.RParen)` elsewhere, producing `Expected ')' after expression. Got Identifier 'x'`. The parser clearly INTENDS to support multi-statement bodies (dedicated branch + comment at 1741), so this is an incomplete dispatch heuristic, not charitable-by-design. Verified by running the exact repro (errors) and the declaration-first form `fn Int x => (Int y = (mul x 2); (print "side"); y)` (works, prints `side` then `10`); also confirmed it blocks the natural `each`/`map` side-effect-first form `(each (list 1 2 3) (fn Int x => ((print (str x)) x)))`. A workaround exists (start the body with a dummy declaration, e.g. `Int _unused = 0;`), which keeps severity at medium rather than high — it is a clear parse-time error with no silent corruption, lost notes, or wrong audio.
repro: dotnet run --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'Function f = fn Int x => ((print "side") x)\n(print (str (f 5)))'  # error: Expected ) after expression. Got Identifier x
suggestedFix: Replace the type-keyword-only lookahead with a structural decision that recognizes any multi-statement body. Concretely, when the token after `=>` is `(`, decide the body shape by scanning the matching parenthesized region (track paren/bracket nesting from the opening `(` to its matching `)`): if at nesting depth 1 there is a top-level statement separator (a `Semicolon`) OR more than one top-level expression/statement (i.e. the inner content does not reduce to a single expression), parse it as a multi-statement block via the existing branch (lines 1742-1752); otherwise treat it as a single parenthesized expression. A lighter-touch alternative that preserves existing behavior: keep the current branch, and additionally enter the multi-statement branch when the region contains a top-level `Semicolon` (since a single parenthesized expression never contains a top-level semicolon). Either way, the existing single-expression path (1757-1758) and the declaration-first multi-statement path must continue to work. Add a parser test covering `fn Int x => ((print "side") x)` and a semicolon-separated expression-first body.

title: Top-level `return` (and `return` inside a top-level for/while loop) silently truncates the rest of the program
finding: ExecuteStatement begins with `if (_returnValue != null) return;`. A ReturnStatement sets _returnValue (ExecuteReturn, line 1215). At top level (no proc on the stack) nothing clears it, so every subsequent top-level statement is silently skipped with NO diagnostic. This is asymmetric with the carefully-fenced blocks: ExecuteMusicalContext / ExecuteTuningContext / ExecuteLiveBlock / ExecuteSectionDeclaration all call ClearLeakedReturn or report+clear a leaked return (lines 89-97, 425-426, 517-518, 597-598, 827-833). But a bare top-level `return` and a top-level for/while loop body containing `return` (ExecuteForStatement line 681 / ExecuteWhileStatement line 714 propagate out with `if (_returnValue != null) return;`) hit neither path. Confirmed: a top-level `for Int i in [1,2,3] { (print (str i)); return i }` followed by `(print "AFTER")` prints only "1" and silently drops "AFTER" — lost program output / lost audio statements with no error.
rootCause: ExecuteStatement guards with `if (_returnValue != null) return;` (line 148-149). ExecuteReturn sets _returnValue (line 1215). At top level (InsideProcCall == false, since `InsideProcCall => _recursionDepth > 0`, line 47) nothing clears _returnValue after a top-level `return` — neither the program-level loop in Execute (lines 137-140) nor ExecuteForStatement/ExecuteWhileStatement, which both propagate out via `if (_returnValue != null) return;` (lines 681, 714). Every subsequent top-level statement is then silently skipped by the guard with no diagnostic. This is asymmetric with the project's OWN documented discipline: ClearLeakedReturn (line 89) emits "'return' is not allowed inside a {blockKind} block at top level — the return was ignored so the rest of the program still runs" and is invoked at top level for musical-context (line 426), tuning (line 518), and live (line 598) blocks — guarded by `!InsideProcCall`. The for/while loop bodies and the bare top-level statement loop miss the same treatment. Verified by repro: top-level `for Int i in [1,2,3] { (print (str i)); return i }` then `(print "AFTER LOOP")` printed only "1" with empty stderr; bare top-level `return 5` between two prints printed only "BEFORE". This is silent truncation of subsequent program output / audio/render statements, NOT charitable-by-design — the existing ClearLeakedReturn proves the project intends a report+clear rather than silent skip.
suggestedFix: Mirror the existing ClearLeakedReturn discipline on the two missing paths. (1) In ExecuteForStatement and ExecuteWhileStatement, when the body sets _returnValue and the interpreter is at top level, call ClearLeakedReturn (gated by `!InsideProcCall`) using the loop's source location instead of (or after) the bare `return;` at lines 681/714, so a leaked return from a top-level loop is reported+cleared while still propagating inside a proc. (2) After the top-level statement loop in Execute (after line 140), if `_returnValue != null` (which can only happen for a top-level bare `return`), report+clear it via ClearLeakedReturn-style diagnostic so the truncation is never silent. Both fixes preserve in-proc semantics (gate on !InsideProcCall) and reuse the existing helper at line 89.

title: Documented negative array index `xs@-1` is unreachable via its natural syntax
line: SimpleLexer.cs:506-532 (isExprStart set); Parser.cs:1358-1362 + ParseUnaryShorthand:1331-1349; ExpressionEvaluator.cs:510 (negative-index handling)
finding: Parser.cs:1360 comment says array indexing 'supports unary minus for negative indices' and EvaluateArrayIndex (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:510) implements `if (indexValue < 0) indexValue = arr.Count + indexValue`. But after `@` (At token, not in TryLexSignedNumber's expr-start set) `-1` lexes as Minus+1; ParsePostfix calls ParseUnaryShorthand which only lowers `-IDENT` (not `-LITERAL`), so `xs@-1` throws 'Unexpected token Minus'. Negative indexing only works via `xs@(neg 1)` or a variable holding -1 (both confirmed to return the last element). This is the same root cause as the negative-literal-after-token bug (At missing from the signed-number expr-start set) and is fixed by the same change.
rootCause: The documented `xs@-1` negative-index syntax is unreachable. After the `@` (TokenType.At) token, TryLexSignedNumber (SimpleLexer.cs:498-533) does NOT include TokenType.At in its isExprStart set (lines 506-532), so when _lastEmittedType == At the `-` falls through to SingleChar(Minus) (SimpleLexer.cs:149) instead of lexing `-1` as one signed IntLiteral. The parser then hits Match(TokenType.At) at Parser.cs:1358 and calls ParseUnaryShorthand (1361) to parse the index, but ParseUnaryShorthand (1331-1349) only lowers `-IDENTIFIER` to (neg IDENT) and has no `-LITERAL` branch, so it descends to ParsePrimary which sees a bare Minus token and throws "Unexpected token Minus". The negative-index semantics are implemented and reachable (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:510), just not via the natural `@-N` surface syntax. Severity corrected from low to medium: `nums@-1` is presented as runnable flow code in three wiki pages (Collections.md:27, Language-Basics.md:175, Tips-and-Tricks.md:510, each stating negative indices count from the end) and advertised in examples/tutorial.flow:1019, yet it produces a hard parse error — a violated documented contract, exceeding the cosmetic/edge low bar. This is not charitable-by-design: it is a parse-time crash on documented public syntax, not a degenerate-input fallback. Both documented workarounds (xs@(neg 1) and a variable holding -1) confirmed returning 3.
repro: dotnet run --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'Ints xs = [1, 2, 3]\n(print (str xs@-1))'  # error: Unexpected token Minus; but xs@(neg 1) returns 3
suggestedFix: Add `or TokenType.At` to the isExprStart disjunction in TryLexSignedNumber (SimpleLexer.cs:506-532). With the existing digit guard (lines 539-541: sign must be followed by a digit), `@-1` then lexes `-1` as a single signed IntLiteral(-1), which reaches ParsePrimary's IntLiteral branch and the already-correct negative-index handling at ExpressionEvaluator.cs:510. This does not affect plain `@1` (no sign) or parenthesized `@(neg 1)` (LParen path). Verified by repro: before the fix `xs@-1` throws "Unexpected token Minus", while `xs@(neg 1)` and a variable holding -1 both return 3. Add a lexer/parser test pinning `xs@-1` == last element. Note: the true defect locus is the lexer expr-start set in SimpleLexer.cs, not Parser.cs as the claim's primary file field implies — same root cause and one-line fix as the broader negative-literal-after-token issue.

title: Named-arg overload resolution picks first name-compatible candidate before type-matching, breaking calls to overloaded builtins
finding: In ResolveCore, the named-arg branch iterates candidates and breaks at the FIRST signature that passes the name/duplicate/arity checks (lines 296-301: 'namedArgCandidate = sig; ... break;'), then sets 'candidates = new[] { namedArgCandidate }' (line 321). Per-slot TYPE matching (sig.Matches) and specificity scoring only run AFTERWARD against that single survivor. For an overload set that shares parameter names and arity but differs by parameter TYPE, the resolver locks onto whichever overload was registered first and never tries the others. When the first survivor's types do not match the supplied args, the whole call fails with 'No matching overload' even though a later overload matches exactly. transpose registers transpose(Sequence, Semitone) before transpose(Sequence, Cent), both named [seq, amount] (TransformFunctions.cs:764-773); the db/hz/ms/sec/cents conversion builtins register Int/Long/Float/Double/tagged overloads all named [x] (ConversionFunctions.cs:80-90 et al). Reproduced: '(transpose s amount=+50c)' fails with 'No matching overload for function transpose with argument types (Sequence, Cent)' while the positional '(transpose s +50c)' succeeds; identically '(db x=12.0)' fails while '(db 12.0)' works. This silently disables the documented universal named-argument surface (D-36-11) for any overloaded builtin reached via a non-first-registered argument type. Note: named-arg calls bypass the overload cache (ExecutionContext.ShouldBypassOverloadCache), so this is purely a resolver defect and reproduces on the very first call regardless of cache state.
rootCause: The named-arg branch of ResolveCore breaks at the first candidate passing only name/duplicate/arity/reorder checks (lines 296-301), then collapses candidates to that single survivor (line 321). Per-slot type matching and specificity ranking run afterward against only that one survivor. For overloads sharing parameter names and arity but differing by type, the resolver locks onto whichever was registered first and never tries the others; if its types do not match, the call errors No matching overload even though a later overload matches exactly. Confirmed by running both repros: (transpose s amount=+50c) fails with (Sequence, Cent) while positional (transpose s +50c) works (transpose registers Semitone overload before Cent, TransformFunctions.cs:764-773); (db x=12.0) fails with (Double) while (db 12.0) works (db registers Int first, ConversionFunctions.cs:80-89). base FlowType.IsCompatibleWith is exact-equality only (FlowType.cs:16-19), so the first-survivor type-check legitimately fails. Positional path runs all candidates through Matches, so it succeeds. Named calls bypass the overload cache, so it reproduces on first call. Breaks the documented universal named-arg surface D-36-11 for any overloaded builtin reached via a non-first-registered arg type.
repro:
printf 'use "@std"
Sequence s = | C4 D4 E4 |
Sequence b = (transpose s amount=+50c)
(print "ok")
' > /tmp/r.flow && dotnet run --project flow-interpreter /tmp/r.flow  # errors 'No matching overload ... (Sequence, Cent)'. Also: (db x=12.0) fails, (db 12.0) works.
suggestedFix: Do not collapse to the first survivor. In the named-arg branch (~268-321), accumulate EVERY candidate that passes the name/duplicate/arity/reorder validation, each paired with its own reordered FlowType array (already computed at 272-293). Filter each pair via sig.Matches(reorderedForThatSig, strictMode) and rank survivors by sig.CalculateSpecificity(reorderedForThatSig), mirroring the positional path at 332-377 — but score each candidate against ITS OWN reordered vector, not one shared argTypes, since different overloads may map the same parameter names to different slots. Keep the single-match fast path and the equal-specificity ambiguity error. Concretely: replace the break at line 301 with appending (sig, reordered) to a list; drop the candidates = new[]{namedArgCandidate} collapse at 321; route the list through Matches and CalculateSpecificity per-candidate-vector before the count==0 / count==1 / ranked branches.

title: TupleType.AnyArity violates Equals/GetHashCode contract (Equals true vs differing hash)
finding: TupleType.Equals returns true whenever EITHER operand IsAnyArity (line 48), so AnyArity.Equals(Tuple<<Int>>) is true. But GetHashCode hashes the literal token "__AnyArity__" for AnyArity (line 63) and the element types for a concrete tuple (line 66), so the two equal instances produce different hash codes. This breaks the .NET invariant that equal objects must hash equally, corrupting any Dictionary<FlowType,...>/HashSet<FlowType> that mixes the AnyArity sentinel with concrete tuple types (e.g. a future overload-cache key carrying an AnyArity param, or any FlowType-keyed dedup set). No active corruption path was found today because runtime VALUE types are always concrete tuples (AnyArity is a param-registration sentinel only) and the OverloadCacheKey is built from value types, so the cache itself is unaffected. Flagging as a latent hazard.
rootCause: TupleType overrides Object's Equals/GetHashCode in a way that violates the .NET invariant "equal objects must have equal hash codes." Equals (line 48) short-circuits to true whenever EITHER operand IsAnyArity, so TupleType.AnyArity.Equals(new TupleType([IntType.Instance])) == true. But GetHashCode hashes the literal "__AnyArity__" for the AnyArity sentinel (line 63) and the element types for a concrete tuple (line 66), so the two Equal instances produce different hash codes. I confirmed: (a) the cited lines match the current source exactly; (b) the contract is genuinely broken at the C# level; (c) the claim's own honesty holds — there is NO active corruption path today. There are zero Dictionary<FlowType,...> or HashSet<FlowType> in flow-lang/flow-interpreter/flow-cli. AnyArity appears only as a parameter-registration sentinel in FunctionSignature.InputTypes (BuiltInFunctions.cs:1202,1220 for unpack) and is consumed via pattern-match `TupleType { IsAnyArity: true }` in ExpressionEvaluator.cs:420,775 and Interpreter.cs:1138 — never via Equals. The OverloadCacheKey (ExecutionContext.cs:109-163) hashes runtime arg types from ToCacheArgTypes(argTypes); a runtime tuple value is always a concrete TupleType with element types, so the AnyArity sentinel never enters a hash key. Hence the defect is a genuine but latent Equals/GetHashCode contract violation.
repro: No .flow repro (the AnyArity sentinel is never a runtime value type). C# level: TupleType.AnyArity.Equals(new TupleType([IntType.Instance])) == true but the two GetHashCode() values differ.
suggestedFix: Remove the AnyArity short-circuit from Equals (delete line 48 `if (IsAnyArity || t.IsAnyArity) return true;`) so Equals becomes a pure structural-equality relation consistent with GetHashCode. AnyArity wildcard matching already lives in IsCompatibleWith (lines 70-73) and CanConvertTo (line 80), which is what the actual overload-matching path uses (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:420/775 pattern-match plus IsCompatibleWith/CanConvertTo at line 424-427) — so removing it from Equals does not affect dispatch. Verified safe against tests: TupleFacts.cs:118-126 (AnyArityMatches_AnyTuple) asserts only IsCompatibleWith, never Equals, so the change keeps the suite green. Optionally add an xUnit fact pinning the invariant: for any two FlowTypes where a.Equals(b), a.GetHashCode() == b.GetHashCode().

title: Long argument fits neither Semitone nor Cent overload of transpose despite Long being in the widening chain
finding: transpose has only Semitone (compatible with Int only, SemitoneType.IsCompatibleWith line 22-26) and Cent (compatible with Double/Float, CentType line 24-27) overloads. A Long argument matches neither: Long.CanConvertTo covers Float/Double/Number (LongType.cs:14-19) but not Semitone or Cent, and neither special type declares compatibility with Long. So '(transpose s longVal)' fails with 'No matching overload for function transpose with argument types (Sequence, Long)' even though Long sits in the documented Int->Long->Float->Double widening chain and the composer reasonably expects a whole-number Long to act like a Semitone count. Ergonomics gap rather than corruption; Int and Double both work.
rootCause: transpose registers exactly two overloads (TransformFunctions.cs:764-773): transpose(Sequence, Semitone) and transpose(Sequence, Cent). Overload acceptance runs through FunctionSignature.SlotMatches (FunctionSignature.cs:197-212), which in non-strict (default) mode accepts a slot when ANY of: arg.IsCompatibleWith(param), arg.CanConvertTo(param), or param.IsCompatibleWith(arg). For a Long argument against the Semitone slot: Long.IsCompatibleWith(Semitone)=false (LongType has no IsCompatibleWith override; base is type-equality only), Long.CanConvertTo(Semitone)=false (LongType.cs:14-19 covers only Float/Double/Number), and Semitone.IsCompatibleWith(Long)=false (SemitoneType.cs:22-25 accepts only IntType). Against the Cent slot all three are likewise false (CentType.cs:24-27 accepts only Double/Float). With both overloads filtered out, OverloadResolver.ResolveCore (line 336-348) reports 'No matching overload'. Verified by live repro: a Long arg yields 'No matching overload for function transpose with argument types (Sequence, Long)', while Int and Double args both succeed. Long sits in the documented Int->Long->Float->Double widening chain, and SemitoneType already accepts Int 'whole-numbers-by-design' (SemitoneType.cs:18-20), so a whole-number Long failing to act as a semitone count is an ergonomics gap inconsistent with the Int path. This is a rejected-input/ergonomics gap, not corruption (no wrong audio, no lost notes, no determinism break; Int/Double recover trivially) — low severity is correct.

Sequence s = | C4 D4 E4 |
Long amt = 2
Sequence b = (transpose s amt)
' > /tmp/l.flow && dotnet run --project flow-interpreter /tmp/l.flow  # 'No matching overload ... (Sequence, Long)'
suggestedFix: Add Long to SemitoneType.IsCompatibleWith, mirroring its existing Int acceptance: change line 24 to `return target is IntType or LongType || base.IsCompatibleWith(target);`. Because SlotMatches tests the inverse-direction clause param.IsCompatibleWith(arg), this makes Semitone.IsCompatibleWith(Long) true and routes a whole-number Long to the Semitone overload — consistent with the documented Int->Long widening chain and the 'whole-numbers-by-design' Int rationale already in the file. (TransposeSemitone must read the underlying CLR long/int charitably, but it already handles the Int/whole-number case.) Alternatively register an explicit transpose(Sequence, Long) overload in TransformFunctions.cs:RegisterTranspose, but the SemitoneType change is the lower-friction, more consistent fix.

title: pitchShift inverts the stretch direction — all upward pitch shifts produce wrong pitch and near-silent/crushed output
finding: PitchShiftEngine.Process computes ratio = 2^(cents/1200), then time-stretches by factor = 1.0/ratio (line 60), then resamples reading srcF = outF * ratio (line 76). For an UPward shift (ratio > 1) the stretch makes the buffer SHORTER (~inFrames/ratio) while the resample tries to read up to outF*ratio = inFrames*ratio samples — i.e. it reads far past the end of the stretched buffer and clamps to the last frame (srcF1/srcF0 clamped at line 81-82). The correct pitch-shift-via-resample identity is: stretch by factor = ratio (LONGER), then resample by ratio — both operations use ratio, not 1/ratio. Measured (mono 1s 440 Hz sine, amplitude 0.5, input RMS 0.354): mode=#vocoder +1200c (octave up) output ~42 Hz (EXPECT 880 Hz), level ratio 0.47 — 72% of the output is the clamped tail. mode=#vocoder +700c (P5 up) ~300 Hz (EXPECT 659 Hz), level 0.64. DEFAULT mode=#auto +1200c via the Flow surface `(pitchShift tone +1200)` 0 zero-crossings in the middle (near-DC/clamp), RMS 0.209. Downward shifts work by luck (stretched buffer is longer than the region the resample reads): -700c is correct (294 Hz, level 0.999), and tiny shifts like +50c look OK because the length mismatch is small. A control simulation that stretches by factor=ratio (not 1/ratio) and resamples by ratio restores both pitch (878 Hz for +1200c) and level (1.0000). All three composer overloads (Double/Cent/Semitone) and #auto/#vocoder/#psola route through this one method, so every upward `pitchShift`/`+Nst`/`+Nc` is affected. Determinism is preserved (deterministic-but-wrong).
rootCause: PitchShiftEngine.Process inverts the stretch direction. It computes ratio = 2^(cents/1200) (line 56) then time-stretches by factor = 1.0/ratio (line 59-60) before resampling at srcF = outF*ratio (line 76). The correct pitch-shift-via-resample identity is stretch by factor = ratio (longer for an upshift), then resample by ratio. With factor = 1/ratio, an UPward shift (ratio>1) makes the stretched buffer SHORTER (length ~= inFrames/ratio + frameSize) while the resample tries to read up to outF*ratio ~= inFrames*ratio samples — far past the end. srcF0/srcF1 clamp to the last frame (lines 81-82), so most of the output is a flat clamped tail (DC). I confirmed this empirically by referencing the built flow-lang.dll and running PitchShiftEngine.Process directly on a 1s 440 Hz sine (amp 0.5, input RMS 0.354): +1200c vocoder -> dominant FFT bin 0.0 Hz (expect 880), RMS ratio 0.599; +700c vocoder -> 0.0 Hz (expect 659), RMS 0.672; DEFAULT mode=#auto +1200c -> 0.0 Hz (expect 880), RMS 0.719. Downshift works by luck (factor>1 makes the buffer longer than the resampled read region): -700c -> 301 Hz, RMS ratio 0.999. Tiny upshifts approximate (+50c -> 452 Hz). A control simulation stretching by factor=ratio and resampling by ratio restored both pitch and level for every case (+1200c -> 882.9 Hz RMS 0.993; +700c -> 667.5 Hz RMS 0.994; -700c -> 301.5 Hz RMS 0.998; +50c -> 452.2 Hz RMS 0.996). All three composer overloads (Double/Cent/Semitone) and #auto/#vocoder/#psola route through this one method (PitchShiftFunctions.cs:174), so every meaningful upward pitchShift/+Nst/+Nc is affected. The bug is also hit indirectly by drum pitch-shift (SfzRenderer.cs:312 calls PitchShiftEngine.Process(..., StretchMode.Auto)). Determinism is preserved (deterministic-but-wrong). The existing CI test PitchShift_Plus5Semitones_PreservesDuration passes only because it uses a small +500c shift and samples a mid-buffer FFT slice that lands BEFORE the clamp boundary (clamp begins at outF ~= 26290 for +500c; mid-buffer slice ~= outF 22050 still holds genuine pitched content). At +1200c the clamp begins at outF ~= 12049, so the mid-buffer slice is entirely in the DC region.
repro:
use "@audio"
Buffer tone = (createSineTone 440Hz 1.0 0.5)
Buffer up = (pitchShift tone +1200)
(writeWav "/tmp/ps_up.wav" up)
# /tmp/ps_up.wav is near-silent / DC, ~0 Hz instead of an 880 Hz octave-up tone.
# Direct: PitchShiftEngine.Process(sine, 1200, StretchMode.Vocoder) -> ~42 Hz, RMS 0.47x.
suggestedFix: In PitchShiftEngine.Process, change the stretch direction from 1/ratio to ratio: replace `StretchEngine.Process(input, factor: 1.0 / ratio, ...)` (line 59-60) with `factor: ratio`. The resample loop (lines 74-90) is left unchanged — it reads srcF = outF*ratio over outFrames = input.Frames; with the now-longer stretched buffer (length ~= inFrames*ratio for upshift) it reads the full buffer for upshift and stays in-bounds for downshift, yielding correct pitch and ~unity level (verified by the control simulation in both directions). title: WAV writer omits the RIFF pad byte after an odd-size data chunk (24-bit odd-frame export is non-conformant)
finding: WriteDataChunk writes the 'data' header + chunkSize + raw samples and then returns. The RIFF spec requires every chunk to be padded to an even byte boundary with a single 0x00 pad byte (not counted in chunkSize). The only bit depth that can produce an odd data size is 24-bit (3 bytes/sample) with an odd total sample count (16-bit and 32-bit are always even). The READER explicitly compensates for this pad byte (LoadWavInternal line 429-431: `if (chunkSize % 2 != 0) remainder++`), so there is a writer/reader asymmetry: Flow's own reader assumes the pad byte exists, but the writer never emits it. Verified: writeWav of a 3-frame 24-bit mono buffer yields a 53-byte file (odd, no pad). Strict third-party parsers (ffmpeg strict, some DAW importers) can reject or misalign on a chunk that follows. Most tolerant readers (and Flow's own reader, by reading one byte into the next chunk) survive, hence medium not high.
rootCause: WriteDataChunk (FileIO.cs:116-127) writes the 'data' chunk header, the chunkSize, and the raw samples via WriteSamples, then returns without emitting the RIFF-mandated even-boundary pad byte. The RIFF spec requires every chunk whose size is odd to be followed by a single 0x00 pad byte (not counted in chunkSize). Of the three supported bit depths only 24-bit (3 bytes/sample, WriteInt24 at lines 184-208) can yield an odd data size; 16-bit (2 B) and 32-bit (4 B) totals are always even. The reader (LoadWavInternal:429-431) explicitly compensates for this pad byte and the inline comment at line 426 even calls it 'the mandatory RIFF odd-chunk pad byte', so there is a real writer/reader asymmetry: Flow's reader assumes the pad exists but the writer never writes it. Empirically verified: createBuffer(3,1,44100) -> writeWav(path, b, 24) produces a 53-byte file (data chunkSize=9, file ends immediately after the 9th data byte, no trailing 0x00). RIFF size field = 0x2D = 45 = 53-8.
repro:
use "@audio"
Buffer b = (silence 0.0001 1)  # craft a buffer whose 24-bit frame count is odd
# writeWav24 path: file length comes out odd (53 bytes for 3 frames), missing RIFF pad byte.
# Direct: FileIO.WriteWavInternal(threeFrame24bitMono, path, 24) -> File length 53, odd.
suggestedFix: In WriteDataChunk, after WriteSamples, pad to an even boundary when the data byte count is odd: `if ((dataSizeLong & 1) == 1) writer.Write((byte)0);`. Additionally, in WriteWavInternal bump the RIFF fileSize field (written at offset 4 by WriteRiffHeader) to include the pad byte when dataSize is odd — i.e. compute `fileSizeLong = 36L + dataSizeLong + (dataSizeLong & 1)` — because the pad byte is part of the file but NOT part of the data chunk's size field. Keep the data chunkSize itself at the true sample byte count. This makes the writer spec-conformant and symmetric with the reader (LoadWavInternal:429-431), and preserves byte-identical two-run determinism since the pad is a constant 0x00. Note: 16/24/32-bit dither RNG behavior is unaffected; only one trailing byte and the RIFF size field change for odd 24-bit exports.

title: Granular with grain longer than the source buffer collapses to near-silence (Hann center lands outside the buffer)
finding: grainSamples is computed as grainSeconds*sampleRate with no clamp against the buffer length, and OverlapAddGrain reads source[sourceFrame + k] starting at the grain's *start* (sourceFrame = t, near 0), applying windowCurve[k] (a Hann window whose peak ~=1.0 is at the grain center). When the grain is longer than the buffer, only the very beginning of the Hann window (values near 0) overlaps the available samples, so the output is dramatically attenuated. Measured: a constant-0.5, 500-sample buffer through `granular(grain=1.0s, density=10Hz, jitter=0)` yields a peak of 0.0006 (effectively silence) instead of ~0.5. This is a degenerate input (grain >> buffer is unusual) so it is low severity, but the result is silently wrong audio rather than a charitable advisory.
rootCause: Confirmed by direct measurement. GranularEngine.cs:82 computes `grainSamples = Math.Max(1, (int)(grainSeconds * sampleRate))` with no clamp against the buffer's `frames`. WindowFunctions.Hann(grainSamples) (WindowFunctions.cs:39-59) builds a Hann curve whose unity peak sits at the grain CENTER (index grainSamples/2) and whose endpoints are ~0. OverlapAddGrain (GranularEngine.cs:150-162) reads `source[sourceFrame+k]` from the grain START (sourceFrame~=t~=0 when jitter=0) and multiplies by `windowCurve[k]`, breaking out of the loop once `srcIdx >= sourceFrames` (line 154). So when the grain is longer than the buffer, only the near-zero LEADING edge of the Hann window (indices 0..frames) ever multiplies any audio; the window's peak (1.0) lands far beyond the buffer end and never applies. Measured directly via GranularEngine.Apply on a constant-0.5, 500-sample, 44100Hz buffer with grain=1.0s, density=10Hz, jitter=0, Hann: output peak = 0.000632 (effectively silence). Same harness on a normal grain (50ms grain, 1.0s buffer) yields peak 0.500000 (energy preserved). Confirmed Hann(44100): hann[0]=0.0, hann[250]=0.000317, hann[499]=0.001263, hann[22050]=1.0. The claim's predicted 0.0006 matches the measured 0.000632. This is not charitable-by-design: there is no clamp and no advisory — the engine silently emits near-silent (wrong) audio for grain>buffer, exactly the "silently wrong audio" defect class. Severity low is correct: grain longer than the entire source buffer is a genuinely pathological/rare input (granular normally uses 10-100ms grains against multi-second material), the result is recoverable, and there is no crash, no data loss, and no determinism violation (the wrong output is deterministic).
repro: Direct: GranularEngine.Apply(new AudioBuffer(500,1,44100){all 0.5}, grainSeconds:1.0, densityHz:10, jitter:0, Hann, prng, site) -> peak 0.0006.
suggestedFix: In GranularEngine.Apply, clamp the grain to the buffer length so the Hann peak stays inside the available material: change line 82 to compute the raw grain, then clamp — e.g. `int rawGrain = Math.Max(1, (int)(grainSeconds * sampleRate)); int grainSamples = Math.Min(rawGrain, frames);`. Because windowCurve is rebuilt from grainSamples (lines 87-93), the window will then span exactly the buffer, putting its unity peak mid-buffer and preserving energy (verified: clamping to frames makes hann[frames/2]~=1.0 land on real samples). Emit a one-shot advisory when the clamp fires, matching the house charitable style and the existing `#auto`/`> 12 st` WarnOnce advisories elsewhere in Phase 37 DSP, e.g. `[granular] grain longer than buffer — clamped to buffer length`. Add a regression test alongside GranularSynthesisTests asserting that a constant-amplitude buffer through a grain>=buffer-length call preserves a peak near the input amplitude rather than collapsing to ~0.

title: SFZ velocity crossfade (xfin/xfout) produces silence/dropout instead of constant power — only one layer ever renders but both gains are applied
finding: SAMP-02 velocity crossfade is structurally incorrect. RenderInternal selects exactly ONE region per (targetMidi, vel) cell via patch.Grid[targetMidi, vel] (last-declared-wins) and renders only that region. The equal-power crossfade design assumes TWO overlapping layers play and sum (cos^2+sin^2=1), but they never both render. Worse, lines 350-364 take the selected region's ComputeXfadeGain (e.g. sin(normVel*pi/2) for an xfin layer) AND, when any sibling in the band also has a crossfade, multiply by an extra 0.7071. Using the repo's own documented fixture (velocity_xfade.sfz: layer1 xfout[60,80], layer2 xfin[60,80]), a real render sweeping velocity 50->90 measured: vel=60 -> RMS 0.00000 (TOTAL SILENCE, -240 dB), vel=65 -> -11.35 dB, vel=70 -> -6.02 dB, vel=80 -> -3.01 dB, with vel<60 and vel>=80 at full level. A composer authoring the standard overlapping-layer velocity-crossfade idiom hears a gaping volume hole (notes vanish) in the middle of the velocity range instead of a smooth equal-power transition. Root cause is two-fold: (1) the grid only stores one region per cell so the xfin layer's sin() curve hits 0 at the band's low edge with no xfout layer summing in to compensate, and (2) the 0.7071 sibling factor double-attenuates the single rendered note.
rootCause: The SFZ velocity-crossfade design is structurally broken because the renderer renders exactly ONE region per (pitch, velocity) cell, not the two overlapping layers the equal-power crossfade math requires. 1. The grid is `SfzRegion?[128,128]` (SfzData.cs:65) built last-declared-wins in SfzParser.cs:428-442. For the fixture's overlap band vel in [60,80], BOTH the xfout layer (region 1) and xfin layer (region 2) cover the cell, but only region 2 (declared last) survives in `grid[60, vel]`. 2. In RenderInternal (SfzRenderer.cs:211-212) `region = PickRoundRobinCandidate(...) ?? patch.Grid[targetMidi, vel]`. PickRoundRobinCandidate returns null (no seq_length>1), so the single winning region 2 (xfin) is rendered alone. 3. ComputeXfadeGain (line 350, helper at 450-467) returns the xfin layer's `sin(normVel*pi/2)`, which is 0 at the band's LOW edge (vel=60). With no complementary xfout layer summing in, the note is multiplied by 0 -> total silence. 4. The sibling-band check (lines 353-361) makes it worse and inconsistent: at vel=60 the sibling region 1's xfout gain is `cos(0)=1.0`, so `!= 1.0` is false -> siblingInBand stays false -> no 0.7071. At vel=65-80 the sibling IS in-band, so the SINGLE rendered note is additionally multiplied by 0.7071 — a spurious double-attenuation of a solo layer. Reproduced the exact claimed RMS curve by computing the gain math against the fixture: vel=60 -> 0.0 (-inf dB silence), vel=65 -> 0.2706 (-11.35 dB), vel=70 -> 0.5 (-6.02 dB), vel=80 -> 0.7071 (-3.01 dB), vel<60 and vel>=81 -> 1.0 (0 dB). This matches the claim's measured values to the digit. Crucially, the only renderer-side test (SfzVelocityCrossfadeTests.cs) verifies opcode PARSING only — its own doc comment defers crossfade correctness to "audible renders" (human ear), and SfzHardSwitchRegression.cs only pins the no-xfade=1.0 case. No automated test exercises the two-layer crossfade RMS, which is why the silent hole shipped undetected. Determinism is preserved (the bug is deterministic), but the audio output is wrong: a composer using the canonical overlapping-layer velocity-crossfade idiom hears notes vanish in the middle of the velocity range.
repro: Parse a 2-region SFZ where region A covers vel 1..80 with xfout_lovel=60 xfout_hivel=80 and region B covers vel 60..127 with xfin_lovel=60 xfin_hivel=80 (the repo fixture flow-lang.Tests/fixtures/Phase37/velocity_xfade.sfz). Load one sample for both regions into an SfzSampleCache and call SfzRenderer.Render for a C4 note at velocity 60/127. Measured RMS = 0 (silent); at vel 70/127 RMS is ~6 dB below the vel-50 baseline. Equal power would hold ~0 dB across [60,80].
suggestedFix: Render and additively SUM the overlapping layers for velocity crossfade instead of picking one. When a (pitch, vel) cell is covered by 2+ regions whose xfin/xfout bands include vel, render each contributing region with its own ComputeXfadeGain and mix them (their sin/cos gains already sum to constant power: cos^2+sin^2=1). Concretely, in RenderInternal enumerate `patch.Regions` matching (targetMidi, vel) where ComputeXfadeGain != 1.0, render each, scale by its own gain, and sum the fitted buffers before the articulation envelope/pan stage — and DELETE the spurious `if (siblingInBand) xfadeGain *= 0.7071;` (line 361), which double-attenuates. If multi-region summing is deferred, the minimum safe fix is: when the picked region is the ONLY contributor at this (pitch, vel) and no complementary layer will be summed, do NOT apply the xfin/xfout fade gain at all (treat it as the hard-switch full-level region) and remove the 0.7071 factor. That eliminates the guaranteed dropout/silence at band edges, falling back to Phase 33 hard-switch behavior rather than a gaping volume hole — though it loses the smooth transition the feature promises. Add an RMS-pinned renderer test that sweeps velocity 50->90 through velocity_xfade.sfz and asserts the band stays within a small dB window (e.g. +/-1.5 dB of 0 dB across [60,80]) so the silent hole can never regress; the existing SfzVelocityCrossfadeTests covers parsing only.

title: SFZ round-robin (seq_position) alternate sample files never eager-loaded — odd triggers render silent
line: 186 (CollectRegionsFromBar reads only patch.Grid[midi,vel]); interacts with SfzRenderer.cs:399-439 PickRoundRobinCandidate and SfzRenderer.cs:322,338 GetVarispeed null -> CreateSilence
finding: EagerLoad/CollectRegionsFromBar collects the set of WAVs to load by dereferencing only patch.Grid[midi, vel], which holds the LAST-declared region for each cell (D-02). But the render path calls PickRoundRobinCandidate FIRST, which walks patch.Regions and selects alternates 1..N by seq_position — and round-robin alternates normally point at DISTINCT sample files (rr1.wav, rr2.wav, ...). Only the grid-winner (the last-declared alternate) has its WAV loaded; the other alternates' samples are absent from _rawCache. At render time GetVarispeed(patch, region.SamplePath, ...) returns null for those alternates -> SfzRenderer returns CreateSilence. Result: a round-robin patch with N distinct alternate samples plays audibly only every Nth note; the rest are silent (with a [sfz] sample-not-loaded WarnOnce buried in stderr). Proven by render test: a 2-alternate patch (seq_position=1 -> C4_sine.wav, seq_position=2 -> G5_sine.wav) yields RawSampleCount=1 after EagerLoad with only G5_sine.wav (the last-declared/grid-winner) loaded; C4_sine.wav (seq_position=1) is missing.
rootCause: SfzSampleCache.CollectRegionsFromBar (SfzSampleCache.cs:186) collects the eager-load set by dereferencing ONLY patch.Grid[midi, vel]. Per D-02 (SfzParser.cs:425-442) the grid cell holds the LAST-declared region covering that (pitch, velocity), so for a round-robin group (multiple <region>s sharing the same lokey/hikey/lovel/hivel with seq_length>1) only the last-declared alternate's WAV is added to `needed` and loaded into _rawCache. At render time SfzRenderer.RenderInternal calls PickRoundRobinCandidate FIRST (SfzRenderer.cs:211) which walks patch.Regions and selects alternates by seq_position, normally pointing at DISTINCT sample files. For every trigger that selects a non-grid-winner alternate, _cache.GetVarispeed (SfzRenderer.cs:322) returns null (sample never loaded) and the renderer returns CreateSilence (SfzRenderer.cs:338) with a one-shot [sfz] sample-not-loaded WarnOnce. Net effect: a round-robin patch with N distinct alternate WAVs plays audibly only on the trigger landing on the last-declared alternate; the rest are silent. Confirmed empirically: a 2-alternate patch (seq_position=1 -> C4_sine.wav, seq_position=2 -> G5_sine.wav) yields RawSampleCount=1 after EagerLoad with only G5_sine.wav loaded; C4_sine.wav (seq_position=1) returns null from GetSample, and PickRegion_TestOnly on trigger 1 picks C4_sine.wav with cacheHit=False. The two existing round-robin tests (SfzRoundRobinTests / SfzRoundRobinDeterminismTests) miss this because the round_robin.sfz fixture deliberately points BOTH alternates at the same C4_sine.wav, so the grid winner happens to cover both; they also only assert SeqPosition selection, never that the alternate's sample was loaded. Determinism is preserved (the same alternate is always silenced) — this is wrong/lost audio, not a two-run violation.
repro: Build an SFZ patch with two <region>s sharing lokey=hikey=60 lovel=1 hivel=127, seq_length=2, where region 1 has sample=A.wav seq_position=1 and region 2 has sample=B.wav seq_position=2. Build a one-note (C4) Song and call SfzSampleCache.EagerLoad(song, patch). cache.GetSample(patch, "A.wav") returns null; only B.wav is loaded. Rendering the C4 note repeatedly through SongRenderer's sampler: path makes every odd trigger (seq_position=1) silent.
suggestedFix: Make CollectRegionsFromBar add EVERY region that could be selected for a note, not just the grid winner. For each non-rest note's clamped (midi, vel), reuse the same candidate-gathering predicate PickRoundRobinCandidate uses — walk patch.Regions and add each region r where r.LoKey<=midi<=r.HiKey AND r.LoVel<=vel<=r.HiVel to `needed`. This unions all round-robin alternates' sample paths into the eager-load set so GetVarispeed never misses at render time. Keep the existing null-cell nearest-pitch fallback contribution as well (and, ideally, also add the nearest-pitch candidates for cells with no exact coverage, mirroring SfzRenderer's FindNearestPitch/FindAnyRegionAtPitch fallback, so fallback-selected alternates are likewise pre-loaded). The sorted load loop (OrderBy SamplePath ordinal, ThenBy PitchKeycenter) at SfzSampleCache.cs:148-150 already dedups via ContainsKey and preserves Pitfall-5 determinism, so adding more regions to `needed` is safe. Add a regression test using DISTINCT sample files per alternate (e.g. C4_sine.wav for seq_position=1, G5_sine.wav for seq_position=2) asserting RawSampleCount==2 and that both GetSample lookups are non-null after EagerLoad — the existing fixture must not be reused since it shares one WAV.

Programmatically: a SampleCache whose EagerLoad found no files still reports HasInstrument("brass")==true, and SampledInstrumentRenderer.Render returns a CreateSilence buffer.

At SampledInstrumentRenderer.cs:161 and :182, before `return SynthUtils.CreateSilence(...)`, emit e.g. `RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce($"sample:missing:{_instrument}", $"[sample] no WAV loaded for '{_instrument}' (nearest MIDI {sampleMidi}) — rendered as rest. On the Web target the U-Iowa MIS bundle is stripped; build with FlowTarget=Desktop or fetch flow-lang/Samples/ to enable sampled playback.");` keyed by instrument (and optionally pitch) so it fires once per process.
