title: SAMP-03 articulation multiplier quartiles span the full buffer including the long release tail — staccato 'attack' bucket smears across the piano tail
finding: The Phase 28 ADSR envelope is shaped against authoredFrames (line 200-205), but the SAMP-03 SamplePathArticulationMultipliers are applied with quartile buckets computed over fitted.Length = authoredFrames + tailSeconds*sampleRate (the full buffer incl. the release tail, up to 1.5s for piano). SamplePathMultiplier.Sample(frameIndex, totalFrames) splits A/D/S/R at totalFrames/4. For a short staccato note with a long tail, frames [0, totalFrames/4) (the 'AttackMult'=0.5 bucket for staccato) cover well past the authored note into the tail region, and the 'ReleaseMult'=0.8 bucket lands at the very end of the tail — so the per-stage scalars no longer align with the actual ADSR stages of the note. The SfzRenderer applies the same multiplier over targetFrames where targetFrames == note duration (no extra tail), so SFZ and bundled-sample paths disagree on what each quartile means. The intended 'brighten the staccato transient' effect is misapplied for sampled instruments with a tail (piano in particular).
rootCause: In SampledInstrumentRenderer.Render, the Phase 28 ADSR envelope is generated with frames: authoredFrames (line 200-203) and applied only over [0, authoredFrames) (line 204). But the SAMP-03 articulation multiplier is sampled with sampleMult.Sample(i, fitted.Length) (line 215), where fitted.Length == targetFrames == authoredFrames + (int)(tailSeconds*sampleRate) (lines 136-138, 191). tailSeconds = clampedRelease defaults to DefaultReleaseSec = 1.5 for ALL sampled instruments (not just piano) via the zero-arg overload at line 96. SamplePathMultiplier.Sample (SamplePathArticulationMultipliers.cs:130-139) splits A/D/S/R quartiles at totalFrames/4. So for a short staccato note (authored window much smaller than the 1.5s tail), the AttackMult (0.5 for staccato) bucket [0, totalFrames/4) covers the entire authored note PLUS the first chunk of the ring-out tail, the DecayMult (1.2) bucket lands in the middle of the tail, and the ReleaseMult (0.8) bucket lands deep in the tail — none of the quartiles align with the note's actual ADSR stages. The intended 'brighten the staccato transient' shaping is misapplied to the post-note tail, and the stepped 0.5 -> 1.2 -> 1.0 -> 0.8 profile overlays a non-monotonic bump on what should be a smooth exponential tail decay (lines 225-234). The SFZ path (SfzRenderer.cs:186 targetFrames = note duration only, no tail; envelope frames: targetFrames line 372; multiplier Sample(i, fitted.Length) line 382 with fitted.Length == targetFrames) keeps the multiplier window equal to the envelope window, so the two sample-based paths disagree on what each quartile means. Verified: no existing test pins the tail-region multiplier behavior — ArticulationOnSampleTests deliberately scans only the authored window (line 217), and SampledStaccatoEnergyTests exercises the multiplier in isolation with frames == buffer length (no tail), so the misalignment is uncaught.
repro: Render a piano staccato note: fitted.Length is authoredFrames + ~1.5s tail. SamplePathMultiplier.For(Staccato).Sample(i, fitted.Length) applies the 0.5 attack scalar across the first quarter of the WHOLE buffer (authored note + start of tail) and the 0.8 release scalar only across the last quarter (deep in the tail), not over the authored note's actual attack/release.
suggestedFix: Bound the SAMP-03 multiplier to the authored-note window so its quartiles align with the ADSR envelope it is meant to reshape, matching the SFZ path (where the multiplier window equals the note duration). Change lines 212-216 to iterate only over the authored region and sample against authoredFrames: `if (sampleMult.IsNontrivial) { int multFrames = Math.Min(authoredFrames, fitted.Length); for (int i = 0; i < multFrames; i++) fitted[i] *= sampleMult.Sample(i, authoredFrames); }`. The post-authored tail (lines 225-234) then stays governed solely by the exponential tail-decay, producing a smooth ring-out. This also makes the sample path consistent with SfzRenderer.cs:378-383 where the multiplier window equals the envelope window. Add an end-to-end regression test that renders a piano staccato note and asserts the tail region [authoredFrames, fitted.Length) decays monotonically (no 1.2x bump partway through), since current tests only scan the authored window.

title: Dead `firstIteration` variable in SFZ loop-crossfade AssembleBody (assigned, never read)
finding: In AssembleBody's sustain-loop path, `bool firstIteration = true;` (line 588) is set to false at line 624 but never read anywhere. The surrounding comment block (lines 582-586) describes special first-iteration handling that the code does not actually implement — every iteration runs the same straight-read + crossfade. This is harmless dead code but signals that the documented 'first iteration plays the full body once' behavior was never wired, so the very first loop seam is treated identically to subsequent seams. Worth confirming the loop crossfade is acoustically correct given the comment/implementation mismatch.
rootCause: In AssembleBody's sustain-loop crossfade path, `bool firstIteration = true;` (line 588) is set to `false` (line 624) but is never read anywhere — confirmed via grep: the identifier appears exactly twice, both writes, zero reads. It is genuinely dead code, a leftover from an earlier implementation approach. It does NOT affect rendered audio or determinism (the build is clean, no warning, the value is never consulted).
repro: Static read of SfzRenderer.AssembleBody — firstIteration has no reader.
suggestedFix: Delete the unused `firstIteration` variable (line 588) and its assignment (line 624). Do NOT add first-iteration branching — the documented special-casing is already correctly implemented through the loop's read-position state: `srcReadPos` is initialized to `region.LoopStart` (line 587) so the FIRST iteration straight-reads the full body from LoopStart, and is only advanced to `region.LoopStart + xfade` at the end of each pass (line 623) so EVERY subsequent iteration resumes at LoopStart+xfade. Optionally tighten the comment (lines 582-586) to state the first/subsequent distinction is carried by `srcReadPos`, not a flag.

title: humanize (uniform) is non-deterministic — static unseeded Random never reset, breaks two-run cmp-clean
finding: `private static readonly Random HumanizeRng = new();` (line 1305) is a process-global, unseeded RNG drawn once per non-rest note in HumanizeUniformBar (line 1337). Unlike SynthUtils.Rng (reset to a fixed seed at every renderSong boundary — SongRenderer.cs:101,160) and unlike humanizeGaussian (which takes an explicit seed and does `new Random(seed)`), HumanizeRng is never reseeded or routed through PrngRegistry. The uniform `humanize` builtin has no seed parameter at all, so a composer cannot make it reproducible. Verified: two separate `dotnet run` invocations of the same script `(humanize mel 0.5)` -> writeWav produced different MD5s (54b2301...vs 459bbf7...). This is an offline (writeWav) transform, so it directly violates the documented 'same source -> byte-identical render' contract. The PrngRegistryNewRandomGateTests gate only forbids `new Random(` in StandardLibrary/{Patterns,Generative,Improv}/, NOT Transforms/, so this slipped through.
rootCause: `private static readonly Random HumanizeRng = new();` (line 1305) is a process-global, wall-clock-seeded RNG drawn once per non-rest note in HumanizeUniformBar (line 1337) to jitter velocity. The uniform `humanize` builtin has no seed parameter, and HumanizeRng is never reseeded — confirmed by grep that the only three references in the entire codebase are its declaration and single use, with no reset hook. By contrast SongRenderer.RenderSong resets PrngRegistry (line 154) and SynthUtils noise RNG (line 160) at the render boundary, and humanizeGaussian uses an explicit `new Random(seed)` (line 1386). humanize velocity directly scales synthesis amplitude, so it changes rendered bytes. The CI gate PrngRegistryNewRandomGateTests scans only StandardLibrary/{Patterns,Generative,Improv}/ (Theory rows lines 32-34), never Transforms/, so this slipped through.
repro:
Run twice and compare: `tempo 120 { timesig 4/4 { Sequence mel = | C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 A4 B4 C5 |
 section a { Sequence v = (humanize mel 0.5) }
 Song sa = [a]
 (writeWav "/tmp/h.wav" (renderSong sa "organ")) } }` — the two WAVs differ in MD5.
suggestedFix: Route uniform humanize through ExecutionContext.PrngRegistry keyed by (SourceLocation, "humanize") like the other unseeded stochastic primitives, so it reseeds at the renderSong/writeWav boundary (ResetAtRenderBoundary already runs there) and preserves two-run cmp-clean. HumanizeStrict already has `ctx` in scope to reach the registry. Concretely: thread a registry-backed Random (or a per-call deterministic stream) from HumanizeStrict -> HumanizeCore -> HumanizeUniformBar instead of the static HumanizeRng, deleting the `static readonly Random HumanizeRng = new()` field. Optionally also add a `(humanize seq amount seed)` overload mirroring humanizeGaussian for explicit reproducibility. Extend PrngRegistryNewRandomGateTests with an InlineData("Transforms") row so future Transforms/ wall-clock Randoms are caught (mark sanctioned explicit-seed uses with // PRNG-SANCTIONED:). Verified: three consecutive `dotnet run flow-interpreter /tmp/h.flow` of the same `use "@audio"` + `(humanize mel 0.5)` -> writeWav source produced three distinct MD5s (64551ee.., 7906088.., 859ea2d..), confirming the offline determinism violation.

title: trill / tremolo on chord brackets collapse upper chord-tones into a single-onset cluster
finding: TrillBar/TremoloBar iterate every entry in bar.MusicalNotes, including non-leading chord tones (IsChordTone=true, e.g. the E and G of [C E G]q). `note.With(...)` preserves IsChordTone, so each chord tone is expanded into N alternations/repeats that ALL keep IsChordTone=true. In BarType.ToTimeline (BarType.cs:194), every IsChordTone note stacks on `lastLeadOnset` (the last lead onset) and does not advance the cursor. Result: only the chord's leading tone actually trills/tremolos over time; the upper voices pile up as a cluster at one tick. Verified via MIDI: `(trill | [C4 E4 G4]h [C4 E4 G4]h | +2st)` produced C4 alternating at ticks 0/240/480/720 but ALL E4(64) and G4(67) trill notes stacked at tick 720: [(720,64),(720,66),(720,64),(720,66),(720,67),(720,69),(720,67),(720,69)]. Same structural collapse confirmed for tremolo. The June-9 audit added chord-bracket coverage for transpose but only single-note coverage for trill/tremolo, so this is untested.
rootCause: TrillBar (TransformFunctions.cs:1505-1544) and TremoloBar (1588-1629) iterate EVERY entry in bar.MusicalNotes, including non-leading chord tones. For [C4 E4 G4]h, NoteStreamCompiler.cs:858 (CompileChordElement) marks E4/G4 with IsChordTone=true. Each chord tone is then expanded into N alternations/repeats, and because note.With(...) preserves IsChordTone (verified NoteType.cs:367 `isChordTone ?? IsChordTone` — neither Trill/TremoloBar passes the slot), every generated subdivision of a chord tone keeps IsChordTone=true. In BarType.ToTimeline (flow-lang/TypeSystem/SpecialTypes/BarType.cs:194-200), all IsChordTone=true notes stack on `lastLeadOnset` (the most-recent lead onset) and do NOT advance the beat cursor. The lead tone's subdivisions advance lastLeadOnset to the LAST subdivision, so every E4/G4 subdivision piles onto that single final onset. Result: only the lead tone trills/tremolos over time; the upper voices collapse into a single-onset cluster. Verified with two live MIDI repros: trill `(trill | [C4 E4 G4]h [C4 E4 G4]h | +2st)` -> C4/D4 alternate at ticks 0/240/480/720, but ALL E4/F#4 and G4/A4 trill note-ons stack at tick 720 (and at 1680 for bar 2): [(720,64),(720,66),(720,64),(720,66),(720,67),(720,69),(720,67),(720,69)]; tremolo `(tremolo | [C4 E4 G4]h ... | 4)` -> C4 repeats at 0/240/480/720 but all four E4 and all four G4 repeats stack at tick 720. Claim's cited BarType path "flow-lang/Runtime/BarType.cs" is wrong (actual: flow-lang/TypeSystem/SpecialTypes/BarType.cs) but the line number (194) and TransformFunctions citations are exact. The June-9 audit test (Audit0609/TransformDataLossTests.cs section 4.2) covers chord-bracket preservation for TRANSPOSE only; section 4.5 trill/tremolo tests all use single notes (C4h, C4h., C4q), so this chord-bracket path is untested.
repro: `tempo 120 { timesig 4/4 { Sequence c = | [C4 E4 G4]h [C4 E4 G4]h |\n section a { Sequence v = (trill c +2st) }\n Song sa = [a] (writeMidi "/tmp/t.mid" sa) } }` — parse note-on ticks: C trills, but E/G note-ons all share one tick.
suggestedFix: Treat a chord group as a unit in TrillBar/TremoloBar. Group bar.MusicalNotes into (lead, [following IsChordTone notes]) runs. For each generated lead subdivision i, emit a FRESH lead note for that subdivision, then re-emit each chord tone WITH the same per-subdivision duration AND isChordTone:true so they stack on THAT subdivision's lead onset (advancing the cursor only on the lead). Concretely in TrillBar: after computing the lead's upperMidi/alternations, for each i emit lead-or-upper (IsChordTone=false), then for each chord tone in the group emit `chordTone.With(durationValue: trillDur, isDotted:false, isTied:false, isChordTone:true)` (and the chord tone's own upper neighbour on odd i). Mirror in TremoloBar with the subDur/subFraction. This makes each subdivision a complete stacked chord, so the timeline advances correctly and the upper voices trill/tremolo in lockstep with the lead. Add a regression test in Audit0609/TransformDataLossTests.cs section 4.5 with a chord-bracket source asserting distinct onsets per subdivision for the upper tones (mirroring the existing Transpose_ChordBracket test).

title: trill on tuplet notes ignores DurationFraction, leaving stale fraction -> severe bar overflow
finding: TrillBar computes the subdivision count and per-note duration purely from the enum DurationValue (TrillSubdivisions reads NoteValueType.ToFraction(DurationValue)), and rebuilds each alternation via `note.With(durationValue: trillDur, ...)` WITHOUT passing a durationFraction. Tuplet notes carry both a 'best-effort enum mirror' DurationValue (QUARTER) AND a real DurationFraction (e.g. 2/3 quarter). Since With's durationFraction param is null, the OLD DurationFraction is preserved and (per GetBeats) overrides the new DurationValue. So every trill alternation keeps the full tuplet-note duration, multiplying the bar length. Verified: `(trill | {3:2 C4 D4 E4}q D4 E4 F4 | +2st)` in 4/4 (bar = 1920 ticks) produced note-ons extending to tick 3240+ — ~6.75 beats crammed into one bar. (TremoloBar avoids this: its else-branch uses BaseQuarterFraction(note) which reads DurationFraction; only TrillBar is broken.)
rootCause: TrillBar derives subdivisions and per-alternation duration purely from the enum DurationValue. TrillSubdivisions (line 1554) reads NoteValueType.ToFraction(DurationValue) and ignores DurationFraction entirely; TrillBar rebuilds each alternation via note.With(durationValue: trillDur, ...) (lines 1528, 1531) without passing durationFraction. MusicalNoteData.With (NoteType.cs:363) coalesces `durationFraction ?? DurationFraction`, so a null arg PRESERVES the source note's old DurationFraction. Tuplet notes carry BOTH durationValue:QUARTER (a "best-effort enum mirror", NoteStreamCompiler.cs:611) AND the real durationFraction:perChildSlot (line 620). Because GetBeats (NoteType.cs:375) takes the DurationFraction branch whenever it HasValue, every trill alternation on a tuplet note keeps the full tuplet-note duration instead of the intended subdivision. Verified end-to-end: `(trill | {3:2 C4 D4 E4}q D4 E4 F4 | +2st)` in 4/4 (PPQ=480, bar=1920 ticks) writes note-ons spaced 160 ticks (= 1/3 quarter, the preserved DurationFraction) for the tuplet portion — the 3 tuplet notes alone span ticks 0..960 (2 full quarters instead of 1) — and the whole bar runs out to tick 3240 (~6.75 beats in one 4/4 bar). The plain-note portion (D4 E4 F4) trills correctly at 120-tick sixteenths, confirming only the rational-duration path is broken. TremoloBar (lines 1604-1617) avoids this by routing dotted/rational/overflow notes through BaseQuarterFraction(note) (line 1635), which reads DurationFraction; TrillBar has no equivalent branch. Render is deterministic (two-run cmp-clean), i.e. deterministically wrong, not a determinism violation.
repro: `tempo 120 { timesig 4/4 { Sequence tup = | {3:2 C4 D4 E4}q D4 E4 F4 |\n section a { Sequence v = (trill tup +2st) }\n Song sa = [a] (writeMidi "/tmp/tt.mid" sa) } }` — note-on ticks run past one 4/4 bar (1920).
suggestedFix: Mirror TremoloBar's rational path in TrillBar. When note.DurationFraction.HasValue, compute the trill subdivision as an exact Fraction = BaseQuarterFraction(note) divided by the alternation count, derive the alternation count from that rational duration (e.g. round BaseQuarterFraction(note) / desired-subdivision-in-quarters, floored to >=2 like TrillSubdivisions), and emit note.With(durationFraction: subFraction, isDotted: false, isTied: false) (and the same plus pitch overrides for the upper neighbour) so GetBeats sees the new duration. Keep the existing enum path (durationValue: trillDur) for plain notes where DurationFraction is null, so non-tuplet trills stay byte-identical. Concretely: add an `if (note.DurationFraction.HasValue)` branch at the top of the per-note loop in TrillBar (before line 1517) that builds alternations with durationFraction; fall through to the current enum code otherwise. BaseQuarterFraction (line 1635) and Fraction arithmetic are already present for reuse.

title: Roman numeral chord quality ignores numeral case — `iv` renders as major, not minor
finding: ResolveRomanNumeral derives chord quality solely from the key's diatonic default table (defaultQualities[degree]) and ignores whether the composer wrote the numeral uppercase or lowercase. RomanNumeralValues maps both 'IV' and 'iv' to degree 3, and the quality comes from MajorQualities[3]='maj' regardless of case. For diatonic-correct case the result happens to be right, but borrowed/chromatic usage is silently wrong: `iv` (minor iv, a very common borrowed chord) in C major produces F-A-C (F major) instead of F-Ab-C (F minor). Verified via MIDI: both `| IV |` and `| iv |` in Cmajor produced notes [65,69,72]. The case carries musical intent (uppercase=major triad, lowercase=minor triad) per the documented examples (I, ii, IV, vi).
rootCause: ResolveRomanNumeral derives chord quality exclusively from the key's diatonic default table (defaultQualities[degree], lines 137-140) and never consults the case of the input numeral. RomanNumeralValues (lines 53-57) maps both "IV" and "iv" to degree 3, and SplitRomanNumeral preserves but does not act on case. So in C major, both `IV` and `iv` index MajorQualities[3]="maj" -> F-A-C. The lowercase case-carried intent (lowercase = minor triad, the standard Roman-numeral-analysis convention also reflected in tests/test_roman_numerals.flow comments lines 6/10/17 and CLAUDE.md "I, ii, IV, V7, vi") is silently dropped for any non-diatonic case. Empirically verified via `dotnet run`: (resolveNumeral "iv" "Cmajor") -> ["F4","A4","C5"] quality "maj" (should be F minor F-Ab-C); (resolveNumeral "v" "Cmajor") -> G-B-D (should be G minor); (resolveNumeral "i" "Cmajor") -> C-E-G (should be C minor). Diatonic-correct case works only by coincidence because the chosen case matches the diatonic default. This is wrong audio for valid, common borrowed/chromatic chords (e.g. the minor iv), not charitable handling of degenerate input.
repro:
`tempo 120 { key Cmajor { Sequence u = | IV |
 Sequence l = | iv |
 section a { Sequence v = u } section b { Sequence v = l }
 Song sa=[a] Song sb=[b] (writeMidi "/tmp/IV.mid" sa) (writeMidi "/tmp/iv.mid" sb) } }` — both MIDIs contain notes [65,69,72] (F major).
suggestedFix: In ResolveRomanNumeral, when no quality extension is supplied (the `else` branch at lines 137-140), override the third based on the numeral's case instead of using only the diatonic default: detect case via char.IsUpper(baseNumeral[0]); if uppercase force a major triad ("maj") and if lowercase force a minor triad ("m"), starting from the diatonic root computed at line 130. Preserve the existing diatonic default ONLY where it encodes a diminished/augmented triad that the case alone cannot express: i.e. keep "dim" when the diatonic default for that degree is "dim" AND the numeral is lowercase (so vii in major still yields the diminished leading-tone triad, and ii in natural minor still yields the diminished supertonic). Concretely: if extension==null, quality = char.IsUpper(baseNumeral[0]) ? "maj" : (defaultQualities[degree]=="dim" ? "dim" : "m"). Leave the extension!=null path untouched (explicit V7/iv7/etc. still override). This keeps every diatonic-correct case byte-identical (verified diatonic outputs already match) while fixing borrowed chords like minor iv, minor v, and minor i in a major key. Add a regression test asserting (resolveNumeral "iv" "Cmajor") -> F-Ab-C and that (resolveNumeral "vii" "Cmajor") stays diminished.

title: Roman numerals in church-mode keys silently resolve to all rests (lost notes)
line: 118 (ResolveRomanNumeral calls TryParseKey) / 154-195 (TryParseKey, major/minor only) / 251 (GetScaleNotes calls TryParseKey)
finding: MusicalContext.ValidKeys accepts all 7 modes (major/minor + dorian/phrygian/lydian/mixolydian/locrian), and ScaleDatabase has the canonical TryParseKeyWithMode that handles modes — but ResolveRomanNumeral (and GetScaleNotes) still call the legacy TryParseKey, which only recognizes the 'major'/'minor' suffixes and returns false for any church mode. ResolveRomanNumeral then returns null, and NoteStreamCompiler.CompileRomanNumeralElement (NoteStreamCompiler.cs:910-915) inserts a rest. Net effect: a composer sets a fully valid `key Ddorian { }` context, writes roman numerals, and EVERY chord silently becomes a rest. Verified: `key Ddorian { | i iv | }` produced an empty MIDI (no note-ons). This is silent note loss, not a charitable degenerate-input case (the key block is accepted as valid).
rootCause: ResolveRomanNumeral (line 112) and GetScaleNotes (line 249) both call the legacy TryParseKey (lines 154-195), which only matches the 'major'/'minor' suffixes and returns false for the five church-mode suffixes (dorian/phrygian/lydian/mixolydian/locrian). A canonical mode-aware parser, TryParseKeyWithMode (line 211), DOES handle all 7 modes, but it is not wired into these two callers — the in-code comment at lines 197-209 explicitly acknowledges TryParseKey stays unchanged and its callers keep the bool isMajor protocol. Meanwhile MusicalContext.BuildValidKeys (MusicalContext.cs:35) admits all 7 modes, so `key Ddorian { }` is accepted as a fully valid context. When ResolveRomanNumeral returns null, NoteStreamCompiler.CompileRomanNumeralElement (NoteStreamCompiler.cs:911-915) inserts a rest with no advisory. Net effect: every roman numeral inside a valid modal key block silently becomes a rest.
repro: `tempo 120 { key Ddorian { Sequence s = | i iv |\n section a { Sequence v = s } Song sa=[a] (writeMidi "/tmp/m.mid" sa) } }` — MIDI has zero note-on events.
suggestedFix: Migrate ResolveRomanNumeral and GetScaleNotes off TryParseKey and onto TryParseKeyWithMode, adding per-mode interval arrays (Dorian/Phrygian/Lydian/Mixolydian/Locrian as rotations of the major scale) and per-mode default chord-quality tables, so numerals and scale notes resolve in modal keys. Concretely: extend ScaleDatabase with a Mode->intervals[] map and a Mode->qualities[] map, then in ResolveRomanNumeral select intervals/qualities by the parsed Tuning.Mode instead of the isMajor bool. As a minimum interim safety net (and good regardless), emit a one-shot WarnOnce stderr advisory at CompileRomanNumeralElement (NoteStreamCompiler.cs:913) when a numeral fails to resolve in the active key (e.g. `[harmony] roman numeral '<n>' unresolved in key '<key>' — rendered as rest`) so the silent-rest fallback becomes visible to the composer instead of dropping notes silently. Verified repro: `key Ddorian { | i iv v | }` rendered an empty MIDI (0 note-on events) vs. `key Aminor { | i iv v | }` rendering 9 note-ons; `(scaleNotes "Ddorian")` returns `[]`; no stderr advisory is printed in either case.

title: chunk's static rotation counter is never reset at render boundary — breaks two-run determinism
finding: _chunkRotationCounters is a process-static Dictionary<SourceLocation,int> that advances on every chunk call at a given site and is cleared ONLY by the test-only hook ResetChunkRotationForTesting(). The comment at lines 405-407 claims it is 'Reset at render-boundary by piggybacking off PrngRegistry (counter map cleared alongside the PRNG state)', but PrngRegistry.ResetAtRenderBoundary() only clears its own _registry/_drawCounts — it has zero knowledge of this separate static field, and grep confirms no production code calls ResetChunkRotationForTesting(). Consequence: any process that builds-and-renders the same chunk-using source more than once (watch-mode re-render, batch script, a host running the same script twice, or the two-run cmp-clean check itself) gets a DIFFERENT chunk rotation each time, producing different audio. I reproduced this: a proc with one chunk call (chunk 4 transposing fn) used to build two sections rendered via renderSong produced byte-different WAVs (cmp differ at byte 49) in a single process — first render transposed bar 0, second render transposed bar 1. By contrast sometimes/sparseSeq/markov (which route through PrngRegistry) stayed byte-identical across the same two-render pattern. Every Phase36 test that touches chunk has to manually call ResetChunkRotationForTesting() in setup (PatternEveryTests.cs:215, PatternDeterminismTests.cs:40, PatternChalkyEdgeCasesTests.cs:36) — the tests work around the leak that production cannot. Secondary hazard: the field is process-global, not per-ExecutionContext, so it also leaks across independent FlowEngine instances (unlike PrngRegistry).
rootCause: `_chunkRotationCounters` is a `private static readonly Dictionary<SourceLocation,int>` (line 408) that advances on every `chunk` call at a given call site (lines 450-453) and is cleared ONLY by `ResetChunkRotationForTesting()` (line 500). grep confirms that hook is called from exactly three test files (PatternEveryTests.cs:215, PatternDeterminismTests.cs:40, PatternChalkyEdgeCasesTests.cs:36) and NEVER from production code. The comment at lines 404-407 claims the counter is 'Reset at render-boundary by piggybacking off PrngRegistry', but `PrngRegistry.ResetAtRenderBoundary()` (PrngRegistry.cs:133-138) clears only its own `_registry` and `_drawCounts` — it has zero reference to the chunk field. The comment is false. Because the counter survives across renders within one process, re-rendering the same source rotates `activeChunk` (counter % n) to a different chunk each time, transposing/transforming a different bar and producing different audio. Verified by repro: a proc with one `(chunk 4 ...)` call built into two sections and rendered twice in one process produced byte-different WAVs (cmp differ at byte 49, immediately after the 44-byte WAV header). The PRNG-routed siblings sparseSeq/sometimes/markov stayed byte-identical across the identical two-render pattern because they route through PrngRegistry, which IS reset at the boundary — confirming the asymmetry. title: lsystemToSequence silently drops every note when the mapper returns a Note literal (documented surface produces empty output)
finding: LsystemToSequence only accepts mapper results where lambdaResult.Data is MusicalNoteData; everything else is charitably skipped with a one-shot advisory. But a bare Note literal (e.g. C4, C4q) evaluates to Value.Note(string) whose .Data is a STRING, not MusicalNoteData. The method's own xmldoc (lines 183-187) explicitly promises this case works: 'a Note literal (e.g. C4q): the parser binds the duration; convert'. That conversion is never implemented. I reproduced: (lsystemToSequence expanded (fn Symbol s => (if (equals s #A) C4 D4))) emits '[lsystemToSequence] mapper returned Note ... expected MusicalNote — skipped' for every symbol and returns an EMPTY sequence. A composer following the most natural documented pattern gets silence with only an advisory — charity hiding a real data-loss defect. The working surface (createMusicalNote C4 4) is what the test corpus uses (test_lsystem_oneshot.flow:61), confirming the bare-Note path was never wired.
rootCause: In LsystemToSequence (flow-lang/StandardLibrary/Generative/LsystemFunctions.cs:173-215) the mapper-result handling at line 188 only accepts results whose .Data is MusicalNoteData. A bare Note literal (C4, D4, etc.) evaluates via ExpressionEvaluator.TryParseSpecialLiteral -> Value.Note(text) (Value.cs:32), whose .Data is a STRING wrapped under NoteType, not MusicalNoteData. So every bare-Note mapper result falls into the else branch (lines 192-206) and is skipped with a WarnOnce advisory. Since notes ends up empty, no bar is added (line 209 guard) and the function returns an empty Sequence. The inline comment at line 185 explicitly documents that this case is supposed to work ('a Note literal (e.g. C4q): the parser binds the duration; convert'), but that conversion was never implemented. Reproduced: the claim's repro emits '[lsystemToSequence] mapper returned Note at /tmp/repro_lsystem.flow:4:16; expected MusicalNote — skipped' for every symbol and prints '(empty sequence)'. The test corpus (tests/test_lsystem_oneshot.flow:61, flow-lang.Tests/Phase36/LsystemModelTests.cs:275, examples/sweep/generative.flow:64) only ever uses createMusicalNote, so the bare-Note path was never exercised. This is charity (skip+advisory) masking total note loss for a documented usage pattern, not charity-by-design.

use "@generative"

Sequence seq = (lsystemToSequence e (fn Symbol s => (if (equals s #A) C4 D4)))
(visualize seq)   -> '(empty sequence)' + per-symbol skip advisory
suggestedFix: Before the charitable-skip else branch in LsystemToSequence, add a NoteType case: when lambdaResult.Type is NoteType (its .Data is a string), call NoteType.Parse(text) to get (name, octave, alteration) and build new MusicalNoteData(name, octave, alteration, durationValue: DefaultDurationValue, isRest: false), then notes.Add(...). Mirror MarkovFunctions.cs:586-598 exactly: reuse DefaultDurationValue = (int)NoteValueType.Value.QUARTER and clamp the duration enum/MIDI range the same way. title: jam's documented sparse named-arg surface fails to parse — (jam over=chords style=#jazz seed=42) is rejected
line: 96-132 (six fixed-arity overload registrations); xmldoc claim at line 26-28
finding: JamFunctions registers six fixed-arity positional overloads (over; over,style; over,style,length; over,style,length,key; +seed; +order) and pushes all defaults INSIDE the C# impl, not into the signatures. Named-arg resolution requires the supplied named params to be a subset of one overload's parameter list AND the remaining positional slots to be fillable — but seed only exists in the 5/6-arity overloads where length and key are mandatory positionals with no signature-level default. So (jam over=chords style=#jazz seed=42) — the exact headline surface advertised in CLAUDE.md ('lets composers call (jam over=chords style=#blues seed=42) directly') and in this file's own xmldoc at line 28-29 — fails with 'unknown parameter seed for function jam'. I reproduced the error directly. Positional (jam chords #jazz 4 "Cmajor" 7) works fine. CLAUDE.md lists 'sparse-named-arg call ergonomics (OverloadResolver relaxation)' as a v1.6 backlog item, so this is a known limitation, but it is presented as a shipped feature in user-facing docs and the function xmldoc.
rootCause: jam registers six fixed-arity positional overloads (over; over,style; over,style,length; over,style,length,key; +seed; +order) and pushes ALL defaults inside the C# Jam() impl via hasOrder/hasSeed/hasKey flags + args.Count checks — never into the FunctionSignature. FunctionSignature (FunctionSignature.cs:32-36) has no default-value field at all, so the resolver cannot fill skipped slots. OverloadResolver.ResolveCore named-arg path (OverloadResolver.cs:259) requires positionalArgTypes.Count + namedArgTypes.Count == sig.InputTypes.Count (exact coverage, no default-fill) AND every named key must be a member of that overload's ParameterNames (line 211). For (jam over=chords style=#jazz seed=42): seed only exists in sig5/sig6, where length+key are still mandatory positionals with no signature-level default — so sig5 fails the arity gate (3 != 5) and sig1-4 fail the unknown-name gate (seed not in their names). All six are rejected. Verified by running the repro: the interpreter emits exactly 'unknown parameter seed for function jam (expected: over, style, length, key)' plus the sibling-overload rejections, then 'Cannot convert Flow type Void ... to Sequence'. Positional (jam chords #jazz 4 "Cmajor" 7) and fully-named-prefix (jam over=chords style=#jazz length=4) both run fine, confirming only the sparse middle-skip path is broken. Note: the claim's aside that 'fully-specified named works' is itself inaccurate — key=<value> fails at PARSE time ('positional argument after named argument is not allowed') because key is a reserved musical-context keyword and cannot be used as a named-arg label; that is a separate, arguably worse, defect outside this claim's scope. It does not weaken the core finding. This is a violated documented contract, not a charity-hidden corruption: it fails loudly, never produces wrong audio.
repro:
use "@std"
use "@improv"
Sequence chords = | Cmaj7 | Am7 | Dm7 | G7 |
Sequence solo = (jam over=chords style=#jazz seed=42)   -> 'unknown parameter seed for function jam (expected: over, style, length, key)'
suggestedFix: Two paths, same as the claim. Immediate honest fix (b): correct the JamFunctions xmldoc at line 26-28 and the CLAUDE.md @improv line (~324) to advertise only currently-parseable+resolvable call shapes — full-prefix positional, or a contiguous named prefix (over=, or over= style=, or over= style= length=) — and drop the '(jam over=chords style=#blues seed=42)' example, since that exact surface is rejected. Proper fix (a), matching the v1.6 'OverloadResolver relaxation' backlog item: give FunctionSignature an optional per-parameter default-value list and teach OverloadResolver's named-arg path to fill skipped middle slots from those defaults instead of demanding exact arity at line 259, then collapse jam to a single 6-param signature carrying defaults so (jam over=chords seed=42) resolves. Separately (independent of this claim) the key= reserved-keyword parser collision should be tracked, since it blocks key= named-arg dispatch for jam entirely.

title: chunk grouping front-loads bars, leaving trailing empty chunks and silent dead cycles; doc example is wrong
finding: chunkSize = ceil(barCount/n) front-loads bars so chunks are uneven and trailing chunks can be empty. The doc comment at line 456 claims 'n=4 with 5 bars makes chunks of 2,1,1,1' but the actual split is {0,1},{2,3},{4},{} = sizes 2,2,1,0. I verified with 5 bars / chunk 4: rotation 0 transposes bars 0+1, rotation 1 bars 2+3, rotation 2 bar 4, rotation 3 is chunkStart=6 >= barCount so a charitable passthrough that transposes NOTHING — i.e. one in every 4 cycles silently does nothing. Tidal's chunk distributes bars evenly (sizes 2,1,1,1) and has no dead cycle. Mild musical surprise rather than corruption, but combined with the rotation-counter determinism bug it makes chunk behaviour hard to reason about.
rootCause: `Chunk` computes `chunkSize = (barCount + n - 1) / n` (ceil-divide) at line 456, then slices contiguous fixed-size windows (chunkStart = activeChunk*chunkSize). For barCount not a multiple of n this FRONT-LOADS the bars: e.g. 5 bars / n=4 yields windows {0,1},{2,3},{4} and a 4th window at chunkStart=6 which is >= barCount, so line 460 (`if (chunkStart >= barCount) return Value.Sequence(seq)`) takes a charitable passthrough that applies the transform to NOTHING. Since the rotation counter (line 451-453) cycles activeChunk = 0,1,2,3,0,1,..., index 3 IS reached on every n-th invocation, so 1 in every n cycles silently does nothing — a dead cycle. The line-460 charity hides this defect: the composer's requested transform never runs that cycle. Verified by re-reading the code and reproducing the integer math: actual chunk sizes are 2,2,1,0 not the 2,1,1,1 the doc comment at line 456 claims. The doc comment is therefore factually wrong — 2,1,1,1 is the even-split distribution the code does NOT produce. Tidal's `chunk` divides the cycle into n equal parts with no dead cycle. Existing tests (PatternEveryTests.ChunkAppliesOneChunkPerCycle, the .flow tests) only ever use barCount == n (4 bars / chunk 4 -> chunkSize=1, perfectly even), so the uneven-split / dead-cycle path is untested.
repro:
use "@std"
use "@patterns"
Sequence s = | C4 | D4 | E4 | F4 | G4 |
proc go ()
  (visualize (chunk 4 (fn Sequence x => (transpose x 12)) s))
end proc
(go) (go) (go) (go)   -> 4th call transposes nothing (dead cycle); chunks are 2,2,1,0 not 2,1,1,1
suggestedFix: Replace the ceil-divide window scheme with an even distribution that hands the remainder out one bar at a time to the first (barCount mod n) chunks, so all n chunks are non-empty whenever barCount >= n (matching Tidal's even split and eliminating the dead cycle). Concretely, precompute chunk boundaries: `int base = barCount / n; int rem = barCount % n;` then chunk i has size `base + (i < rem ? 1 : 0)`, with `chunkStart` = sum of preceding sizes. Compute chunkStart/chunkEnd for `activeChunk` from this table instead of `activeChunk * chunkSize`. With this, for 5 bars / n=4 the sizes become 2,1,1,1 and every rotation index transforms a real (non-empty) chunk. Keep the `chunkStart >= barCount` guard only for the genuinely-degenerate barCount < n case (where some trailing chunks legitimately have zero bars). Also fix the doc comment at line 456: it currently claims ceil-divide yields 2,1,1,1, which is false (it yields 2,2,1 plus a dead 4th chunk); update it to describe the even-split behavior.

title: Markov pitch+duration bit-layout doc and 'quarter-note units' description contradict the implementation
finding: The class xmldoc (lines 49-53) and FeatureModePitchDuration comment (75-78) describe the packed state as '(pitch << 20) | duration' with pitch in the low 12 bits and duration in the high 20 bits. The actual EncodePitchDurationState (line 92) does (d << 12) | p — duration in the high bits, pitch in the low 12 — and DecodePitchDurationState mirrors it, so encode/decode are mutually consistent and round-trip correctly (verified: durations vary correctly in a generated pitch+duration sequence). Separately the doc says duration is in 'quarter-note units', but ExtractStates (line 429) actually stores the NoteValueType enum slot (0..7: WHOLE=0..ONETWENTYEIGHTH=7, e.g. QUARTER=2), and BuildSequenceFromStates clamps it back to that enum range — not quarter-note count. No behavioral bug, but the documentation would mislead a future maintainer about both the bit layout and the duration encoding.
rootCause: Two documentation-vs-implementation mismatches confirmed by re-reading the source. (1) Bit layout: the class xmldoc (line 50) and the FeatureModePitchDuration constant comment (lines 75-76) state the packed state is "(pitch << 20) | duration" with "pitch occupies the low 12 bits; duration ... occupies the high 20 bits." This contradicts itself (pitch<<20 would put pitch high, yet it claims pitch is low) AND contradicts the code: EncodePitchDurationState (line 92) does `(d << 12) | p` — duration shifted into the high bits, pitch masked into the low 12 bits via `midiPitch & 0xFFF`. DecodePitchDurationState (lines 101-102) mirrors it (`p = state & 0xFFF`, `d = (state >> 12) & 0xFFFFF`), so encode/decode round-trip correctly. The doc's shift amount (20) and operand placement are both wrong. (2) Duration encoding: the doc repeatedly calls the duration component "quarter-note units"/"duration in quarter-note units" (lines 50-51, 76), but ExtractStates (line 429) stores `note.DurationValue`, which is the NoteValueType enum slot (WHOLE=0, QUARTER=2, ... ONETWENTYEIGHTH=7 per NoteValueType.cs:24-31), and BuildSequenceFromStates clamps it to [WHOLE, ONETWENTYEIGHTH] = [0,7] (lines 590-592). It is an enum slot, not a quarter-note count. Both are documentation-only defects with no behavioral impact — the encode/decode pair is internally consistent and the duration value is treated as an enum slot consistently throughout.
repro: N/A — documentation vs code mismatch; behaviour is self-consistent.
suggestedFix: Correct both doc passages to match the code. In the class xmldoc (lines 50-51) and the FeatureModePitchDuration comment (lines 75-76), change "(pitch << 20) | duration_quarter_units ... Pitch occupies the low 12 bits; duration in quarter-note units occupies the high 20 bits" to: "(durationEnumSlot << 12) | (pitch & 0xFFF) — pitch occupies the low 12 bits; the NoteValueType enum slot (0..7: WHOLE=0 .. ONETWENTYEIGHTH=7, e.g. QUARTER=2) occupies the next 20 bits." Also fix the EncodePitchDurationState parameter name `durationQuarterUnits` and the DecodePitchDurationState tuple field `DurationQuarterUnits` to e.g. `durationEnumSlot`/`DurationEnumSlot` so the API surface stops implying a quarter-note count. No behavioral change required; the encode/decode/extract/build logic is already correct and consistent.

title: oscBundle cannot wrap messages — referenced oscSendMessage builtin does not exist
finding: oscBundle requires every argument to be an OscHandle whose PendingPacket is non-null, and its own error message says these must be 'built via oscSendMessage or oscBundle'. But there is NO oscSendMessage builtin (grep across all .cs and .flow confirms it does not exist; only oscSend/oscListen/oscStop/oscPump/oscBundle/oscSendBundle are registered). The only Value carrying a non-null PendingPacket comes from oscBundle itself, which always wraps an OscBundle — never a leaf OscMessage. Therefore a composer can never construct a bundle that CONTAINS messages: `(oscBundle ...)` can only nest empty/other bundles. Verified live: `(oscBundle)` then `(oscSendBundle ...)` sends an empty bundle successfully, but there is no language-level way to put a message into it. CLAUDE.md documents `oscBundle(...packets)` / atomic bundle delivery as a shipped Phase 38 feature, so this is a documented capability that cannot perform its stated purpose.
rootCause: There is no builtin that produces an OscHandle carrying a leaf OscMessage. Grep across all .cs and .flow confirms only six OSC names are registered (__enableOscModule, oscSend, oscListen, oscStop, oscPump, oscBundle, oscSendBundle) — no oscSendMessage or oscMsg. oscSend returns Value.Void() (OscFunctions.cs:224), so it produces no packet handle. The ONLY site that sets OscHandleData.PendingPacket to a non-null value is the oscBundle body (OscFunctions.cs:310-318), and it always wraps a Rug.Osc.OscBundle — never an OscMessage. oscBundle then requires every argument's PendingPacket to be non-null (line 296), so the only thing it can ingest is another bundle handle. Net result: a bundle can only ever nest other (ultimately empty) bundles; a composer can never place a NOTE/CC message inside a bundle. Verified empirically on Linux/localhost: `(oscBundle)` then `(oscSendBundle "127.0.0.1" 9999 b)` sends an empty bundle, and `(oscBundle inner)` nests an empty bundle, but no path injects a message. The error text at line 298 names oscSendMessage, a builtin that does not exist (dead reference). This breaks a documented Phase 38 capability: osc.flow line 6 advertises `oscBundle(...packets)`, the OscHandleData doc anticipates a 'single OscMessage' in PendingPacket (OscHandleData.cs:56-57), and the in-repo tutorial examples/live/osc_controller.flow:33 documents the intended call `(oscBundle msg1 msg2 ...)` — none of which is constructible.
repro:
use "@osc"
OscHandle b = (oscBundle)
(oscSendBundle "127.0.0.1" 9999 b)   Note: works, but sends an EMPTY bundle
Note: there is no builtin to build a single-message packet to pass into oscBundle, so a bundle of NOTE messages is impossible.
suggestedFix: Add the missing message-constructor builtin. Register `oscMsg(String path, ...args) -> OscHandle` (signature: [StringType, VoidType-vararg-element], IsVarArgs, names ["path","args"]) whose body builds `var msg = new Rug.Osc.OscMessage(path, InferOscArgs(payload));` and returns `Value.OscHandle(new OscHandleData { Port=0, Path=path, Receiver=null, Cts=new CancellationTokenSource(), ListenerTask=Task.CompletedTask, PendingPacket=msg })` — mirroring the oscBundle discriminator pattern and reusing the existing InferOscArgs/SendOscMessage plumbing. Declare it in flow-lang/osc.flow. Two follow-on edits are required: (1) oscSendBundle at line 332 currently rejects any handle whose PendingPacket is not an OscBundle — relax it to also accept a bare OscMessage handle (send it directly via SendOscPacket); and (2) fix the now-accurate-but-incomplete error string at line 298 to read 'built via oscMsg or oscBundle'. With this, the documented `(oscBundle (oscMsg "/a" 1) (oscMsg "/b" 2))` form (and the osc_controller.flow tutorial) becomes constructible. Charitable note: the listener-handle rejection path at 296-298 currently accumulates the ArgumentException without aborting (the line after it still ran in my repro) — worth confirming that injecting a non-packet handle does not silently yield a malformed bundle once oscMsg exists.

title: flow watch plain-line mode silently swallows distinct advisories/errors after the first (WarnOnce process-lifetime dedup)
line: 276-278 (PublishAdvisory plain-line branch routes through RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce; dedupKeys defined at flow-interpreter/LiveReloadManager.cs:600 and :540-543)

title: Every clean oscStop logs a spurious '[osc] receive error ... socket has been disconnected'
finding: The receive loop only breaks cleanly on OperationCanceledException (584) and ObjectDisposedException (585). The cts.Token.Register callback (552) disposes the Rug.Osc OscReceiver to unblock Receive(), and the comment claims this 'forces ObjectDisposedException'. In Rug.Osc 1.2.5, Receive() on a closed/disposed receiver actually throws a generic Exception with the localized message 'The receiver socket has been disconnected' (Rug.Osc.Strings.Receiver_SocketIsClosed), NOT ObjectDisposedException. It therefore falls through to the generic catch (586-594) which writes `[osc] receive error on port N: The receiver socket has been disconnected` to stderr and `continue`s; the loop then exits on the next !cts.IsCancellationRequested check. Result: every normal oscStop prints a scary error. Reproduced consistently across multiple live runs.
rootCause: The receive loop expects a disposed Rug.Osc OscReceiver to throw ObjectDisposedException (caught cleanly at line 585). The comment at lines 546-552 explicitly asserts disposing the receiver 'forces ObjectDisposedException in Receive()'. That premise is false in Rug.Osc 1.2.5: calling Receive() on a disposed/closed OscReceiver throws a GENERIC System.Exception with message 'The receiver socket has been disconnected' (Rug.Osc.Strings.Receiver_SocketIsClosed), not ObjectDisposedException. It therefore falls through to the generic catch at 586, which Console.Error.WriteLine($"[osc] receive error on port {port}: {ex.Message}") and continues, exiting only on the next !cts.IsCancellationRequested check. Net effect: every normal oscStop emits one spurious '[osc] receive error on port N: The receiver socket has been disconnected' to stderr. Confirmed empirically with a standalone net10 probe mirroring the exact loop: output was 'generic catch: IsCancellationRequested=True msg=The receiver socket has been disconnected' — the ObjectDisposedException branch never fires, and cts.IsCancellationRequested is True at the point of logging.
repro:
use "@osc"
OscHandle h = (oscListen 9999 "/test" (fn Int x => (print (str x))))
(oscStop h)
Note: stderr shows: [osc] receive error on port 9999: The receiver socket has been disconnected
suggestedFix: In the generic catch at line 586, short-circuit clean teardown before logging: `if (cts.IsCancellationRequested) break;` as the first statement (a Receive() failure during a requested cancel is normal shutdown, not an error). The probe confirmed cts.IsCancellationRequested is True at this point during oscStop, so this break path is reached for every clean stop. As belt-and-suspenders, the dead-receiver case can also be matched explicitly (e.g. `catch (Exception ex) when (cts.IsCancellationRequested) { break; }` placed above the logging catch) so genuine mid-session receive errors still surface. Also worth correcting the now-inaccurate comment at 546-552 that claims dispose 'forces ObjectDisposedException'.

title: Multi-line note streams cannot be entered in the REPL — completeness check ignores the Pipe token
finding: IsInputComplete tracks brace/proc/paren/bracket nesting but never counts the note-stream delimiter TokenType.Pipe (SimpleLexer.cs:195 emits one Pipe per '|'). So an unterminated note stream is judged complete. Verified directly via the public ReplInputCompleteness seam: `Sequence s = | C4q D4q` -> True and `| C4 D4 E4` -> True (both lack a closing '|'), while `(add 1 2` -> False and `[intro verse` -> False are correctly incomplete. Consequence: a composer typing a note stream across lines presses Enter after `| C4 D4` and the REPL submits it immediately; the parser charitably closes the open stream into a truncated 1-bar sequence (or errors), and the intended continuation `E4 F4 |` becomes a separate, broken statement. Song/chord bracket literals are handled (bracketDepth); note streams are the gap. Both the legacy Console.ReadLine path (ReadCompleteInput) and the PrettyPrompt soft-newline path (TransformKeyPressAsync) call this same helper, so both editors are affected.
rootCause: ReplInputCompleteness.IsInputComplete (ReplLineEditor.cs:629-644) tracks LBrace/RBrace, Proc/EndProc, LParen/RParen, and LBracket/RBracket nesting depth, but the token loop never inspects TokenType.Pipe. The lexer emits one Pipe per '|' (SimpleLexer.cs:195), and '|' is the note-stream delimiter (a stream opens and closes with the same '|'). Because the loop ignores Pipe, an unterminated note stream is judged complete (return blockDepth<=0 && procDepth<=0 && parenDepth<=0 && bracketDepth<=0 — pipes never considered). I confirmed this by running the public seam against the built DLL: IsInputComplete("Sequence s = | C4q D4q") returns True (1 unbalanced pipe), IsInputComplete("| C4 D4 E4") returns True (1 pipe), while the correctly-handled controls (add 1 2 -> False, [intro verse -> False, balanced | C4 D4 E4 | -> True) behave as expected. Both editor surfaces call this helper: the legacy Console.ReadLine path via Repl.cs:312 (NeedsMoreLines -> ReadCompleteInput line 250) and the PrettyPrompt soft-newline path via ReplLineEditor.cs:550 (TransformKeyPressAsync). The defect is harmful (not benign charity) because Parser.NoteStream.cs:404-408 charitably auto-closes an unterminated stream into a valid-but-truncated NoteStreamExpression with NO error ('the last bar is incomplete but still valid'): pressing Enter after a partial stream silently submits and truncates the bar, orphaning the composer's intended continuation as a separate statement. That is silent input truncation hidden by charity.

Direct: ReplInputCompleteness.IsInputComplete("Sequence s = | C4q D4q") returns true.
suggestedFix: In the token loop add a pipe counter alongside the existing depth counters and treat an odd count as incomplete. e.g. add `int pipeCount = 0;` and `else if (token.Type == TokenType.Pipe) pipeCount++;`, then return `blockDepth <= 0 && procDepth <= 0 && parenDepth <= 0 && bracketDepth <= 0 && (pipeCount % 2 == 0);`. This is safe against false positives: '|' is exclusively a balanced delimiter in Flow (note streams `| ... |`, `pickup | ... |`, `progression | ... |`; arithmetic is prefix-only, no infix bitwise-or per TokenType.Pipe uses in Parser.cs/Parser.NoteStream.cs), so every complete input has an even pipe count. Multi-line streams stay correct: a single bar across lines (`| C4 D4` then `E4 F4 |`) shows odd=incomplete on line 1 and even=complete after the closer, while fully-typed multi-line `| ... |` per line is even on each line. Add an xUnit case mirroring ReplMultiLineTests.cs asserting IsInputComplete("Sequence s = | C4q D4q") == false and IsInputComplete("| C4 D4 E4 |") == true.

title: LiveStatusPanel ANSI panel repaints absolute terminal rows 1-4, colliding with scrolling log output
finding: In ANSI+stdout mode the panel positions itself with absolute cursor escapes (\x1b[1;1H ... \x1b[4;1H) and the 2Hz heartbeat redraws there continuously. But LiveReloadManager.Run writes scrolling lines to the same terminal (Console.WriteLine 'Watching ... for changes', the Ctrl+C handler's 'Stopping playback...', 'Live reload ended.') and there is no DECSTBM scroll-region reservation. The fixed top-4-rows panel and the scrolling log therefore overwrite each other: log lines land under the panel and the heartbeat stomps whatever scrolled into rows 1-4. (lines 260-261), and 'Live reload ended.' (line 290). suggestedFix: Reserve a scroll region below the panel so logs scroll under the fixed rows. Add a Console-redirected-with-forceTtyMode test that asserts the emitted byte stream contains a scroll-region setup before the first \x1b[1;1H to pin the fix (the existing StringWriter seam already exercises the ANSI path via forceTtyMode).

title: midiOut silently drops ALL voice-block notes (ParallelVoices) — breaks .mid/audio parity

title: openMidiOutput handle is never closed — native device + ALSA port leak on the low-level escape-hatch path

MidiDevice d = (openMidiOutput "Synth")

title: clockMaster reads a frozen MusicalContext snapshot — composer tempo blocks after start never change the clock rate
finding: clockMaster passes `context.GetMusicalContext()` (MidiClockFunctions.cs:57) to StartMaster. GetMusicalContext (ExecutionContext.cs:901-963) returns a freshly-built, MEMOIZED resolved MusicalContext object; entering a later `tempo N { }` block invalidates the cache and builds a DIFFERENT object — it never mutates the snapshot the clock holds. The master's RunMasterLoop re-reads `_context.Tempo` (via ReadTempoOrDefault, MidiClock.cs:222-232) at each bar boundary, but `_context` is the frozen snapshot, so the value never changes. The MidiClock docstring and midi.flow both say 'tempo changes apply only at the NEXT bar boundary', implying live composer tempo edits propagate — they do not (only SetLiveTempo from a slave/JACK changes the rate, because ReadTempoOrDefault checks the live sink first). The ClockMasterTests pass only because they construct and mutate a raw MusicalContext directly rather than going through GetMusicalContext.
rootCause: clockMaster passes context.GetMusicalContext() (MidiClockFunctions.cs:57) into StartMaster. Verified at ExecutionContext.cs:901-963: GetMusicalContext() always builds `var resolved = new MusicalContext()` — a fresh, standalone, MEMOIZED resolved object that is never any frame's own MusicalContext. The clock stores it as `_context` (MidiClock.cs:97). The master loop re-reads `_context.Tempo` at each bar boundary via ReadTempoOrDefault (MidiClock.cs:142,158,222-232) precisely to honor the documented 'tempo changes apply at the next bar boundary' contract (MidiClock.cs:22-26 and midi.flow:63). But composer tempo edits never mutate that snapshot: ExecuteMusicalContext (Interpreter.cs:230-264) always does PushFrame() then `var musicalCtx = new MusicalContext()` and writes .Tempo onto that NEW frame object, then invalidates the GetMusicalContext cache (ExecutionContext.cs:961/969). So a later `tempo 120 { }` builds a different object and the cache rebuilds — the frozen snapshot the clock holds keeps its original Tempo forever. The only path that can change the master's rate is MusicalContext.SetLiveTempo (MusicalContext.cs:75), which ReadTempoOrDefault checks first (MidiClock.cs:227) and which is written only by the clock slave (MidiClock.cs:381) / JACK. The existing test MidTempoChange_DeferredToBarBoundary (ClockMasterTests.cs:113-158) passes ONLY because it constructs a raw `new MusicalContext{Tempo=60}` and mutates `ctx.Tempo = fastBpm` on that exact instance (line 134) — it bypasses GetMusicalContext entirely, so it never exercises the production composer path. The bar-boundary re-read mechanism is functional but reads a value no composer code can change.

MidiDevice d = (openMidiOutput "Synth")
tempo 60 { ClockHandle c = (clockMaster d) }   Note: later tempo 120 { } blocks do not change the emitted 0xF8 rate.
suggestedFix: Decide the intended contract and make code + docs agree. Option A (honest minimal): the master runs on a background thread decoupled from the interpreter's call stack, so true block-scoped tempo propagation is impossible by reading the live stack anyway; document the master tempo as frozen-at-clockMaster-time. Update MidiClock.cs:22-26 and midi.flow:63 to say 'the tempo is captured when clockMaster is called; to retune the running clock, drive it through the live-sync channel (slave/JACK) or stop+restart the handle.' Option B (propagating): give clockMaster a tempo-read delegate `() => context.GetMusicalContext().Tempo` and call it (not a frozen snapshot field) inside ReadTempoOrDefault each bar — this lets file-scope/global tempo edits reach the clock (it still cannot see a transient block frame the interpreter has since popped). Either way, add a test that goes through the real ExecutionContext: register @midi, run `tempo 60 { (clockMaster d) }`, then push a later tempo frame and assert whether the emitted 0xF8 interval changes — asserting the chosen contract. Do NOT rely on mutating a hand-built MusicalContext, which is what masks the bug today. requiresHardware is false: StartMaster takes a managed IMidiOutputHandle (the test's TimestampingHandle / a null handle both run the full loop + ReadTempoOrDefault with no ALSA/librtmidi), so the defect is fully reproducible in-process.

title: JACK/clock tempo validation has no upper bound — pathological transport BPM is accepted and busy-spins the master
