title: midiOut overrides= Dict silently ignores non-Int channel values (e.g. Long)
finding: ReadOverrides only accepts entries where `kv.Value.Data is int ch` (MidiFunctions.cs:379). Flow's numeric widening means a channel value produced by arithmetic or written as a larger literal can be a Long, not an Int. Such an entry is silently dropped from the override map (no advisory), so the documented overrides= channel remap is silently ignored and the sequence falls back to its GM default channel — a confusing silent no-op rather than the intended remap.
rootCause: ReadOverrides (MidiFunctions.cs:373-383) only admits dict entries where `kv.Value.Data is int ch` (line 379). C# pattern matching `is int` does NOT match a boxed `long` (or `double`/`float`), and Value.As is likewise strict (Value.cs:388-398, plain `is T` else throw). A channel value typed as Long — produced by `(long 3)` (the real builtin; the claim's `(toLong 3)` is the OSC-doc name and does not exist), by Long arithmetic (StdLib.cs:342 AddLong returns Value.Long), or by an int-overflowing literal (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:67) — is therefore silently skipped from the override map. Dict values are stored as raw Value objects (DictFunctions) with no coercion, and the overrides= signature uses a dictWildcard so the values bypass the overload-resolver's per-param Int coercion that protects the low-level midiNoteOn path. Downstream, ScheduleOneSequence does `overrides.TryGetValue(seqName, out var ovCh)` (line 499); a dropped entry makes TryGetValue return false, so `channel` stays at the GM default (line 498) and is clamped (line 501) with NO advisory. Net: the documented overrides= remap is silently ignored -> the sequence plays on the wrong (default GM) MIDI channel. This is a charity-hides-defect case (silently wrong routing, no stderr advisory), not charitable-by-design. NOTE: a plain channel literal like `3` evaluates to Value.Int (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:66) and IS accepted, so the trigger is uncommon — it requires an explicitly Long-typed channel value — which keeps this low severity.
repro: use "@midi" with `(midiOut s "port" overrides=(dict "piano" (toLong 3)))` — the override is dropped and piano stays on channel 0.
suggestedFix: In ReadOverrides, replace the strict `kv.Value.Data is int ch` with charitable numeric coercion before clamping to 0..15: e.g. `int? ch = kv.Value.Data switch { int i => i, long l => (int)l, double d => (int)Math.Round(d), float f => (int)Math.Round(f), _ => null };` then `if (kv.Key.Data is string name && ch is int c) map[name] = Math.Clamp(c, 0, 15);`. Optionally WarnOnce (RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce) when an override entry has a non-numeric value so a genuine typo isn't swallowed. This matches Flow's numeric-widening ergonomics and keeps the existing Int path byte-identical.

title: MIDI note velocity silently discarded on midi2flow conversion (data loss)
finding: MidiParser reads per-note velocity, Quantizer threads it through NoteSpan -> NoteElement.Velocity / ChordElement.Velocity (it even computes avgVelocity for chords at Quantizer.cs:707), but FlowGenerator.FormatElements never emits any dynamic marking. Every note/chord is emitted as just pitch+duration. Flow note streams DO support per-note dynamics (Parser.NoteStream.cs:507 TryParseDynamicMarking maps pp->0.25, mf->0.625, ff->0.875, etc.), so the velocity is fully expressible and recoverable, but it is thrown away. REPRO: created a Format-1 MIDI with C4 at velocity 20 (pp) then D4 at velocity 120 (ff) then E4 pp then F4 ff; `flow midi2flow x.mid` emits `| C4q D4q E4q F4q |` with zero dynamics, and `flow-midi x.mid` likewise. All four notes render at the default 0.63 velocity, flattening the entire dynamic shape of any imported MIDI. This violates the SPEC-5 round-trip-fidelity intent (Midi2FlowCommand comment claims 'flat, round-trippable output').
rootCause: MidiParser reads per-note velocity (NoteOnEvent.Velocity, MidiTypes.cs:9) and Quantizer threads it all the way through NoteSpan -> NoteElement.Velocity / ChordElement.Velocity (Quantizer.cs:686, 709, 711), even averaging it for chords (avgVelocity at Quantizer.cs:707). But FlowGenerator.FormatElements (lines 280-337) emits only NoteName/[notes] + duration suffix + dotted + tied. It NEVER reads or emits the .Velocity field for either NoteElement or ChordElement. Flow note streams fully support inline dynamics: Parser.NoteStream.cs:507 TryParseDynamicMarking maps ppp->0.125, pp->0.25, p->0.375, mp->0.5, mf->0.625, f->0.75, ff->0.875, fff->1.0 (sticky per-bar, reset at line 78), so the velocity is recoverable in the target syntax. Because the emitted stream carries no dynamic token, NoteStreamCompiler.cs:615/777 defaults note.Velocity ?? 0.63 — every imported note collapses to a uniform 0.63, flattening the entire dynamic shape. This is data loss masked by a charitable default (no advisory is emitted), not charity-by-design. Confirmed by both source re-reads and a live repro.
repro: python3 hand-rolled Format-1 MIDI: track1 = NoteOn C4 vel20 / off / D4 vel120 / off / E4 vel20 / off / F4 vel120 / off. Then: flow midi2flow x.mid  -> output is `Sequence track1_seq = | C4q D4q E4q F4q |` (no pp/ff). Same with standalone `flow-midi x.mid`.
suggestedFix: Add a velocity->dynamic bucketer in FlowGenerator that maps a MIDI 0-127 velocity onto the same eight-step ladder used by TryParseDynamicMarking (ppp/pp/p/mp/mf/f/ff/fff), then in FormatElements emit a leading dynamic token before a NoteElement/ChordElement whenever its bucketed dynamic differs from a running "sticky" dynamic carried across the bar (matching the parser's per-bar sticky reset, so the bucketer state resets at FormatBar boundaries to stay consistent with stickyVelocity=null at each pipe). For chords use the already-computed avgVelocity. To keep two-run cmp-clean, bucketing is pure-deterministic (integer thresholds). Concretely: pick bucket edges that round-trip the parser's eight values (e.g. <16->ppp, <32->pp, <48->p, <64->mp, <80->mf, <96->f, <112->ff, else fff) and emit e.g. `pp C4q` only when the bucket changes. This restores dynamic fidelity with zero new syntax and satisfies the SPEC-5 round-trip intent that Midi2FlowCommand.cs:14-18 documents.

title: Format-1 track with any channel-9 note is flagged all-drum and dropped, losing melody
finding: Drum detection uses Any(channel==9). A single stray ch9 hit in an otherwise melodic Format-1 track marks the ENTIRE track IsDrumTrack=true. FlowGenerator then filters out all drum tracks (FlowGenerator.cs:50 `.Where(t => !t.IsDrumTrack)`), so all melodic notes on that track are silently discarded. Many real-world MIDIs put a drum part and a melody part in the same MTrk, or have stray percussion. REPRO: Format-1 track with C4/D4/E4 on ch0 plus one snare (note 38) on ch9 -> `flow midi2flow mixed.mid` prints `Note: Converted from mixed.mid — no playable tracks found` and `flow-midi mixed.mid --dump` confirms `Channels: 0, 9` with 4 noteOns present. The 3 melody notes are lost. Note: line 202 also derives `channel` from the FIRST noteOn, which can mismatch the drum flag. Format 0 does NOT have this bug (SplitByChannel isolates ch9 correctly).
rootCause: On the Format-1/2 path, drum classification is all-or-nothing: `bool isDrum = track.Events.OfType<NoteOnEvent>().Any(e => e.Channel == 9)` (Quantizer.cs:198). A SINGLE channel-9 noteOn anywhere in a track marks the ENTIRE MTrk as a drum track. EmitTrackAsVoices (lines 222-227) then passes the whole span list (melody + drums together) through as one QuantizedTrack with IsDrumTrack=true; the Format-1 path never splits by channel the way Format 0 does (SplitByChannel, line 176). FlowGenerator.cs:48 `.Where(t => !t.IsDrumTrack ...)` discards that track wholesale, so all melodic notes on channels 0-8/10-15 are silently dropped. Reproduced end-to-end: a Format-1 track with C4/D4/E4 on ch0 plus one snare (note 38) on ch9 yields `flow-midi --dump` showing 4 noteOns on `Channels: 0, 9`, but `flow midi2flow mixed.mid` (and the standalone `flow-midi`) both print `Note: Converted from mixed.mid — no playable tracks found` — the 3 melody notes are lost. Real-world Type-1 MIDIs that merge a drum part into a melodic MTrk, or carry a stray ch9 hit, hit this. Format 0 is unaffected (SplitByChannel isolates ch9). No existing test guards this classification, so the behavior is not a locked contract.
repro: Format-1 MIDI, track1: NoteOn ch0 C4, ch0 D4, ch9 note38 (snare), ch0 E4. Run: flow midi2flow mixed.mid  -> 'no playable tracks found'. Melody silently dropped.
suggestedFix: Make the Format-1/2 path channel-aware exactly like Format 0 instead of classifying the whole track on a single ch9 hit. In Quantizer.Quantize's else branch (lines 185-207), replace `PairNotes(track.Events)` + `Any(channel==9)` with a per-track `SplitByChannel(track)`: route the ch9 sub-spans to a `drums` QuantizedTrack (isDrum=true) and emit every non-ch9 channel's sub-spans as melodic track(s) via EmitTrackAsVoices(isDrum=false), preserving the existing track.Name/index naming for the dominant melodic channel. (SplitByChannel already pairs notes per (channel,pitch), so it can be reused directly.) Minimal alternative if a full split is too invasive: keep PairNotes but compute `isDrum` only when the strong majority of noteOns are ch9 (e.g. `>= 0.9`), and when a track is mixed, emit the ch9 spans as a separate `drums` track and the non-ch9 spans as the melodic track — never let one stray ch9 note suppress an entire melodic track. Either way the result must keep two-run cmp-clean determinism (channel iteration order should be sorted).

title: midi2flow reports success (exit 0) when it produced a comment-only file with all notes dropped
finding: When FlowGenerator finds no playable tracks it returns only the line `Note: Converted from <file> — no playable tracks found` and Midi2FlowCommand still writes it to -o, prints `Converted <in> -> <out>`, and returns 0. The resulting .flow `check`s OK (it is a valid comment-only program) and renders silence. Combined with the drum-detection bug above, a user converting a normal MIDI gets a success message and a silent file with no indication their notes were dropped. The conversion 'succeeded' by exit code while losing all musical content.
rootCause: FlowGenerator.Generate (flow-midi/Conversion/FlowGenerator.cs:53-57) returns ONLY the line `Note: Converted from <file> — no playable tracks found` when every track is filtered out by the playable-tracks predicate (FlowGenerator.cs:47-50 drops drum tracks, empty tracks, and all-rest tracks). `Note:` is a valid Flow line comment (SimpleLexer.cs:1314-1323), so the artifact is a syntactically valid comment-only program that renders silence. Both consumers — Midi2FlowCommand.cs:45-57 and the standalone flow-midi/Program.cs:92-105 — write that string to -o, print `Converted <in> -> <out>` (to STDERR, not stdout as the claim states), and `return 0` with no check on whether any musical content survived. Total content loss is reported as success. The drum-skip itself is intentional/documented (Flow uses different drum notation); the defect is that the conversion as a whole gives no failure signal when it produced zero notes. Note: drum detection (Quantizer.cs:179,198 — channel 9 = GM percussion) is the correct convention, NOT an over-firing bug; the claim's reference to a separate 'drum-detection bug above' is unnecessary — a drum-only/all-rest/empty MIDI is itself a legitimate, common input (e.g. an exported drum loop) that triggers this path. Verified by repro: a drum-only Type-1 MIDI produced exit 0, stderr 'Converted ...', and an output file containing only the comment, which the interpreter then ran clean with no audio.
repro: flow midi2flow mixed.mid -o out.flow  -> prints 'Converted ... -> out.flow', exit 0; out.flow contains only the no-playable-tracks comment.
suggestedFix: Have FlowGenerator.Generate signal the no-playable-tracks case to callers instead of folding it into normal output — e.g. return a result struct (`(string Source, int PlayableTrackCount)`) or expose a bool. Then in Midi2FlowCommand.cs (around line 45-57) and flow-midi/Program.cs (around line 92-105), when playableTrackCount == 0: write a clear stderr warning such as `Warning: no playable tracks found in <input> — output is a comment-only file (all tracks were drums/empty/rests)` and `return 2` (distinct non-zero exit) so scripts and users see the failure. Keep writing the comment-only file (charitable) but make the exit code and message honest. Optionally also surface the count of dropped drum tracks in the warning so a drum-only source is explicitly explained.

title: flow-interpreter prints stale 'v0.1' banner to stdout, polluting -e/pipe output
finding: The interpreter entry hardcodes `Flow Language Interpreter v0.1` and writes it to STDOUT unconditionally on every invocation, including `-e`/`--eval` and stdin-pipe modes. Two problems: (1) version stamping is wrong — it says v0.1 while the project is v1.5.x; (2) it is on stdout, so `flow-interpreter -e '(print "X")'` emits the banner mixed with program output, breaking any tool capturing stdout. REPRO confirmed: `flow-interpreter -e '(print "RESULT")'` prints `Flow Language Interpreter v0.1\n\nRESULT`. (The newer flow-cli does NOT print this banner, so `flow run`/`flow eval` are clean, but CLAUDE.md still documents the `dotnet run --project flow-interpreter` path.)
rootCause: flow-interpreter/Program.cs:9-10 unconditionally calls Console.WriteLine("Flow Language Interpreter v0.1") followed by Console.WriteLine() at the very top of Main(), BEFORE flag parsing (ParseFlags at line 13). Because the banner write precedes any dispatch, it executes on every invocation path including -e/--eval (lines 35-38 -> RunFromString) and stdin (lines 40-43 -> RunFromStdin). Two concrete defects: (1) the banner goes to STDOUT (Console.WriteLine, not Console.Error), so it is interleaved with the Flow program's own stdout (e.g. results of (print ...)); (2) the version literal is stale: the project ships at 1.5.0 (flow-cli sets AssemblyInformationalVersion to 1.5.0; see flow-cli/obj/Debug/net10.0/flow-cli.AssemblyInfo.cs:16 and flow-cli/Commands/VersionCommand.cs:18 which reads it via reflection), while the interpreter hardcodes "v0.1".
repro: flow-interpreter -e '(print "RESULT")' 2>/dev/null  -> 'Flow Language Interpreter v0.1' then blank then 'RESULT'.
suggestedFix: Route the banner to stderr and suppress it in non-interactive modes, or drop it entirely (flow-cli already omits it). Minimal targeted fix: delete lines 9-10 (`Console.WriteLine("Flow Language Interpreter v0.1"); Console.WriteLine();`). If a banner is desired for the interactive REPL only, move it inside the no-argument REPL branch (after the `if (Console.IsInputRedirected)` guard at lines 24-27, just before `var repl = new Repl();` at line 30) and emit via Console.Error.WriteLine, reading the real version with `System.Reflection.Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly().GetCustomAttribute<AssemblyInformationalVersionAttribute>()?.InformationalVersion` exactly as flow-cli/Commands/VersionCommand.cs:18 does (strip the +commit suffix). This keeps -e/--eval/--stdin stdout clean and stops emitting a stale version.

title: uninstall.sh FLOW_VERSION default is stale 0.1.0 (dead/misleading)
finding: uninstall.sh sets FLOW_VERSION defaulting to 0.1.0 while install.sh defaults to 1.5.0. The variable is never read anywhere else in uninstall.sh (it `rm -rf`s the whole $SHARE_ROOT), so it is dead code — but it is misleading version cruft inconsistent with the rest of the install tooling and at odds with the task's version-stamping requirement (must reflect 1.5.x, not 0.1.0).
rootCause: scripts/uninstall.sh line 10 declares FLOW_VERSION with a stale default of 0.1.0. grep confirms the variable appears only once in the file (the assignment) and is never read again — the uninstall path uses `rm -rf "$SHARE_ROOT"` (line 39) which removes the entire share/flow tree regardless of version. Meanwhile its sibling scripts/install.sh:25 defaults FLOW_VERSION to 1.5.0 and uses it heavily to build the versioned install dir (flow-v${FLOW_VERSION}), the tarball URL, and console output. The 0.1.0 default in uninstall.sh is therefore dead, misleading version cruft inconsistent with the project's actual 1.5.x version. Verified test-install.sh does not source uninstall.sh or otherwise consume the variable. Functionally harmless (uninstall still works) but cosmetically wrong.
repro: grep -n FLOW_VERSION scripts/uninstall.sh -> only line 10; variable never used.
suggestedFix: Delete the unused line 10 (`FLOW_VERSION="${FLOW_VERSION:-0.1.0}"`) entirely, since the variable is never read in uninstall.sh. If a version stamp is desired for the console banner, instead align the default to 1.5.0 to match install.sh:25 and actually print it (e.g. add `echo "==> Flow uninstaller v${FLOW_VERSION}"`). The minimal, safest fix is removal.

title: VersionCommand.cs comment claims version is 0.1.0-phase30 (stale)
finding: The doc comment states the InformationalVersion is `0.1.0-phase30`, but flow-cli.csproj is now stamped 1.5.0 and `flow version` correctly prints `flow 1.5.0+<commit>`. The code is correct; only the comment is stale and contradicts the actual stamping. Harmless at runtime but misleads future maintainers auditing version stamping.
rootCause: The doc comment at VersionCommand.cs:7-8 states the InformationalVersion is "set in flow-cli.csproj to `0.1.0-phase30`", but flow-cli.csproj:10-11 is now stamped `<Version>1.5.0</Version>` / `<InformationalVersion>1.5.0</InformationalVersion>`. Verified at runtime: `dotnet run --project flow-cli -- version` prints `flow 1.5.0+bbbe3824288e6ae64d60256d803839f8c566e4a1` (the +commit suffix is the .NET SDK default IncludeSourceRevisionInInformationalVersion behavior, not SourceLink — there is no SourceLink package in the repo). The code (reading AssemblyInformationalVersionAttribute with a fallback chain) is correct; only the comment is stale and contradicts the actual stamping. Pure documentation drift with no runtime effect.
repro: flow version -> 'flow 1.5.0+...' while the comment says 0.1.0-phase30.
suggestedFix: Update the comment at VersionCommand.cs:7-8 to reference 1.5.0 instead of 0.1.0-phase30, e.g. "Prints the assembly's InformationalVersion (set in flow-cli.csproj to `1.5.0`)". Note for accuracy: the displayed `+<commit>` suffix is produced by the .NET SDK default (IncludeSourceRevisionInInformationalVersion), not SourceLink. If a clean `flow 1.5.0` is desired, either set `<IncludeSourceRevisionInInformationalVersion>false</IncludeSourceRevisionInInformationalVersion>` in flow-cli.csproj, or strip everything after the first `+` before printing in VersionCommand.cs. No functional fix is required.

title: RunResult.midi is a Base64 string, not a Uint8Array — corrupt MIDI download on Web
line: 48 (Midi is byte[]) + 337 (Serialize via FlowWasmJsonContext); JS side flow-lang/wasm/flow-runtime.js:247-265 (run, no decode) + typedef 339
finding: RunResult.Midi is byte[]. RunFromJs serializes the whole RunResult through the source-generated FlowWasmJsonContext (line 337). System.Text.Json serializes byte[] as a Base64-encoded STRING, not a JSON number array — I confirmed this with a standalone net10 source-gen repro: {"midi":"TVRoZAABAv8=",...}. The flow-runtime.js run() method does only JSON.parse(json) and returns the object verbatim (lines 248-264) — it performs NO base64 decode. Yet the documented contract says the opposite: the JS typedef at flow-runtime.js:339 declares `@property {Uint8Array} [midi]`, and CLAUDE.md D-48-17/D-48-18 states 'writeMidi works on the Web target -> RunResult.midi as Uint8Array. Phase 49 wires the Blob download.' The C# test WasmContractTests.cs:106 even decodes with Convert.FromBase64String, proving C# knows it is base64 — but nothing bridges base64->Uint8Array for the JS consumer. A Phase 49 consumer doing `new Blob([result.midi])` gets a Blob containing the literal base64 text, producing a corrupt, unplayable .mid download. The C->JS contract is broken; result.midi is the wrong type.
rootCause: System.Text.Json (including the source-generated FlowWasmJsonContext used at WasmEntry.cs:337) serializes byte[] as a Base64-encoded STRING, never a JSON number array. I verified this empirically with a standalone net10 source-gen repro using the same [JsonSourceGenerationOptions] shape: it emitted {"midi":"TVRoZAABAv8=",...} — a string — for MThd-prefixed bytes (matching the exact base64 the claim cited). RunResult.Midi (WasmEntry.cs:48) is byte[], so RunResult.midi crosses the C->JS boundary as a Base64 string. The frozen flow-runtime.js run() (lines 247-265) only does JSON.parse(json) with NO base64 decode — grep for atob/FromBase64/charCodeAt across flow-runtime.js and the playground MIDI path returns nothing. The advertised contract is the opposite: the JS typedef at flow-runtime.js:339 and the consumer type at flow-site/src/lib/runtime.ts:33 both declare midi as Uint8Array, and CLAUDE.md D-48-17/18 says "RunResult.midi as Uint8Array". The C# test WasmContractTests.cs corroborates the bug: its own comment (line 99) says "serializes byte[] as base64url per System.Text.Json default" and it decodes via Convert.FromBase64String (line 106) — so the test only passes because it knows to decode, while the JS consumer does not. Real downstream corruption is confirmed in the Phase 49 consumer: state.svelte.ts:128 assigns result.midi straight to this.midi (typed Uint8Array|null), and download.ts:30-38 checks `bytes instanceof Uint8Array` — FALSE for a string — so it falls through to `part = bytes as BlobPart` and new Blob([base64String]) yields a Blob containing the literal base64 TEXT, i.e. a corrupt, unplayable .mid download.
repro:
use "@audio"
Sequence sq = | C4q D4q E4q |
section verse { sq }
Song s = [verse]
(writeMidi "out.mid" s)  — then in JS: const r = await runtime.run(src); typeof r.midi === 'string' (base64), NOT a Uint8Array; new Blob([r.midi]) yields a corrupt file.
suggestedFix: The C->JS midi value MUST become a Uint8Array to honor the typedef + D-48-18. Note the frozen-runtime constraint (CLAUDE.md + HANDOFF section 8 forbid hand-editing flow-runtime.js), so the cleanest options are: (A) decode in the SvelteKit consumer wrapper — in flow-site/src/lib/runtime.ts bootRuntime() wrap run() so that after it returns, if (typeof result.midi === 'string') result.midi = Uint8Array.from(atob(result.midi), c => c.charCodeAt(0)); (do the same for any future wav string). This respects the frozen runtime and fixes every consumer. (B) If editing the runtime is acceptable in a future WASM-runtime phase, do the decode inside flow-runtime.js run() right after JSON.parse, or change WasmEntry to expose midi via a dedicated [JSExport] byte[] getter (marshalled as a real typed array) and null the Midi field in the serialized RunResult. Add a Node/vitest assertion in flow-site that result.midi instanceof Uint8Array after a writeMidi run, and that its first 4 bytes are 0x4D 0x54 0x68 0x64 ("MThd") — the existing C# WasmContractTests passes only because it decodes base64 itself, so it cannot catch the JS-side gap.

title: RunFromJs reuses one FlowEngine across all runs — second run of any script with a top-level declaration throws 'already declared'
finding: GetEngine() lazily creates a process-static _sharedEngine and RunFromJs reuses it on every call (line 279). FlowEngine.Execute (FlowEngine.cs:338-405) only clears the ErrorReporter (line 340) — it never resets the interpreter's global StackFrame or section registry. StackFrame.DeclareVariable throws InvalidOperationException 'Variable X already declared in this scope' (StackFrame.cs:73-74) and Interpreter throws 'Section X is already defined' (Interpreter.cs:788) on re-declaration. The JS run() (flow-runtime.js:247) never disposes between runs. So the very common playground loop — edit a script, click Run again — fails on the SECOND run for ANY script with a top-level `Buffer x = ...`, `Song s = [...]`, `section ...`, or `proc ...`. The exception is caught at FlowEngine.cs:400 and surfaces as errors[{kind:'runtime', message:'Unexpected error: Variable x already declared in this scope'}]. This is masked in CI: WasmContractTests.cs:82,87 explicitly calls DisposeFromJs() before each run 'to avoid false failures from section/variable re-declaration errors in the long-lived singleton' — acknowledging the bug in C# tests, but the JS run() does NOT replicate that dispose.
rootCause: RunFromJs reuses one process-static FlowEngine across every call (WasmEntry.cs:185-193 GetEngine lazy singleton; reused at lines 279/289). FlowEngine.Execute (FlowEngine.cs:338-405) only clears the ErrorReporter (line 340) and the block tuning stack (line 383) — it never clears the persistent global scope or section registry. ExecutionContext.GlobalFrame is created once in the constructor (ExecutionContext.cs:671-672) and SectionRegistry (ExecutionContext.cs:242) is a persistent dictionary; Interpreter.Execute(program) (Interpreter.cs:126-141) iterates statements on that persistent context without pushing a fresh frame. Top-level variable declarations call _context.DeclareVariable unconditionally (Interpreter.cs:1071), and StackFrame.DeclareVariable THROWS InvalidOperationException 'Variable X already declared in this scope' on re-declaration (StackFrame.cs:73-74). That throw is caught at FlowEngine.cs:400-403 and surfaced as errors[{kind:'runtime', message:'Unexpected error: Variable X already declared in this scope'}]. The duplicate-section case is similar but REPORTS rather than throws (Interpreter.cs:787-789 'Section X is already defined') — still an error entry. The JS run() (flow-runtime.js:247-265) calls RunFromJs directly with no dispose between calls, so the common playground loop (edit, click Run again) fails on the second run for any script with a top-level `Buffer/Sequence/Song x = ...` or `section ...`. The bug is self-documented: WasmContractTests.cs:61-64 + 82-88 explicitly call DisposeFromJs() before every RunFromJs 'to avoid false failures from section/variable re-declaration errors in the long-lived singleton' — the C# test works around it but the JS run() never replicates that dispose. (Minor claim inaccuracy: the section case reports an error rather than throwing, and `proc` redeclaration is tolerated via function overloading; the variable and section cases are definitive and cover the overwhelmingly common playground patterns.)
repro: Run twice through the same runtime without dispose: const r1 = await runtime.run('Buffer t = (createSineTone 440Hz 1.0 0.5)\n(play t)'); const r2 = await runtime.run(SAME_SOURCE); r2.errors[0].message === 'Unexpected error: Variable t already declared in this scope'.
suggestedFix: Make each run() independent. Preferred: have RunFromJs build a fresh FlowEngine per call (Dispose the previous one), so each run re-runs the constructor's stdlib bootstrap (@std + style packs) and starts with a clean GlobalFrame + empty SectionRegistry — exactly the semantics WasmContractTests already emulates with DisposeFromJs() before each RunFromJs(). Concretely, in RunFromJs, before Execute: under _lock, dispose _sharedEngine and set _sharedEngine = new FlowEngine(verbose:false) (or call GetEngine() after nulling it). A plain ResetGlobalScope() that only clears GlobalFrame variables + SectionRegistry is NOT sufficient on its own because it would wipe the stdlib bindings loaded in the constructor — any reset path must re-bootstrap (@std import + StyleRegistry.LoadShippedAndUserPacks), which fresh-engine-per-run gives for free. Avoid option (b) (making JS run() call dispose) — it leaves the C# contract unsafe for any other caller and forces callers to remember to dispose. Keep DisposeFromJs idempotent (it already is). After the fix, drop the per-test DisposeFromJs workaround in WasmContractTests so the test actually exercises the production reuse path.

title: WarnOnce dedup is process-static and never reset per run — RunResult.stderr diverges on two runs of the same source (D-48-16 violation)
line: WasmEntry.cs:258-348 (RunFromJs has no diagnostics reset; only MidiExport.DrainInMemorySink at 271); RenderingDiagnostics.cs:21,33 (process-static _emitted; WarnOnce dedups per-process)
finding: Composer-facing advisories ([tuning], [stretch] mode=#auto, granular unknown-windowing, [midi] non-EQ, etc.) route through RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce, which writes to Console.Error (captured into RunResult.stderr per D-48-15) but dedups on a process-static HashSet _emitted (RenderingDiagnostics.cs:21) that is emitted-once-per-process. RunFromJs never calls ResetForTesting() (or any per-run reset) at the top of a run. The WASM runtime is one long-lived process with a reused engine, so: run 1 of an advisory-emitting script -> advisory present in stderr; run 2 of the IDENTICAL source -> advisory suppressed -> stderr differs. This breaks the D-48-16 'same source -> byte-identical RunResult JSON (excluding durationMs)' contract for the stderr field. WasmDeterminismTests passes only because its fixture is pure print+add with no advisory builtins (it explicitly notes this at lines 53-58).
rootCause: Advisories like [tuning] (ScalaBuiltins.cs:154), [stretch] mode=#auto (StretchEngine.cs:206), [fast]/granular (PatternFunctions.cs) route through RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce, which writes Console.Error and dedups on the process-static HashSet _emitted (RenderingDiagnostics.cs:21) keyed by a sentinel that is STABLE across runs of identical source. RunFromJs redirects Console.Error into a per-call StringWriter during engine.Execute (WasmEntry.cs:267,289,316), so advisories ARE captured into RunResult.stderr (D-48-15). The WASM runtime reuses one long-lived _sharedEngine (WasmEntry.cs:185-193). RunFromJs clears the MIDI sink per run (line 271) but never resets the diagnostics dedup state. The only caller of RenderingDiagnostics.ResetForTesting() is ExecutionContext.RestoreState (ExecutionContext.cs:1378), a TEST-ONLY snapshot-restore invoked by TestRunner, NOT by production FlowEngine.Execute. So run 1 of an advisory-emitting source emits the advisory into stderr; run 2 of the identical source through the same runtime dedups it away, so StripDurationMs(json1) != StripDurationMs(json2) -- a D-48-16 two-run cmp-clean violation for the stderr field. Confirmed the advisory channel by running a degenerate script on the Desktop engine: stderr emitted '[fast] factor must be > 0 and finite (got 0); sequence unchanged'. WasmDeterminismTests (WasmDeterminismTests.cs:57-58) uses an advisory-free fixture (print+add) and compares full JSON minus only durationMs, so it passes vacuously and cannot catch this.
repro: Two runs through one runtime of: use "@audio"\nSequence s = | (? C4 E4 G4) |\n... (or any non-EQ tuning / #auto stretch). run1.stderr contains the advisory; run2.stderr does not -> StripDurationMs(json1) != StripDurationMs(json2).
suggestedFix: In WasmEntry.RunFromJs, call FlowLang.Diagnostics.RenderingDiagnostics.ResetForTesting() at the START of the method, alongside the existing MidiExport.DrainInMemorySink() clear at line 271, so WarnOnce dedup state is per-run not per-process. This mirrors the per-run MIDI-sink clear and restores two-run cmp-clean for the stderr field. Optionally rename ResetForTesting to ResetForRun and also clear ExecutionContext.StrictAdvisoryDedup (same per-process posture), but the diagnostics reset is the minimal correct fix for D-48-16. Then add a determinism test whose fixture actually emits an advisory (use @patterns; Sequence s = | C4 D4 E4 F4 |; (degrade (fast s 0.0))) and assert StripDurationMs(run1) == StripDurationMs(run2) including stderr so the gate stops being vacuous.

title: loop()/stream() silently produce no audio on Web (Task.Run never executes on single-threaded WASM)
finding: `(loop buf)` registers to LoopBufferInfiniteAsync and `(stream ...)` to StreamBuffer/StreamSequence, all of which dispatch via Task.Run(() => ...) (lines 116, 163, 211, 104). RunFromJs runs FlowEngine.Execute SYNCHRONOUSLY on the single Mono-WASM main thread (WasmEntry.cs:289, documented at lines 280-289). Task.Run queues the body to that same thread, which is blocked for the whole synchronous run — so the queued loop/stream body NEVER executes during the run, and after RunFromJs returns the body would (if scheduled) enter the blocking `while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)` loop in LoopBufferInfinite (line 191) that would hang the tab. Net effect on Web: `(loop ...)` and `(stream ...)` are silently no-ops (no audio), with no advisory. `(play ...)` works because PlayBuffer calls PlaySamples synchronously (line 92) and WebAudioBackend.Play is fire-and-forget. CLAUDE.md only promises `(play buffer)` audible on Web; loop/stream silence is undocumented and surprising.
rootCause: All non-blocking playback builtins dispatch their work via Task.Run: loop(Buffer) -> LoopBufferInfiniteAsync at line 163, loop(Buffer,Int) -> LoopBufferNAsync at 211, stream(Sequence) at 104, stream(Buffer) at 116. PlaybackFunctions.Register is called unconditionally (BuiltInFunctions.cs:81, no #if !FLOW_WEB guard), so loop/stream ARE registered on the Web target and DetectBackend (AudioPlaybackManager.cs:161-162) returns a WebAudioBackend whose Play (WebAudioBackend.cs:131) is fire-and-forget. WasmEntry.RunFromJs (WasmEntry.cs:289) runs FlowEngine.Execute SYNCHRONOUSLY on the single Mono-WASM main thread — the code itself documents (lines 280-289, and WebAudioBackend.cs:37-47) that Mono-WASM is single-threaded by default and that the prior Task.Run+Wait pattern deadlocked there. Consequently the Task.Run-queued loop/stream body cannot run during the synchronous Execute. By contrast play(Buffer) -> PlayBuffer -> PlaySamples (line 92) calls backend.Play synchronously, so (play ...) is audible. The defect is that loop/stream produce no correct audio on Web with NO advisory: either the queued body never gets pumped (silent no-op), or if pumped after RunFromJs returns, LoopBufferInfinite's tight while(!ct.IsCancellationRequested){ backend.Play(...) } (line 191) over a fire-and-forget Play would spawn unbounded overlapping AudioBufferSourceNodes / hang the tab. This is Web-specific: on Desktop the PulseAudio/CoreAudio Play blocks on a real background thread so the loop behaves. CLAUDE.md only promises (play buffer) audible on Web; loop/stream silence is undocumented — charity (silent return of Void) hides lost audio output rather than the intended behavior.
repro: use "@audio"\nBuffer b = (createSineTone 440Hz 1.0 0.5)\n(loop b)  — on Web produces no sound and no diagnostic; the Task.Run body never runs on the single WASM thread.
suggestedFix: Add a Web-target branch to the four non-blocking builtins. Option A (preferred for loop): on OperatingSystem.IsBrowser(), route loop/stream to the synchronous fire-and-forget path — for loop, build a JS-side AudioBufferSourceNode with source.loop=true (a new FlowRuntimeInterop [JSImport] PlayStereoFloat32Looping, or a looping flag on the existing one) so the browser loops natively without a C# while-loop; for stream, just call PlaySamples synchronously (Play already returns immediately on Web). Option B (minimum viable): in LoopBufferInfiniteAsync/LoopBufferNAsync/StreamBuffer/StreamSequence, when OperatingSystem.IsBrowser() emit a one-shot WarnOnce stderr advisory like "[target] loop/stream fall back to a single synchronous play under FlowTarget=Web (no background thread) — line N" and call the synchronous single-play path instead of Task.Run, so composers get audio + a diagnostic instead of silence. Either way, do NOT Task.Run on the Web target.

title: Parse-stage and runtime FlowErrors are all labeled kind='eval'; SourceSnippet always null despite registered SourceMap
finding: MapFlowErrors maps EVERY Error-level FlowError to kind='eval' (line 232) and always sets SourceSnippet=null (line 237). But D-48-14 pins kind in {parse|eval|runtime|cancel|platform-not-supported} and says 'Phase 49 renders Rust-style diagnostic boxes' off these fields. Parse errors (e.g. the live-block Web reject at Parser.cs:269, or any syntax error) reach engine.ErrorReporter.Errors via Parser.Parse catch at Parser.cs:91 with a real CurrentToken.Location — so Line/Column ARE populated — but they get mislabeled as 'eval', and the source line is never quoted into SourceSnippet even though FlowEngine.Execute registers the full source in SourceMap under '<wasm>' (FlowEngine.cs:347, retrievable via SourceMap.TryGetSource). The XML doc at lines 218-225 acknowledges parse-vs-eval tagging as a v1.6 backlog, but the null SourceSnippet undercuts the Rust-style-diagnostic promise that the contract documents as already-supported.
rootCause: MapFlowErrors (WasmEntry.cs:227-239) maps every Error-level FlowError to SourceSnippet=null and never consults the engine's SourceMap, even though FlowEngine.Execute registers the full source under the "<wasm>" key (FlowEngine.cs:347) and SourceMap.TryGetSource (SourceMap.cs:77) can retrieve it. Parse and runtime errors DO carry a real SourceLocation with Line/Column (verified by repro `(print` -> `<eval>:1:7`, reported via Parser.cs:91 ReportError(ex.Message, CurrentToken.Location)). Phase 49's playground actually built the snippet+caret render path (flow-site/src/routes/playground/+page.svelte:511-516, gated `{#if err.sourceSnippet}`), so with SourceSnippet always null that branch is dead code and the advertised Rust-style diagnostic box degrades to heading + bare lines with no quoted source line or caret. The data is reachable but deliberately left null; no test pins null-snippet as intended (WasmJsonSerializationTests.cs:92-93 only verifies JSON null-omission, using a fabricated RunError). NOTE: the SECOND half of the claim — parse errors mislabeled kind="eval" — is by-design and NOT a defect: FlowError (FlowError.cs:8-12) carries only a DiagnosticLevel, no parse/eval/runtime stage discriminator, and WasmEntry.cs:217-225 documents per-stage tagging as a v1.6 backlog item the claim itself acknowledges.
repro: runtime.run('(print') -> errors[0].kind === 'eval' (should be 'parse') and errors[0].sourceSnippet === undefined even though the offending line is available in the SourceMap.
suggestedFix: Thread the engine SourceMap into MapFlowErrors so it can populate SourceSnippet. In RunFromJs (where `engine` is already in scope at line 279) call `MapFlowErrors(engine.ErrorReporter.Errors, engine.SourceMap)`; in MapFlowErrors, for each error with a positive Location.Line, do `if (sourceMap.TryGetSource("<wasm>", out var src)) { var lines = src.Split('\n'); if (line >= 1 && line <= lines.Length) snippet = lines[line - 1]; }` and pass `snippet` instead of null. Keep null when no line / no registration (matches the documented "null when no snippet is available" semantics at WasmEntry.cs:73-74). The kind="eval" -> "parse" relabel is correctly deferred to a future FlowError stage discriminator (v1.6 backlog) and need not block this fix. No existing test pins SourceSnippet=null, so this is non-breaking; WasmJsonSerializationTests.cs:93 continues to pass because that test fabricates its own null-snippet RunError.

title: Buffers with >2 channels are marshalled to WebAudio as stereo, garbling playback
line: 331 (PromoteToStereo channels>=2 pass-through), 187 (hardcoded channels: 2 marshal); JS de-interleave flow-runtime.js:138,146-147
finding: WebAudioBackend.Play calls PromoteToStereo(samples, channels) (line 154), which for channels>=2 returns the input UNCHANGED (line 331), then unconditionally marshals to JS with channels: 2 (line 187). For a true stereo buffer (channels==2) this is correct. But IAudioBackend.Initialize accepts channels 1..8 (line 86-87), so a 3+ channel interleaved buffer is passed through by PromoteToStereo and then de-interleaved JS-side (flow-runtime.js:142-149) as 2 channels — frames = samples.length/2 and L/R picked from a 3+-wide interleave, producing garbled/mistimed audio. Edge case (Flow rarely emits >2ch buffers) but a real correctness gap given the 1..8 channel surface.
rootCause: PromoteToStereo (WebAudioBackend.cs:328-340) returns the input array UNCHANGED for any channels>=2 (line 331), including 3+ channels. Play then unconditionally marshals to JS with hardcoded channels: 2 (WebAudioBackend.cs:186-187). On the JS side, playStereoFloat32 (flow-runtime.js:118-163) computes frames = samples.length / channels with channels==2 (line 138) and de-interleaves with stride 2 (lines 142-148). For a true 3-channel interleaved buffer (length = frames*3), JS reads frames = floor(frames*3/2) and picks L/R from a 3-wide interleave — producing garbled, mistimed audio. A >2-channel buffer is user-constructible and reaches Play unclamped: AudioBuffer's constructor only rejects channels<1 (AudioCore.cs:60), the `buffer` builtin (CreateBuffer, AudioCore.cs:112-119) takes channels straight from args with no upper clamp, and `noise` (SignalGeneration.cs:193-209) clamps only the lower bound. Play path: PlayBuffer (PlaybackFunctions.cs:92) passes buffer.Channels -> PlaySamples (line 361) -> backend.Play(samples, sampleRate, channels). Initialize accepts channels 1..8 (WebAudioBackend.cs:86-87) so channels==3 does not short-circuit. AudioPlaybackManager applies no downmix. The original claim's only inaccuracy is citing line 154 (the PromoteToStereo call) as the pass-through; the actual pass-through is the `if (channels >= 2) return samples;` at line 331 — the call at 154 is correct.
repro: A 3-channel interleaved AudioBuffer reaching WebAudioBackend.Play plays back garbled because PromoteToStereo passes it through unchanged but the JS marshal treats it as stereo.
suggestedFix: In PromoteToStereo (WebAudioBackend.cs:328), keep the channels==2 reference-equal pass-through but add a downmix branch for channels>2: de-interleave the N-channel input and average all channels into both L and R (or front L/R for >2 if a layout convention is desired), returning a true 2-channel interleaved array of length frames*2. This honors D-48-07 'stereo always' so the JS-side channels:2 assumption holds. Add a one-shot stderr advisory (e.g. '[webaudio] downmixed N-channel buffer to stereo for browser playback') per the charitable-default convention. Alternatively, pass the true channel count to PlayStereoFloat32 and let JS createBuffer with the real channel count plus a ChannelMergerNode/downmix to ctx.destination — but the in-PromoteToStereo downmix is the smaller, lower-risk change and keeps the frozen JS marshal contract intact. Repro: build FlowTarget=Web and run `(play (noise 0.5 0.5 3 44100))` or `(play (buffer 22050 3 44100))` in the playground — playback is garbled/mistimed vs. the correct stereo case.

title: FEATURES.md claims raw oscillators saw/square are PolyBLEP band-limited; createSawTone/createSquareTone are naive
finding: FEATURES.md:169 lists under 'Raw oscillators | Fully': '`sine`, `saw`/`sawtooth` (PolyBLEP band-limited), `square` (PolyBLEP band-limited), `triangle`'. But the actual raw oscillator builtins are naive: flow-lang/StandardLibrary/Audio/SignalGeneration.cs `GenerateSaw` (line 61-81, comment 'Sawtooth: ramps from -1 to 1 linearly', no BLEP) and `GenerateSquare` (line 86-106, comment 'Square wave: -1 for phase < 0.5, +1...', no BLEP); `CreateSineTone`/`createSawTone`/`createSquareTone` likewise contain no PolyBLEP. PolyBLEP only applies to the *synthesizer-instrument* path (SawSynthesizer/SquareSynthesizer in NoteSynthesizer.cs:130-187, via BlepOscillator.PolyBlep), which is the renderSong dispatch, NOT the raw oscillator builtins. The wiki Audio-and-Synthesis.md:89 correctly states 'Raw oscillator waveforms ... are aliased and naive', directly contradicting FEATURES.md.
rootCause: FEATURES.md:169, under a row explicitly titled 'Raw oscillators', claims `saw`/`sawtooth` and `square` are '(PolyBLEP band-limited)'. The actual raw-oscillator builtins are naive. The Flow procs `createSawTone`/`createSquareTone`/`createTriangleTone` (flow-lang/audio.flow:372-420) call the `generateSaw`/`generateSquare` builtins, registered in flow-lang/StandardLibrary/BuiltInFunctions.cs:811-821 to flow-lang/StandardLibrary/Audio/SignalGeneration.cs `GenerateSaw` (lines 61-81: `(2.0 * state.Phase - 1.0)`, comment 'ramps from -1 to 1 linearly') and `GenerateSquare` (lines 86-106: `(state.Phase < 0.5 ? -1.0 : 1.0)`), neither of which contains any BLEP correction. `CreateSineTone` (SignalGeneration.cs:146-164) is likewise a plain sine. The alternative helper `SynthUtils.GenerateSaw`/`GenerateSquare` (SynthUtils.cs:67-98) is also naive (no BLEP) and is not even on the raw-oscillator builtin path. PolyBLEP exists ONLY in the synthesizer-instrument path: `SawSynthesizer.RenderNote` (NoteSynthesizer.cs:130-139, `naive - BlepOscillator.PolyBlep(phase, dt)`) and `SquareSynthesizer.RenderNote` (NoteSynthesizer.cs:175-184), which back the `saw`/`square` instruments dispatched by renderSong, NOT the raw oscillator builtins. The project's own wiki (wiki/Audio-and-Synthesis.md:89) states the opposite and correct fact: 'Raw oscillator waveforms (`sine`, `saw`/`sawtooth`, `square`, `triangle`) are aliased and naive — no anti-aliasing by design.' So FEATURES.md:169 is a confirmed documentation inaccuracy that directly contradicts the wiki. (Note: the same false 'PolyBLEP band-limited' claim is independently repeated in C# docstrings flow-lang/StandardLibrary/BuiltInDocs.cs:105 and :110 for createSawTone/createSquareTone — surfaced by the REPL `:help` meta-command — but the claim under review cites FEATURES.md:169, which is accurate as cited.)
repro: grep -n 'ramps from -1\|phase < 0.5 ? -1.0' flow-lang/StandardLibrary/Audio/SignalGeneration.cs  # naive; grep -n PolyBlep flow-lang/StandardLibrary/Audio/SignalGeneration.cs  # 0 hits
suggestedFix: Fix FEATURES.md:169 to stop attributing PolyBLEP to the raw oscillators. Either (a) drop the '(PolyBLEP band-limited)' parentheticals so the 'Raw oscillators' row reads `sine`, `saw`/`sawtooth`, `square`, `triangle` and add a note 'aliased/naive — no anti-aliasing by design' matching wiki/Audio-and-Synthesis.md:89; or (b) split into two rows — 'Raw oscillator builtins (createSawTone/createSquareTone/generateSaw/generateSquare): naive, aliased' and 'Synthesizer instruments "saw"/"square" used by renderSong: PolyBLEP band-limited (Sound Design 2.0)'. Separately (not part of this claim's cited line but worth folding into the same docs pass) correct the matching false strings in flow-lang/StandardLibrary/BuiltInDocs.cs:105 and :110 so `:help createSawTone`/`:help createSquareTone` no longer claim band-limiting.

title: Uppercase note-name typo in a note stream silently drops notes and emits a misleading location-less error (asymmetric with charitable lowercase path)
line: 401 (the `break` arm); the asymmetric charitable path is at 383-395
finding: Inside `| ... |`, the main loop turns a LOWERCASE unknown identifier into a VariableReferenceElement (line 383-395) which the compiler charitably renders as a rest with a clear stderr warning. An UPPERCASE identifier that is not a roman numeral (the shape of a mistyped note name, e.g. `Z9`, `H4`, `C9x`) matches none of the branches and hits `break` at line 401, abandoning the rest of the stream. Repro `Sequence s = | C4 D4 Z9 E4 |` prints ONLY `/tmp/erg-6.flow:1:28: error: Empty note stream` — col 28 is the CLOSING pipe, the typo `Z9` is never named, and C4/D4/E4 are all gone (bars.Count==0 path at line 410). Repro `Sequence s = | C4 D4 Z9 E4` (no closing pipe) instead silently keeps only [C4 D4] and reports `error: Function 'Z9' not found` at the leftover token. Either way: a single mistyped note name SILENTLY DELETES surrounding notes and the message points at the wrong place / wrong concept. This is exactly the case CLAUDE.md's charitable-interpretation memory should cover, and the lowercase path already does it correctly — the uppercase path is an inconsistent gap that produces wrong audio (lost notes) with a cryptic diagnostic.
rootCause: In ParseNoteStream's main loop, the Identifier branch (lines 368-398) only handles two cases: roman numerals (ScaleDatabase.IsRomanNumeral, line 371) and lowercase-initial identifiers treated as variable references (line 383, `char.IsLower(identText[0])`). An UPPERCASE identifier that is not a roman numeral — the exact shape of a mistyped note name like `Z9` or `H4` — is lexed as a plain Identifier (SimpleLexer.cs:1113-1114 rejects any first char outside A-G as a NoteLiteral) and matches NO branch, so control falls through to the unconditional `break` at line 401. The break abandons the rest of the stream. The leftover dangling pipe(s) then re-enter note-stream parsing in the surrounding expression parse, producing an `Empty note stream` error whose `location` is the opening/closing pipe (col 28 = the CLOSING pipe in the repro), never the offending token at col 22. Net effect: the typo silently deletes its neighboring notes (C4/D4/E4 all gone) and the diagnostic points at the wrong place and never names `Z9`. The lowercase path is charitable (compiler emits `Warning: undefined variable ... inserting rest`, NoteStreamCompiler.cs:1021, and preserves all notes), so the two paths are inconsistent. Confirmed by running the exact repro: `| C4 D4 Z9 E4 |` => only `error: Empty note stream` at 1:28, while `| C4 D4 z9 E4 |` => warning + `Sequence[1 bars, 4 beats total]` (all 4 kept). Note: the claim's tertiary example `C9x` does NOT trigger the bug — `C9` is a valid note in octave 9 and `x` is a valid duration suffix (TryParseDurationSuffix, line 427), so it parses charitably; only the `Z9`/`H4` shapes (first char outside A-G) reproduce. This minor mis-citation does not affect the finding.
repro: printf 'Sequence s = | C4 D4 Z9 E4 |\n(print (str s))\n' > /tmp/erg.flow && dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- /tmp/erg.flow   # => only 'error: Empty note stream' at col 28; Z9 never named; C4/D4/E4 dropped. Compare lowercase 'z9' => 'undefined variable z9 ... inserting rest', notes preserved.
suggestedFix: At Parser.NoteStream.cs:401, before the unconditional `break`, detect an unconsumed Identifier (or note-shaped token) that no element branch interpreted and recover instead of bailing. Preferred (keep symmetry with the lowercase var-ref path): if the current token is an uppercase A-G-leading identifier that failed NoteType.Parse, emit it as a charitable rest with a located WarnOnce advisory `[note-stream] unrecognized note name '<X>' at line N:col — rendered as rest` and `Advance()` past it so the remaining notes (E4 etc.) keep parsing — mirroring the VariableReferenceElement -> rest-insertion behavior in NoteStreamCompiler.cs:1021. Minimum acceptable fix: replace the bare `break` with a LOCATED diagnostic naming the token (`_errorReporter.ReportError($"Unrecognized element '{CurrentToken.Text}' in note stream", CurrentToken.Location);`) followed by `Advance(); continue;` so the offending token is named at its real column (22) and surrounding notes are not silently deleted. Either way, a single note-name typo must never silently drop neighboring notes nor point the diagnostic at the closing pipe.

title: Integer division by zero throws to the catch-all and renders as a location-less 'Unexpected error'; the charitable ReportDivisionByZero handler is dead code
line: 390 (IDivInt throw), 400 (DivIntPromote throw); dead handler ExpressionEvaluator.cs:1035; uncaught at ExpressionEvaluator.cs:450; catch-all FlowEngine.cs:402
finding: `(div N 0)` and `(idiv N 0)` call StdLib.DivIntPromote/IDivInt, which `throw new InvalidOperationException("Division by zero")` (lines 400 / 390). That exception is not caught locally — it propagates to FlowEngine.cs:402's catch-all which reports it at `SourceLocation.Unknown` with an 'Unexpected error:' prefix. Repro `Int a = (div 5 0)` prints `0:0: error: Unexpected error: Division by zero` — no file, no line, and the 'Unexpected error' framing reads like an interpreter bug rather than a composer mistake. Meanwhile ExpressionEvaluator.ReportDivisionByZero (line 1035) already implements the charitable located form (`_errorReporter.ReportError("Division by zero", location)` + return Void) but has ZERO call sites — it is dead code. The most-likely arithmetic mistake gets the worst diagnostic while a good handler sits unused.
rootCause: All division builtins in StdLib.cs throw InvalidOperationException on a zero divisor (IDivInt:390 "Integer division by zero", DivIntPromote:400, plus DivFloat:264, DivDouble:305, DivLong:351, DivNumber:366 — the claim understates the scope to idiv/div-int but the defect is shared across every div builtin). The interpreter invokes the internal implementation at ExpressionEvaluator.cs:450 (`overload.Implementation!(argValues)`) inside a try/FINALLY with no catch — the finally only restores CurrentCallSite/CallerStrictMode. No catch exists anywhere between StdLib and FlowEngine.Execute's catch-all at FlowEngine.cs:402, which reports the message at SourceLocation.Unknown prefixed with "Unexpected error:". Meanwhile ExpressionEvaluator.ReportDivisionByZero (line 1035) — which already does the located, charitable form (`_errorReporter.ReportError("Division by zero", location)` + `return Value.Void()`) — has exactly zero call sites (verified via grep: only its definition matches). So the most common arithmetic mistake gets the worst possible diagnostic (no file, no line, "Unexpected error" framing that reads like an interpreter bug) while the purpose-built handler is dead. Verified by repro: `dotnet run --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'Int a = (div 5 0)'` prints `0:0: error: Unexpected error: Division by zero`; `(idiv 5 0)` -> `0:0: error: Unexpected error: Integer division by zero`; `(div 5.0 0.0)` -> same location-less framing.
repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'Int a = (div 5 0)' 2>&1   # => 0:0: error: Unexpected error: Division by zero
suggestedFix: Route the zero-divisor case through a located diagnostic and wire up the existing dead handler. Cleanest: in ExpressionEvaluator's internal-call dispatch (around line 447-456), wrap the `overload.Implementation!(argValues)` call in a `catch (InvalidOperationException ex) when (ex.Message contains "ivision by zero")` that calls `ReportDivisionByZero(call.Location)` (returning Value.Void per the charitable report-and-continue contract used by ReportUnknownMember). That single catch covers ALL six div builtins at once and gives `file:line: error: Division by zero`. Alternatively, have the StdLib div functions signal a recoverable located error rather than throwing to the global catch, but the evaluator-side catch is simpler and centralizes it. Note ReportDivisionByZero returns Void, which means `Int a = (div 5 0)` will bind Void to an Int annotation — acceptable and far better than the current location-less crash framing, and consistent with how other charitable error paths return Void. While here, consider widening the catch message match (the integer path says "Integer division by zero", the rest say "Division by zero").

title: Failed expression feeding a typed declaration produces a SECOND, location-less cascade error that leaks internal C# language ('underlying CLR type null')
line: 1049-1051 (ConvertTo on Void); throw at flow-lang/Runtime/Value.cs:382; caught at flow-lang/Core/FlowEngine.cs:402
finding: When the RHS of a typed declaration fails (e.g. `(add 1)` -> reported 'No matching overload' and returns Value.Void()), ExecuteVariableDeclaration proceeds: Void.CanConvertTo(target) returns true (VoidType is a wildcard, VoidType.cs:24-28), so line 1050-1052 calls value.ConvertTo(target). Void's data is null, so Value.ConvertTo hits the final `throw new InvalidCastException(...)` at Value.cs:382, which is NOT caught here and propagates to FlowEngine.cs:402 -> `0:0: error: Unexpected error: Cannot convert Flow type 'Void' with underlying CLR type 'null' to Flow target type 'Int'`. Every failed overload that feeds a declaration produces this second, location-less, C#-implementation-leaking line. Observed on `Int y = (add 1)`, `Int z = (add 1 2 3 4)`, `Chord c = Xyz9`, `Buffer b = (createSineTone 440Hz)`. The first error is fine; the cascade is pure noise that talks about CLR types a composer never sees.
rootCause: VERIFIED by re-reading code and running all four repro cases. When a typed declaration's RHS fails (e.g. `(add 1)` reports "No matching overload" and the evaluator returns Value.Void()), ExecuteVariableDeclaration does NOT bail out. At Interpreter.cs:1020-1021, typeCompatible = value.Type.IsCompatibleWith(target) || value.Type.CanConvertTo(target); VoidType.CanConvertTo returns true unconditionally (wildcard, VoidType.cs:24-28), so typeCompatible=true and the "Cannot assign" guard at 1040 is skipped. Execution reaches line 1049: `!value.Type.Equals(varDecl.Type) && value.Type.CanConvertTo(varDecl.Type)` = (!Void.Equals(Int)=true) && (Void.CanConvertTo(Int)=true) = true, so line 1051 calls value.ConvertTo(Int). Value.ConvertTo has no Void/null special case (confirmed top at 231-234 only short-circuits same-type); a Void value has Data=null so no `Data is X` branch fires, and it falls through to the unconditional throw at Value.cs:382: InvalidCastException("Cannot convert Flow type 'Void' with underlying CLR type 'null' to Flow target type 'Int'"). The narrowing try/catch at Interpreter.cs:1024-1035 only wraps the IsNumericNarrowing path, not line 1051, so this throw is uncaught here and propagates to FlowEngine.Execute's catch at FlowEngine.cs:400-403, emitted at SourceLocation.Unknown as "0:0: error: Unexpected error: ...". Ran the repro: `Int y = (add 1)`, `Int z = (add 1 2 3 4)`, `Chord c = Xyz9`, and `Buffer b = (createSineTone 440Hz)` ALL produce the correct first error followed by the location-less CLR-leaking second line. NOT a charitable-by-design case: the first error is the real one; the second is a duplicate, location-less cascade that surfaces internal C# implementation language ("underlying CLR type 'null'") to composers on every failed typed declaration. Severity medium (not high): the first diagnostic is correct and no audio/data is corrupted, but it violates the diagnostics-quality contract for this ergonomics-first language and the cascade is confusing.
repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'Int y = (add 1)' 2>&1   # => 'No matching overload ...' THEN '0:0: error: Unexpected error: Cannot convert Flow type Void with underlying CLR type null to Flow target type Int'
suggestedFix: In ExecuteVariableDeclaration (Interpreter.cs:997), special-case a Void RHS before the ConvertTo at 1049. Since VoidType only reaches the assignment boundary when the RHS already failed and reported a real error, skip the conversion entirely: add `if (value.Type is TypeSystem.PrimitiveTypes.VoidType) { return; }` immediately after `var value = _evaluator.Evaluate(varDecl.Value);` at line 999 (the composer already got the accurate first error; declaring nothing is correct since no usable value exists). Guarding on `_errorReporter.HasErrors` is optional but defensible if some legitimate path can yield Void. Separately, the Value.cs:382 message leaks "underlying CLR type 'null'" to composers; move the CLR-type detail behind a verbose flag and emit a plain "cannot convert Void to <T>" for the user-facing path. Both changes eliminate the location-less, implementation-leaking cascade.

title: User procs and all Flow-defined stdlib procs silently lack named-arg support (parameter names dropped at declaration)
finding: ExecuteProcDeclaration builds the FunctionSignature from parameter TYPES only: `var inputTypes = proc.Parameters.Select(p => p.Type).ToList(); ... var signature = new FunctionSignature(proc.Name, inputTypes, isVarArgs);`. It never passes the parameter NAMES (proc.Parameters[i].Name), so signature.ParameterNames stays null for every user-defined proc and every Flow-level stdlib proc. OverloadResolver.cs:198-204 then rejects any named-arg call with `function 'X' does not yet support named arguments (parameter names not yet declared on this signature)`. Verified by running `proc addThem(Int: a, Int: b) (add a b) end proc` then `(addThem a=3 b=4)` -> error; and `(createSineTone duration=1.0 frequency=440.0 amplitude=0.5)` -> same error even though audio.flow:341 declares those exact names. This contradicts CLAUDE.md's 'Universal named args (Phase 36 D-36-11): at language level; ~150 builtins backfilled'. The backfill only covered C#-registered signatures; 46 Flow-defined stdlib procs plus ALL user procs are excluded. The inconsistency is invisible to composers: `(lowpass t cutoff=1000Hz)` works but the sibling `(createSineTone duration=1.0 ...)` in the same @audio module does not, purely because one is C#-registered and the other is a Flow proc.
rootCause: ExecuteProcDeclaration builds the FunctionSignature from parameter TYPES only (`var inputTypes = proc.Parameters.Select(p => p.Type).ToList(); var signature = new FunctionSignature(proc.Name, inputTypes, isVarArgs);`), never passing parameter NAMES. The FunctionSignature 4th constructor parameter `ParameterNames` (FunctionSignature.cs:32-36) thus defaults to null for every user-defined proc and every Flow-level stdlib proc. OverloadResolver.cs:198-205 then rejects any named-arg call against such a signature with the misleading message 'does not yet support named arguments (parameter names not yet declared on this signature)' — even though the names ARE declared on the Parameter records (ProcDeclaration.cs:92-95). The Phase 36 named-arg backfill only touched C#-registered signatures; Flow-defined stdlib procs (e.g. createSineTone at audio.flow:341) and all user procs were excluded. The entire downstream named-arg machinery (validation + type reorder in OverloadResolver.cs:207-294, value reorder in ExpressionEvaluator.cs:360-382) is fully generic and keys solely off Signature.ParameterNames — nothing else is missing, only the population at the declaration site. Confirmed by repro: `(addThem a=3 b=4)` and `(createSineTone duration=1.0 frequency=440.0 amplitude=0.5)` both error. This is a silently-violated documented 'universal named args' contract with a wrong error message, not charitable-by-design (it produces a hard error, not a sane default + advisory).
repro:
printf 'proc addThem(Int: a, Int: b)
    (add a b)
end proc
Int r = (addThem a=3 b=4)
(print (str r))
' > /tmp/n.flow && dotnet run --project flow-interpreter /tmp/n.flow
suggestedFix: At Interpreter.cs:938-941, thread the parameter names through to the signature constructor: `var paramNames = proc.Parameters.Select(p => p.Name).ToList(); var signature = new FunctionSignature(proc.Name, inputTypes, isVarArgs, paramNames);`. Verified: this makes `(addThem a=3 b=4)` return 7 and `(createSineTone duration=1.0 frequency=440.0 amplitude=0.5)` succeed, with no regressions in the named-args/lambda test scripts. Safe because (a) FunctionSignature.Equals/GetHashCode (FunctionSignature.cs:51-75) intentionally exclude ParameterNames, so overload identity, the InternalFunctionRegistry de-dup, and overload caching are unperturbed; (b) the named-args+varargs combination is rejected earlier in OverloadResolver.cs:190-197 before the ParameterNames check, so populating names for varargs procs is harmless.

title: Music literals (Cent/Decibel/Millisecond/Second) parse with locale-dependent double.TryParse — silent 10x value corruption in comma-decimal locales
finding: The lexer parses Cent, Decibel, Millisecond, and Second music literals with bare `double.TryParse(numberPart, out double v)` (no CultureInfo), while Beat (line 848), Hertz (631/645/783/795), and all plain numbers (411/562/872) correctly pass CultureInfo.InvariantCulture. In a culture where '.' is the group separator (de-DE, fr-FR, es-ES, etc.), `double.TryParse("2.5")` returns true with value 25 — the decimal point is read as a thousands separator. Empirically reproduced: `LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8 DOTNET_SYSTEM_GLOBALIZATION_INVARIANT=0 dotnet run flow-interpreter loc.flow` prints `2.5s`->25s, `-12.5dB`->-125dB, `100.5ms`->1005ms, `50.5c`->505c. These are silent, error-free 10x wrong values that flow straight into reverb decay, delay time, gain, and microtonal transpose — wrong audio with no diagnostic. The Desktop target (default, what composers use) does NOT set InvariantGlobalization (that property is set only under Condition FlowTarget==Web in flow-lang.csproj:34, and is an apphost property that only applies to the executable anyway — neither flow-interpreter nor flow-cli sets it or pins CurrentCulture). This also violates the CLAUDE.md 'Music Types Quick Reference' contract that `2.5s` = 2.5 seconds. The static helpers CentType.Parse/DecibelType.Parse/MillisecondType.Parse/SecondType.Parse share the same defect but the lexer is the live path.
rootCause: Cent/Decibel/Millisecond/Second music literals are parsed with bare `double.TryParse(numberPart, out double v)`, which uses CultureInfo.CurrentCulture and the default NumberStyles (Float | AllowThousands). In a comma-decimal locale (de-DE, fr-FR, es-ES, ...), CurrentCulture sees '.' as the THOUSANDS group separator, so `double.TryParse("2.5")` returns true with value 25 — a silent 10x corruption. Hertz (SimpleLexer 631/645/783/795, ExpressionEvaluator 147/155), Beat (676/848), and plain floats (872) correctly pass NumberStyles.Float + InvariantCulture; the four time/microtone/gain literal families do not. Verified empirically: under new CultureInfo("de-DE"), bare double.TryParse returned 2.5->25, -12.5->-125, 100.5->1005, 50.5->505, while the invariant call returned 2.5 correctly. The corruption reaches the runtime in TWO places. The lexer call is only a VALIDATION gate (Cent/Time/Decibel tokens route to LiteralExpression carrying RAW TEXT per Parser.cs:1423-1430), but the actual numeric Value is produced at eval time in ExpressionEvaluator.TryParseSpecialLiteral (lines 108/118/126/136), which has the identical bare-parse defect and feeds Value.Cent/Millisecond/Second/Decibel directly (Value.cs:35/37 store the double verbatim). So the claim's lines are correct but the truly LIVE value path is the ExpressionEvaluator, which the claim under-cited. Desktop is the default composer target and does NOT set InvariantGlobalization (csproj:34 is gated to FlowTarget==Web only); neither flow-interpreter nor flow-cli pins CurrentCulture. The static helpers (SecondType.Parse:45, CentType/DecibelType/MillisecondType.Parse) share the defect. Result: 2.5s reverb decay becomes 25s, -12.5dB gain becomes -125dB, 100.5ms delay becomes 1005ms, +50.5c transpose becomes +505c — silent wrong audio with no advisory, and a cross-locale determinism break.
repro:
Write loc.flow:
  Second s = 2.5s
  (print (str s))
Run: LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8 LANG=de_DE.UTF-8 DOTNET_SYSTEM_GLOBALIZATION_INVARIANT=0 dotnet run --project flow-interpreter loc.flow
Observed: prints 25s (should be 2.5s). Same for -12.5dB->-125dB, 100.5ms->1005ms, 50.5c->505c.
suggestedFix: Pass `System.Globalization.NumberStyles.Float, System.Globalization.CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` to every bare double.TryParse for Cent/Decibel/Millisecond/Second in BOTH places: SimpleLexer.cs lines 692, 707, 722, 736, 808, 821, 833, 862 (the validation gate) AND ExpressionEvaluator.cs lines 108, 118, 126, 136 (the live value path that actually builds Value.Cent/Millisecond/Second/Decibel) — matching the existing Hertz/Beat/plain-float sites. Also fix the static helpers SecondType.Parse:45, CentType.Parse, DecibelType.Parse, MillisecondType.Parse for defense-in-depth. Strongest belt-and-suspenders: pin CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentCulture/CurrentCulture = InvariantCulture at flow-interpreter Program.Main and flow-cli startup so all numeric parse/format is locale-independent regardless of any future bare-parse sites. Add a regression test that runs the four literals under a forced comma-decimal culture (CultureInfo.CurrentCulture = new("de-DE")) and asserts Value equals 2.5/-12.5/100.5/50.5.

title: (str 440Hz) fails with ambiguous-overload while every other music literal stringifies — missing str(Hertz) overload
line: 236-244 (gap between strDecibel @234-236 and strBeat @242-244; no str(Hertz) registered)
finding: There are dedicated str overloads for Int/Float/Double/Long/Number/String/Bool/Note/Symbol/Bar/Semitone/Cent/Millisecond/Second/Decibel/Beat/Array/Sequence/Chord/Section/Song/Tuning, but NONE for Hertz. HertzType.IsCompatibleWith returns true for both DoubleType and FloatType (HertzType.cs:32-35), so (str 440Hz) matches str(Float) and str(Double) at equal convertible specificity and the OverloadResolver reports 'Ambiguous overload for function str with argument types (Hertz). Candidates: str(Float), str(Double)'. This is exactly the case StrBeat's own doc comment (StdLib.cs:165-173) flags as REQUIRING a dedicated overload — the developers handled it for Beat but missed Hertz. Every other music literal in the table stringifies fine; only Hertz, a first-class music type per the Quick Reference, cannot be printed. Empirically reproduced: (print (str 1.5kHz)) and (print (str 440Hz)) both error; workaround (str (double 440Hz)) works.
rootCause: There is no `str` overload registered for HertzType. The `str` registry (BuiltInFunctions.cs:175-256, plus ScalaBuiltins/HarmonyFunctions for Tuning/Chord/Section/Song) covers Int/Float/Double/Long/Number/String/Bool/Note/Symbol/Bar/Semitone/Cent/Millisecond/Second/Decibel/Beat/Array/Sequence/Chord/Section/Song/Tuning — but Hertz is missing. HertzType.IsCompatibleWith (HertzType.cs:32-35) returns true for BOTH DoubleType and FloatType, so (str 440Hz) scores equal convertible specificity against str(Float) and str(Double), and OverloadResolver reports an ambiguous overload. This is the exact ambiguity class the StrBeat doc comment (StdLib.cs:165-173) documents as REQUIRING a dedicated overload — handled for Beat, missed for Hertz.
