title: Rest with explicit duration suffix (`_q`, `_h`, `_e`, etc.) causes 'Empty note stream' parse error
finding: The lexer's underscore branch checks `!char.IsLetterOrDigit(PeekNext())` to decide whether `_` is a standalone rest token. Because the duration suffix characters `q`, `h`, `w`, `e`, `s` are all letters, `_q` / `_h` / `_e` / `_s` / `_w` are consumed as a single identifier token instead of `Underscore` + identifier. The note-stream parser then never sees `TokenType.Underscore`, so the rest element is never recognised and the bar appears empty. Repro: `timesig 4/4 { Sequence s = | _q | }` -> parse error 'Empty note stream'. CLAUDE.md documents `_` as supporting duration suffixes (`q`/`h`/`w`/`e`/`s`) — `_h` is used in tutorial.flow prose. The workaround is bare `_` (duration inferred from bar fill), but that silently changes rhythmic meaning when the rest must be a specific duration.
rootCause: The lexer's `_` case (SimpleLexer.cs:197-203) only emits a standalone `TokenType.Underscore` when the next char is NOT a letter/digit and not `_`. Because every note-duration suffix (`w h q e s t x y`) is a letter, `_q`/`_h`/`_e`/`_w`/`_s` fall through to identifier scanning (line 203) and are consumed as a single identifier token (e.g. `"_q"`). Note LITERALS avoid this because ScanNumberOrSpecialLiteral (SimpleLexer.cs:1037-1054) explicitly rewinds position by 1 to split the trailing duration suffix into a separate token — but that path only fires for `text.Length >= 3` (e.g. `C4q`), so the 2-char `_q` never reaches it. The note-stream parser (Parser.NoteStream.cs:90-96) expects `_` as `TokenType.Underscore` followed by a SEPARATE duration-suffix identifier consumed by TryParseDurationSuffix (Parser.NoteStream.cs:422-434, looks for an Identifier whose text is `w/h/q/e/s/t/x/y`). The single `_q` identifier instead reaches the identifier branch at Parser.NoteStream.cs:368-398: it is not a roman numeral, and `char.IsLower('_')` is false so the variable-reference branch (line 383) is skipped — the loop breaks. For a pure-rest bar this leaves currentBarElements empty -> bars.Count==0 -> ErrorReporter "Empty note stream" (Parser.NoteStream.cs:410-412). Confirmed live: `| _q |`, `| _h |`, `| _e |`, `| _w |` all error "Empty note stream"; `| C4q _q _ _ |` errors "Unexpected token Underscore"; whereas `| C4q _ _ _ |` (bare rest) and `| C4q _ q |` (underscore + space + suffix) both parse cleanly — proving the parser already supports separated tokens and the defect is purely lexical. The repo itself documents this at examples/jazz/combo.flow:26-29 ("REST-WITH-SUFFIX `_q` / `_w` IS A LEXER BUG").
repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'use "@std" timesig 4/4 { Sequence s = | C4q _q _ _ | (print (str s)) }' -> parse error 'Empty note stream'
suggestedFix: In SimpleLexer.cs's `_` case (line 197-203), treat `_` as a standalone Underscore rest token when it is immediately followed by exactly one duration-suffix letter that does not begin a longer word. Concretely, add a guard before the existing fall-through: if PeekNext() is one of {w,h,q,e,s,t,x,y} AND the char two ahead (call a PeekNext2 helper / `_position+2` bounds-checked) is NOT a letter/digit/underscore, return SingleChar(TokenType.Underscore). SingleChar consumes only the `_`, leaving the suffix letter to be re-scanned as its own Identifier token on the next ScanToken pass — exactly what Parser.NoteStream.TryParseDurationSuffix expects. Keep the existing `PeekNext() != '_'` clause so `__enableSfzModule`-style internal markers still lex as identifiers. This preserves the documented note-stream rest grammar (CLAUDE.md:291) and matches the suffix-split behavior already applied to note literals at SimpleLexer.cs:1045-1046. Add a regression test asserting `| _q |` / `| _h |` parse to a RestElement with DurationSuffix set (compiled by NoteStreamCompiler.CompileRestElement at NoteStreamCompiler.cs:808-825, which already honors rest.DurationSuffix).

title: `(invert seq)` is a silent no-op when all notes are in voice blocks
finding: The `Invert` function finds the axis note by iterating `bar.MusicalNotes` only. For a voice-block sequence, `bar.MusicalNotes` is empty (all notes live in `bar.ParallelVoices`); no axis is found (`axisMidi` remains null), so the function hits the 'all rests' early-return path and calls `TransformNotes(seq, n => n)` — an identity clone. The voice-block notes ARE preserved (TransformBar recurses into ParallelVoices), but the inversion arithmetic is never applied. Result: `(invert voiceBlockSeq)` returns a byte-identical copy of the input, producing identical audio. Two-run cmp-clean is technically preserved (same wrong output both times), but the function violates its documented contract. Repro: build a voice-block sequence, call `(invert ...)`, render both, diff the WAVs — they are byte-identical.
rootCause: In Invert (TransformFunctions.cs:861-900) the axis-finding loop at lines 867-878 iterates only `bar.MusicalNotes`. For a voice-block-only bar, NoteStreamCompiler.cs:208-211 inserts a single whole-bar REST into the parent bar's MusicalNotes and hangs the audible notes off `bar.ParallelVoices` (CompileVoiceBlock returns the real notes in each voice sub-bar's own MusicalNotes). The axis loop's `if (!note.IsRest)` skips that lone rest, so `axisMidi` stays null and the function hits the early-return at line 882: `Value.Sequence(TransformNotes(seq, n => n))`. TransformNotes/TransformBar (607-645) DO recurse into ParallelVoices, so the voice notes are preserved verbatim — but the inversion arithmetic (`2*axis - midi`) at line 890 is never reached. Result: `(invert voiceBlockSeq)` returns a byte-identical clone, violating the documented contract ("Inverts a sequence around its first note", BuiltInDocs.cs:184). Confirmed empirically: voice-block invert produced two byte-identical 352844-byte WAVs (cmp clean), while a control plain sequence `| C4q E4q F4q G4q |` invert produced WAVs differing at byte 88257.
repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'use "@std" use "@audio" tempo 120 { timesig 4/4 { key Cmajor { Sequence vb = | {voice C4w} {voice E4q F4q G4q A4q} | Sequence inv = (invert vb) section s1 { Sequence v = vb } section s2 { Sequence v = inv } Song song1 = [s1] Song song2 = [s2] Buffer b1 = (renderSong song1 "piano") Buffer b2 = (renderSong song2 "piano") (writeWav "/tmp/a.wav" b1) (writeWav "/tmp/b.wav" b2) } } }' ; diff /tmp/a.wav /tmp/b.wav && echo BUG
suggestedFix: Extend the axis search to recurse into ParallelVoices. Add a helper mirroring CountAudibleNotes' parent-then-voices traversal order (to keep the axis deterministic / two-run cmp-clean): a recursive FindFirstNonRestMidi(BarData bar) that first scans bar.MusicalNotes for the first non-rest note (returning its MIDI), then recurses into each bar.ParallelVoices sub-bar, returning the first match. Then in Invert replace the lines 866-878 loop with a loop over seq.Bars calling FindFirstNonRestMidi(bar) and breaking when it has a value. The early-return at 881-882 and the TransformNotes inversion at 885-897 already recurse into ParallelVoices correctly, so only the axis-finding step needs fixing. No other transform is affected (transpose uses a per-note delta, not an axis).

title: `(visualize seq)` / `(inspect seq)` reports '(no notes in sequence)' for voice-block sequences
finding: The `Visualize` function iterates `bar.MusicalNotes` only and never recurses into `bar.ParallelVoices`. Because voice-block bars have an empty `MusicalNotes` list (all content is in `ParallelVoices`), `noteEvents` remains empty and the function prints '(no notes in sequence)'. Audio rendering is unaffected; this is a display-only bug in the REPL tool. Repro: `timesig 4/4 { Sequence vb = | {voice C4w} {voice E4q F4q G4q A4q} | (visualize vb) }` -> '(no notes in sequence)'.
rootCause: The `Visualize` function's per-bar loop iterates only `bar.MusicalNotes` (line 72) and never inspects `bar.ParallelVoices`. Voice-block bars compiled by NoteStreamCompiler carry their audible content exclusively in `ParallelVoices`; the parent bar's `MusicalNotes` holds a single whole-bar rest placeholder (NoteStreamCompiler.cs:208-211). That placeholder rest is skipped by the `if (!note.IsRest)` guard at line 76, so `noteEvents` stays empty and line 93-95 prints "(no notes in sequence)". Confirmed by repro and by the control case (a plain `| C4q D4q E4q F4q |` sequence renders a correct piano roll). Audio (BarRenderer.cs:62), MIDI (MidiExport.cs:483), MusicXML (MusicXmlExport.cs:247), and LilyPond (LilyPondExport.cs:159) all branch on ParallelVoices correctly — only this REPL display tool omits the branch.
repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'use "@std" timesig 4/4 { Sequence vb = | {voice C4w} {voice E4q F4q G4q A4q} | (visualize vb) }' -> prints '(no notes in sequence)'
suggestedFix: After the `foreach (var note in bar.MusicalNotes)` loop (line 84), add a parallel-voice pass: when `bar.ParallelVoices` is non-null/non-empty, iterate each voice sub-bar and run the SAME note-event collection logic, but with a FRESH per-voice beat cursor that starts at `offsetBeats` (all voices share the bar onset, mirroring BarRenderer.cs:62-77 which renders each voice from offset 0 within the bar). Use each voice sub-bar's own `MusicalNotes` and its own `TimeSignature` (falling back to `bar.TimeSignature` when null, as BarRenderer does at line 71-72). This makes overlapping voices stack on their respective pitch rows. Note that when ParallelVoices is present the parent bar's MusicalNotes is just the placeholder rest, so the existing line-72 loop is effectively a no-op for those bars and the two passes do not double-count.

title: euclidean throws InvalidOperationException on degenerate inputs instead of charitable WarnOnce advisory
finding: All three euclidean overloads (lines 1651, 1725, 1748) use throw new InvalidOperationException(...) for hits<=0, steps<=0, steps>1024, and hits>steps. This violates the project-wide D-v1.5-05 charitable interpretation policy (degenerate inputs -> sane default + stderr advisory, not an error). The exception bubbles up as '0:0: error: Unexpected error: euclidean: hits must be > 0' with no line number, losing the source location. Every other generative primitive (markov, lsystem, cellular, lorenz) uses RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce and returns an empty result or clamped value.
rootCause: All three `euclidean` overloads guard degenerate inputs (hits<=0, steps<=0, steps>1024, hits>steps) with `throw new InvalidOperationException(...)`. These throws are uncaught until FlowEngine.Execute's top-level catch (flow-lang/Core/FlowEngine.cs:400-403), which reports `Unexpected error: {ex.Message}` at `SourceLocation.Unknown`. Confirmed by running the repro: `(euclidean 0 8 C4)` yields `0:0: error: Unexpected error: euclidean: hits must be > 0` — the source line is lost (always 0:0) and the whole script halts. This contradicts the documented project-wide generative contract: CLAUDE.md's Generative section lists euclidean among the generative primitives and states "Charitable interpretation throughout (D-v1.5-05 + PAT-02) — degenerate inputs -> input + advisory, never throws." Every sibling generative primitive follows that contract via `RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce` plus a Phase-44 Pattern-S3 strict-mode `ctx.ErrorReporter.ReportError` branch: CellularFunctions.cs (ClampDimensionWithAdvisory / WrapRuleWithAdvisory at lines ~388/416/432, including an identical `> 1024` DoS guard handled by clamp+WarnOnce), ChaosFunctions.cs (length<=0 -> empty + WarnOnce, length>100_000 -> clamp + WarnOnce), LsystemFunctions.cs, and MarkovFunctions.cs. euclidean is the lone outlier because its guards were authored in Phase 15 (planning docs 15-04-PLAN.md explicitly specify the throws) before the charitable-generative policy was uniformly applied in Phase 36. This is NOT charitable-by-design and is NOT a 'should error instead of being charitable' complaint — it is the inverse: a documented-contract violation plus a broken diagnostic (0:0 'Unexpected error' with no line number).
repro: dotnet run --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'use "@generative" Sequence eu = (euclidean 0 8 C4)'
suggestedFix: Replace the four `throw new InvalidOperationException(...)` statements in each of the three overloads (lines 1651-1654, 1725-1728, 1748-1751) with charitable clamp/empty-return plus advisory, mirroring CellularFunctions.ClampDimensionWithAdvisory. Thread the ExecutionContext (already captured by RegisterEuclideanOverloads; the 3-arg overload registered around line 1645 needs it passed in too) and follow Pattern S3: when ctx.CallerStrictMode is true, call ctx.ErrorReporter.ReportError(...) at ctx.CurrentCallSite (preserving the source location instead of 0:0); otherwise RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce. Specifically: hits<=0 or steps<=0 -> emit `[euclidean] hits/steps must be > 0 at {site}; returning empty sequence` and return Value.Sequence(new SequenceData()); steps>1024 -> clamp steps to 1024 + WarnOnce (matching the T-36-19 cellular DoS-guard wording, which preserves the original security intent while staying charitable); hits>steps -> clamp hits to steps + advisory `[euclidean] hits {hits} > steps {steps}; clamped to {steps}`. This brings euclidean in line with the documented generative contract, restores the source line in diagnostics, and keeps the Phase-15 T-15-08 DoS protection (the >1024 case becomes a clamp rather than an unbounded Bjorklund allocation).

title: NoteStreamCompiler weight-sum warnings spam stderr via Console.Error.WriteLine instead of WarnOnce
finding: CompileRandomChoiceElement calls Console.Error.WriteLine directly (lines 965, 972, 1010, 1021, 1036, 1059) rather than using RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce. The weight-sum warning at line 972 fires once per note element: a bar with four (? C4:30 E4:30)q elements produces four identical 'Warning: random choice weights sum to 60, not 100. Normalizing.' lines on stderr. Confirmed by running the repro. This also bypasses the WASM redirect that Phase 48 routes stderr advisories through (D-48-15 stdout/stderr split), so these warnings do not appear in RunResult.stderr on the Web target.
rootCause: CompileRandomChoiceElement is called once per (?...) element in a note stream (call sites at NoteStreamCompiler.cs:143 and :275) with no deduplication. The weight-sum advisory at line 972 (and the sum-to-0 advisory at 965) uses Console.Error.WriteLine directly instead of the project's canonical RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce sentinel-dedup channel. Every element whose weights do not total 100 emits an identical line, so a bar of four (? C4:30 E4:30)q elements prints four identical 'Warning: random choice weights sum to 60, not 100. Normalizing.' lines. Repro confirmed: the cited CLI command emits exactly 4 identical lines. This contradicts the documented dedup discipline: RenderingDiagnostics.cs:16-17 states the wrapper exists 'so iterative REPL workflows don't flood the console,' and ExecutionContext.cs:546-551 (Phase 44 CR-03) explicitly calls out hot-loop advisory sites that 'bury any real problem the composer was looking for' as the reason to gate on a per-key sentinel. The render itself is correct and deterministic (the warnings fire deterministically and do not affect audio bytes, voices, or note selection) — this is console noise only, hence low severity. The same direct-Console.Error pattern at the variable-reference sites (1010, 1021, 1036, 1059) is per-element too but is a lesser case (those usually indicate a genuine one-off authoring mistake).
repro: dotnet run --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'use "@std" use "@audio" tempo 120 { timesig 4/4 { Sequence s = | (? C4:30 E4:30)q (? C4:30 E4:30)q (? C4:30 E4:30)q (? C4:30 E4:30)q | section main { Sequence v = s } Song song = [main] Buffer mix = (renderSong song "piano") (writeWav "/tmp/t.wav" mix) } }' 2>&1 | grep Warning
suggestedFix: Route the random-choice advisories through RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce keyed by choice.Location so each distinct stream site warns at most once per process. E.g. at line 972: RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce($"random-choice-weight:{choice.Location}", $"[note-stream] random choice weights at {choice.Location} sum to {totalWeight} (not 100); treating as relative weights and normalizing"); and at line 965 similarly with key "random-choice-weight0:{choice.Location}". Add 'using FlowLang.Diagnostics;'. Optionally reword to drop the implication that 100 is required, since normalizing relative weights is intended behavior.

title: MarkovFunctions.EncodePitchDurationState documents parameter as 'quarter-note units' but stores NoteValueType enum slot — misleading naming risks future corruption
finding: EncodePitchDurationState parameter is named durationQuarterUnits and the class xmldoc says 'duration in quarter-note units occupies the high 20 bits'. In reality, the caller passes note.DurationValue which is a NoteValueType.Value enum integer (WHOLE=0, HALF=1, QUARTER=2, EIGHTH=3, SIXTEENTH=4, etc.) — NOT quarter-note units (where quarter=1, half=2, whole=4). The round-trip works correctly because the same enum integer is encoded and decoded unchanged, but if any future code path interprets the stored value as actual quarter-note units it will produce wrong pitches/durations. Confirmed: ExtractStates (line 429) passes note.DurationValue directly as durationQuarterUnits.
rootCause: The misnomer is real and exactly as described. EncodePitchDurationState's second parameter is named durationQuarterUnits (line 87) and the class xmldoc (lines 50-51, 75-76) says "duration in quarter-note units occupies the high 20 bits." But ExtractStates (line 429) passes note.DurationValue, which is a NoteValueType.Value enum slot — verified in TypeSystem/SpecialTypes/NoteValueType.cs:24-31 as WHOLE=0, HALF=1, QUARTER=2, EIGHTH=3, SIXTEENTH=4, THIRTYSECOND=5, SIXTYFOURTH=6, ONETWENTYEIGHTH=7 — NOT quarter-note units (where quarter=1, half=2, whole=4). MusicalNoteData.DurationValue is confirmed to be that enum slot (NoteType.cs:392 casts it directly as (NoteValueType.Value)DurationValue.Value; ProgressionCompiler.cs:213 comments "DurationValue=0 = WHOLE"). The decode tuple field is named DurationQuarterUnits (line 99) and BuildSequenceFromStates (line 598) re-stores it as an enum slot. This is purely a naming/documentation defect with NO behavioral impact: the round-trip is lossless because the same integer is encoded and decoded unchanged, and grep confirms the only callers are ExtractStates/BuildSequenceFromStates plus a round-trip test (MarkovModelTests.cs:309-323 using values 2 and 7, consistent with enum-slot semantics). No code path interprets the stored value as actual quarter-note units, so the "future corruption" risk is hypothetical. This is the lowest-impact kind of finding — a cosmetic naming/doc discrepancy, not wrong audio, lost notes, truncation, or a wrong-type defect; charity does not hide a real behavioral bug here.
repro: Read flow-lang/StandardLibrary/Generative/MarkovFunctions.cs lines 87-93 and 418-438; compare the NoteValueType.Value enum definition (WHOLE=0..ONETWENTYEIGHTH=7) against the stated 'quarter-note units' semantic.
suggestedFix: Documentation/naming-only change, no behavioral edit. Rename the parameter at line 87 from durationQuarterUnits to durationEnumSlot and the local at line 91 accordingly; rename DecodePitchDurationState's return field (line 99) from DurationQuarterUnits to DurationEnumSlot. Fix the xmldoc at lines 50-51 and 75-76 to read "NoteValueType.Value enum slot (WHOLE=0, HALF=1, QUARTER=2, ... ONETWENTYEIGHTH=7) occupies the high bits" and correct the bit-layout text (the code is (d << 12) | p — pitch low 12 bits, duration shifted by 12 — so the doc's "(pitch << 20)" is also inaccurate and should say "(durationEnumSlot << 12) | pitch12"). title: flow-interpreter never loads ~/.config/flow/config.toml — sfz_root and all other config keys silently ignored
finding: flow-interpreter/Program.cs (and ScriptRunner.cs / LiveReloadManager.cs) never call FlowConfigLoader.LoadFromXdg(). FlowConfig.Active stays at its Defaults singleton (all null) for every script run via 'dotnet run --project flow-interpreter'. As a result, sfz_root is always null — loadSfz #violin fires the WarnOnce advisory and immediately throws 'SFZ root directory not configured', even though ~/.config/flow/config.toml contains a valid sfz_root entry. The same miss silently drops default_tempo, default_timesig, default_audio_device, and stdlib_search_path for the interpreter path. Only flow-cli/Program.cs calls FlowConfigLoader.LoadFromXdg() (at line 16). Confirmed: 'dotnet run --project flow-interpreter -- examples/sweep/sfz_articulation.flow' exits 1 with the sfz_root error; 'dotnet run --project flow-cli -- run examples/sweep/sfz_articulation.flow' exits 0 and produces a 7.2 MB WAV.
rootCause: flow-interpreter/Program.cs Main() (line 7) never calls FlowConfigLoader.LoadFromXdg(), so for every `dotnet run --project flow-interpreter <script>` invocation FlowConfig.Active stays pointed at FlowConfigPoco.Defaults (all keys null — confirmed flow-lang/Runtime/FlowConfig.cs:69 and SfzRoot default null at FlowConfig.cs:39/48). Only flow-cli/Program.cs:16 loads the TOML. Because FlowConfigLoader (Tomlyn-backed) lives in flow-cli/Config/FlowConfigLoader.cs and flow-cli already references flow-interpreter (flow-cli.csproj:16), the interpreter cannot reference it without a circular dependency, and Tomlyn 2.3.2 is referenced only by flow-cli.csproj:23. Net effect: ~/.config/flow/config.toml is silently ignored on the interpreter path. The most visible symptom is SFZ: ResolveSfzRoot (flow-lang/StandardLibrary/Audio/Sfz/SfzBuiltins.cs:271-301) sees SfzRoot==null and throws InvalidOperationException("SFZ root directory not configured") — a hard exit-1 — even though config.toml contains a valid sfz_root. default_tempo / default_timesig / default_audio_device / stdlib_search_path are also dropped (degrade silently to baked-in 120 BPM / 4/4 / no override).
repro:
dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- examples/sweep/sfz_articulation.flow
# Output: [sfz] sfz_root not configured ... error: SFZ root directory not configured
# Even though ~/.config/flow/config.toml has sfz_root = "/home/noah/.flow/samples/VSCO-2-CE-1.1.0"
suggestedFix: Make the interpreter load config before constructing any FlowEngine, exactly as flow-cli does. title: SViolinVib.sfz uses 'ampeg_dynamic' and 'tune' opcodes not in the 20-opcode whitelist — charitably ignored but may affect timbre
finding: SViolinVib.sfz declares two opcodes not in the KnownOpcodes whitelist: 'ampeg_dynamic' (controls the ADSR response to velocity, i.e. how much ampeg_attack / ampeg_release scale with velocity) and 'tune' (fine pitch offset in cents, equivalent to Flow's centOffset). The SFZ parser charitably WarnOnce-advisories them and continues. The ampeg_dynamic miss means the sampled violin does not vary its envelope shape with velocity as intended — all velocities share the same ADSR shape. The tune miss means the patch's per-region fine-tuning (VSCO-CE uses tune to compensate for slight pitch drift in samples) is ignored, potentially causing subtle out-of-tune artifacts on notes far from the sample keycenter.
rootCause: VERIFIED by running the code. The canonical #violin patch /home/noah/.flow/samples/VSCO-2-CE-1.1.0/SViolinVib.sfz declares two opcodes outside the 20-opcode KnownOpcodes whitelist (SfzParser.cs:84-108): `ampeg_dynamic=1` (file line 18, <global>) and `tune=-20` (file line 75, a single <region> for sample LLVln_ArcoVib_C4_p.wav covering MIDI 59-61, vel 0-62). Loading it by absolute path emitted exactly: "[sfz] unrecognized opcode 'ampeg_dynamic' in 'SViolinVib' — ignoring" and "[sfz] unrecognized opcode 'tune' in 'SViolinVib' — ignoring" (SfzParser.cs:340-356 WarnOnce path). The `tune` miss is a genuine wrong-audio defect that charity hides: SfzRenderer computes pitch as integer `semitonesShift = targetMidi - region.PitchKeycenter` (SfzRenderer.cs:239) and SfzRegion has no TuneCents field, so the -20-cent correction VSCO authored to compensate that sample's recorded pitch drift is silently dropped — Flow renders that one region ~20 cents sharp. The `ampeg_dynamic` half is effectively a non-issue: Flow layers its own Phase 28 articulation ADSR on top of the sample, so VSCO's velocity-dynamic-envelope flag is largely subsumed by Flow's envelope model. Determinism is preserved (deterministic ignore). Scope is narrow: 1 of 30 regions, vel<=62, ~3-semitone band, 20 cents subtle — hence low. Note: examples/sweep/sfz_articulation.flow could not drive the repro via #violin because sfz_root resolution failed in this env ('sfz_root not configured' despite config.toml), so I reproduced via the loadSfz absolute-path overload instead — same parser path, advisories confirmed.
repro:
dotnet run --no-build --project flow-cli -- run examples/sweep/sfz_articulation.flow 2>&1 | grep 'unrecognized'
# [sfz] unrecognized opcode 'ampeg_dynamic' in 'SViolinVib' — ignoring
# [sfz] unrecognized opcode 'tune' in 'SViolinVib' — ignoring
suggestedFix: Add `tune` (and optionally `transpose`) to KnownOpcodes; parse via ReadDouble as signed cents (SFZ range -100..+100). Add `double TuneCents = 0.0` to the SfzRegion record and set it in BuildRegion (`double tuneCents = ReadDouble(region, "tune", 0.0, patchDescription);`). In SfzRenderer.RenderInternal, fold region.TuneCents into the playback pitch alongside semitonesShift: convert to a fractional-semitone varispeed ratio multiplier using the existing RatioMath.CentOffsetMultiplier(region.TuneCents) (already used by Phase 23/32 cent-offset paths), applied to the varispeed ratio before resampling. Keep TuneCents=0 byte-identical to today (Phase 33/34 baselines: CentOffsetMultiplier(0)=1.0 is an exact identity, so pinned WAVs are unaffected). For `ampeg_dynamic`, the claim's no-op-with-advisory is the right call — add it to the whitelist parsed as an ignored flag with a one-shot 'recognized but not modeled — Flow applies its own articulation envelope' advisory, so it stops surfacing as 'unrecognized opcode'.

title: Non-4/4 time signatures render at wrong wall-clock speed (6/8 is 2x too slow, 2/2 is 2x too fast)
finding: GetBeats(timeSigDenominator) returns fraction-of-whole x denominator (denominator-unit beats), but SynthUtils.BeatsToSeconds(beats, bpm) and MixVoicesToStereoBuffer both treat the result as quarter-note beats (secondsPerBeat = 60/bpm where bpm is quarters-per-minute). This is accidentally correct only for 4/4 (denominator=4, scaling factor=1). For 6/8 (denom=8): quarter note returns GetBeats(8)=2.0, BeatsToSeconds(2.0,120)=1.0s, but correct is 0.5s — 2x too long. For 2/2 (denom=2): half note returns GetBeats(2)=1.0, BeatsToSeconds(1.0,120)=0.5s, but correct is 1.0s — 2x too short. Same factor applies to BarLengthBeats (uses Numerator as quarter-beats) and MixVoicesToStereoBuffer (totalFrames = totalBeats x secondsPerBeat x sampleRate). Confirmed: a single C4e in a 6/8 bar at 120BPM produces 3.0s WAV; expected 1.5s bar duration.
rootCause: NoteType.GetBeats(int timeSigDenominator) (line 392-394) returns `NoteValueType.ToFraction(value) * timeSigDenominator`. ToFraction returns the note's fraction-of-a-WHOLE-note (QUARTER=0.25, EIGHTH=0.125, HALF=0.5 — verified NoteValueType.cs:67-90). Multiplying by the denominator yields DENOMINATOR-UNIT beats (number of beats where one beat = one denominator-unit note), NOT quarter-note beats. This is internally self-consistent across BarType.ToTimeline/GetActualBeats/ValidateDuration and SequenceType.BarLengthBeats (all in denominator-units, bar total == Numerator), but every wall-clock/tick conversion assumes QUARTER-note beats: SynthUtils.BeatsToSeconds = beats/bpm*60 and SongRenderer.MixVoicesToStereoBuffer secondsPerBeat = 60/bpm (SongRenderer.cs:372-378) treat bpm as quarters-per-minute; MidiExport.cs:494/502/555/562 multiply GetBeats(denom) by ticksPerQuarter against a per-quarter SetTempoEvent (line 400). The factor (denominator/4) is exactly 1.0 only for denominator=4, so it is accidentally correct for 4/4 and wrong for every other meter. The codebase even documents the intended contract incorrectly: MidiFunctions.cs:489-490,512 and NoteType.cs:377-379 assert GetBeats returns "quarter-relative" beats, but the power-of-2 path does not. Empirically verified by rendering: 4/4 four quarters @120BPM = 2.0000s (correct); 6/8 six eighths @120BPM = 3.0000s (should be 1.5s, 2x too slow); 2/2 two halves @120BPM = 1.0000s (should be 2.0s, 2x too fast). This is wrong audio AND wrong MIDI for all non-4/4 meters, not charitable-by-design. Note the beat-true-to-sig pragma in the repro is a red herring — it only affects Beat literals and (beat N) via BeatConstructorFunctions.cs:29, never note-stream durations through GetBeats.
repro: Run examples/beat/intro.flow and measure /tmp/beat_intro.wav. The 6/8 jig (4 bars x 6 eighths at 120BPM) should be 4 x 1.5s = 6.0s. Actual is 12.0s — 2x too long. Alternatively: tempo 120 { timesig 6/8 { section s { Sequence x = | C4e C4e C4e C4e C4e C4e | } Song g=[s] Buffer b=(renderSong g "piano") (writeWav "/tmp/t68.wav" b) } } -> actual 3.0s, expected 1.5s.
suggestedFix: Make GetBeats return universal quarter-note units. In NoteType.cs:392-394 change `return fraction * timeSigDenominator;` to `return fraction * 4.0;` (the timeSigDenominator parameter becomes unused on the power-of-2 path; keep the signature for the DurationFraction branch which is already quarter-correct). Then convert the companion bar-capacity/validation sites from raw Numerator (denominator-units) to quarter-units so internal consistency holds: SequenceType.cs:64 `double numerator = bar.TimeSignature!.Numerator * 4.0 / bar.TimeSignature.Denominator;` (and the ParallelVoices branch line 66 returns the same converted value); BarType.GetActualBeats (BarType.cs:148) fallback `TimeSignature?.Numerator ?? 4` -> `(TimeSignature != null ? TimeSignature.Numerator * 4.0 / TimeSignature.Denominator : 4.0)`; BarType.ValidateDuration (BarType.cs:170) compare `totalBeats <= TimeSignature.Numerator * 4.0 / TimeSignature.Denominator`; NoteStreamCompiler.CalculateAutoFitDuration totalBeats (NoteStreamCompiler.cs:542) `double totalBeats = timeSig.Numerator * 4.0 / timeSig.Denominator;`. (NoteStreamCompiler.cs:325 barCapacity is already correct: Numerator*4/Denominator.) No change needed in BeatsToSeconds, MixVoicesToStereoBuffer, MidiExport, or MidiFunctions — once GetBeats and Numerator-derived totals are all quarter-units, the existing 60/bpm and ticksPerQuarter math becomes correct. Verify with RMS baselines under flow-lang.Tests/baselines/Phase28 (4/4 fixtures must stay byte-identical since factor=1) and re-render the three repros to confirm 6/8 bar = 1.5s and 2/2 bar = 2.0s. The change is deterministic, so two-run cmp-clean is preserved.

title: (str 1.0) drops the decimal point — prints '1' not '1.0'
finding: (str Double) uses C#'s default double-to-string conversion which omits the trailing .0 for whole-number doubles. (str 1.0) -> '1', (str 2.0) -> '2', (str 0.5) -> '0.5'. This makes the beat-literal display in the sweep print '1 quarters' and '2 quarters' where the file comments expect '1.0 quarters' and '2.0 quarters'. Low impact but can confuse composers comparing values.
rootCause: Whole-number doubles print without a trailing ".0". Confirmed live: `(str 1.0)`->`1`, `(str 2.0)`->`2`, `(str 0.5)`->`0.5`; and examples/sweep/tuplets_beat.flow prints `2b = 1 quarters` / `1b = 2 quarters` / `2b = 4 quarters` where the inline comments anticipate `1.0`/`2.0`/`4.0`. The claim's behavior is REAL but its cited location is WRONG: `StdLib.StrDouble` (flow-lang/StandardLibrary/StdLib.cs:57-60) merely delegates to `Value.ToString()`, which formats doubles with `d.ToString("G10")` at flow-lang/Runtime/Value.cs:425 — and `G10` strips the trailing `.0` for integral values. The beat-literal sweep actually exercises a SECOND, independent path: `StdLib.StrBeat` (flow-lang/StandardLibrary/StdLib.cs:174-177) uses `$"{args[0].As<double>()}"` (default shortest-round-trip format), which likewise drops `.0`. Both paths verified to produce `1`/`2` for 1.0/2.0 via an isolated C# program. This is purely cosmetic: the stored numeric value is correct (2b genuinely equals 1 quarter), no audio is wrong, no notes/voices lost, and formatting is deterministic (no two-run cmp violation). It is NOT charitable-by-design — there is no advisory and no documented contract requiring `.0` to be dropped; D-14 (StdLib.cs:166) only says (str Beat) prints the quarter-relative double, which it does. So it does not hide a defect and is correctly rated low/cosmetic.
repro:
dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'Double x = 1.0; (print (str x))'
# Output: 1
# Expected: 1.0
suggestedFix: If `.0` display is desired, fix at BOTH double-formatting sites, not the str registration in BuiltInFunctions.cs (which the claim misnames). The claim's proposed `d.ToString("F0") + ".0"` is unsafe — F0 truncates fractional precision near integers and mishandles large/scientific magnitudes, breaking round-trip. Use a precision-preserving integral check instead. In flow-lang/Runtime/Value.cs:425 replace `return d.ToString("G10");` with: `var s = d.ToString("G10"); return (double.IsFinite(d) && !s.Contains('.') && !s.Contains('E') && !s.Contains('e')) ? s + ".0" : s;`. Apply the equivalent guard in flow-lang/StandardLibrary/StdLib.cs:176 (StrBeat) on its interpolated string. Given low/cosmetic severity, an acceptable alternative is to leave the engine as-is and simply correct the inline `(expect 1.0 ...)` comments in examples/sweep/tuplets_beat.flow to match the shortest-form output (`expect 1`, `expect 2`, `expect 4`).

title: JI/Pythagorean pragma produces wrong frequencies for non-C-major keys
finding: When `enable justIntonation;` or `enable pythagorean;` is active and a `key X { }` block with X != C is in scope, every note renders at a musically wrong frequency. The root cause is in `NoteToFrequency(MusicalNoteData note, RenderTuning tuning)` at lines 98-112: `tonicHz = RatioMath.TonicHzFromKey(tuning.TonicLetter, 0, note.Octave)` gives the 12-TET frequency of the TONIC LETTER at the note's octave, then multiplies by a C-relative ratio from TuningTables. For key=Cmajor this is correct (tonic letter is C, C_ratio=1.0). For key=Gmajor, G4's tonic_hz = 12TET-G4 = 392 Hz, then multiplied by G's C-relative ratio (3/2), giving 588 Hz (D5) instead of G4 (392 Hz). G3 in G major JI renders at ~294 Hz (D4) instead of ~196 Hz. All JI/Pythagorean unit tests (PitchConversionTuningFacts, TuningRatioFacts, SpellingAwareTuningFacts) use only tonic='C'; no non-C key tests exist. The C-relative ratio tables in TuningTables.cs are correct; the bug is in how the tonic anchor is applied.
rootCause: In NoteToFrequency(MusicalNoteData, RenderTuning) the non-12-TET path computes freq = TonicHzFromKey(tonicLetter, tonicAlteration, octave) * LookupRatio(system, mode, noteLetter, alteration). The anchor (tonicHz) is the 12-TET frequency of the TONIC LETTER, but the ratio from TuningTables is C-RELATIVE — every table in TuningTables.cs has ['C']=1.0 and lists each letter's ratio measured from C, not from the tonic. The product therefore double-counts the tonic's own interval from C for any key whose tonic != C. For C major the bug is invisible because C's ratio is 1.0. Confirmed end-to-end: SongRenderer.ResolveRenderTuning (SongRenderer.cs:256-272) sets TonicLetter='G'/Mode=Major for `key Gmajor`, RatioMath.TonicHzFromKey (RatioMath.cs:15-16) returns 12-TET G, and LookupRatio('G' in JI Major) returns 3/2 — so the tonic G renders 1.5x too high. Empirically reproduced: G4 under `enable justIntonation; key Gmajor` peaks at 588 Hz (a D5) instead of ~392 Hz (the G4 tonic); the C-major control renders G4 correctly at 392.44 Hz (Goertzel power 4.99e15 at 588Hz for Gmajor vs 2.92e15 at 392Hz for Cmajor). The same defect applies to Pythagorean and to every mode/key with a non-C tonic. No existing test exercises a non-C tonic through NoteToFrequency: every `new RenderTuning(...)` in flow-lang.Tests/Unit/Phase23 + Integration/Phase23 uses tonic 'C'; TuningModeShiftFacts only tests LookupRatio letter-by-letter (which confirms the tables are C-relative, e.g. JI Dorian 'A' -> 5/3).
suggestedFix: Normalize the looked-up ratio by the tonic's OWN C-relative ratio so the result becomes tonic-relative: at PitchConversion.cs line ~99, compute `double tonicRatio = TuningTables.LookupRatio(tuning.System, tuning.Mode, tuning.TonicLetter, tuning.TonicAlteration);` then divide every ratio by it: `ratio = TuningTables.LookupRatio(tuning.System, tuning.Mode, note.NoteName, note.Alteration) / tonicRatio;` (and apply the same `/ tonicRatio` in the KeyNotFoundException chromatic-fallback branch at line 110). This makes freq = tonic_12TET_hz * (note_C_ratio / tonic_C_ratio), so the tonic renders at exactly its 12-TET reference Hz and intervals are measured from the tonic. C major stays byte-identical (tonicRatio = 1.0). Caveat the claim itself notes and which is correct: the C-anchored mode tables encode mode-specific commas relative to C, so for a transposed key the divided ratios reproduce the correct tonic and overall interval skeleton but a few non-tonic diatonic degrees can land on the wrong comma (e.g. the second above the tonic comes out 10/9 rather than 9/8); a fully correct fix builds a per-tonic table by rotating the mode pattern onto the new root. Add regression tests with a non-C tonic (e.g. assert G4 ~= 392 Hz under JI/Pyth Gmajor) since none exist today.

title: `(loadScala "path.scl")` resolves paths CWD-relative, unlike `use "file.flow"` which is script-relative
finding: ScalaBuiltins.LoadScalaOneArg calls `File.ReadAllText(sclPath)` directly at line 77 (and line 89 for the two-arg overload). This resolves `sclPath` relative to the process CWD, not relative to the calling .flow script's directory. By contrast, `use "file.flow"` goes through ModuleLoader.ResolvePath (ModuleLoader.cs:438) which uses `Path.GetDirectoryName(currentFile)` to resolve relative to the importing script. A composer placing a .scl file next to their .flow script and writing `(loadScala "my_scale.scl")` will succeed only when run from that script's directory; running with an absolute path like `dotnet run --project flow-interpreter /path/to/piece.flow` from a different directory will produce `error: Unexpected error: Could not find file '/cwd/my_scale.scl'`. The error message does not mention the path resolution asymmetry, making debugging difficult.
rootCause: ScalaBuiltins.LoadScalaOneArg (line 77) and LoadScalaTwoArg (lines 89, 91) call File.ReadAllText(sclPath/kbmPath) on the raw composer-supplied string with no path resolution. For a relative path this resolves against the process CWD (Directory.GetCurrentDirectory), not the calling .flow script's directory. By contrast, `use "file.flow"` is resolved script-relative through ModuleLoader.ResolvePath (ModuleLoader.cs:436-440: `Path.GetDirectoryName(currentFile)`). So colocating a .scl next to a .flow and running it from any other directory fails. The script path IS available to the engine — FlowEngine.Execute(source, fileName) (FlowEngine.cs:338) receives it from ScriptRunner.cs:24 — but it is never threaded down to the loadScala registry lambda. The not-found case is not charitable: File.ReadAllText throws FileNotFoundException, which is caught at FlowEngine.cs:402 and surfaced as a hard `Unexpected error: Could not find file '...'` that blocks the whole script and does not mention the resolution asymmetry.
repro:
# Create /tmp/test.flow with content: (loadScala "relative.scl")
# Run from project root: dotnet run --project flow-interpreter /tmp/test.flow
# -> error: Could not find file '/home/.../project_root/relative.scl' (looked in CWD, not /tmp/ where test.flow lives)
suggestedFix: Resolve relative .scl/.kbm paths against the current script directory, mirroring ModuleLoader.ResolvePath. Add a `string? CurrentScriptFile` property to ExecutionContext and set it in FlowEngine.Execute (the fileName param is already plumbed in from ScriptRunner.cs:24). Then in both LoadScalaOneArg (line 77) and LoadScalaTwoArg (lines 89, 91), before File.ReadAllText do: `if (!Path.IsPathRooted(p) && ctx?.CurrentScriptFile is string sf) p = Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(Path.GetDirectoryName(sf) ?? Environment.CurrentDirectory, p));` — falling back to CWD when no script context (REPL/eval). Optionally reuse ModuleLoader's AdditionalSearchPaths search-then-fallback ordering for parity with `use`. Verified empirically: from the script's own dir `(loadScala "relative.scl")` loads ('Tuning("12-tone equal temperament", 12 steps, ...'); from project root the identical script fails with 'Could not find file .../flow-sharp/relative.scl'.

title: `length` is documented in BuiltInDocs and CLAUDE.md but is not a callable function — only `len` is registered
finding: BuiltInDocs.cs line 36 has a documentation entry `["length"] = new("Returns the number of elements in an array or characters in a string.", ...)`. CLAUDE.md's collections builtin list also names `length`. However, BuiltInFunctions.cs only registers `"len"` for both String (line 162) and Array (line 579); no `"length"` function is registered. The REPL's `:help length` command will display documentation for a function that does not exist. Composers following the CLAUDE.md reference will write `(length arr)` and get `error: Function 'length' not found`. Verified: `(len (list 1 2 3))` returns 3; `(length (list 1 2 3))` errors.
rootCause: A documentation/registration mismatch. BuiltInDocs.cs:36 documents `length`, and CLAUDE.md:371 lists `length` in the Collections builtin reference, but the actual callable function is only ever registered as `len` (BuiltInFunctions.cs:164 for String, :581 for Array via StdLib.LenString / Collections.Len). A source-scoped grep (`*.cs` + `*.flow`, excluding bin/obj) confirms zero `proc length` declarations and zero `Register("length"...)` calls. Runtime repro confirmed: `(length (list 1 2 3))` -> `error: Function 'length' not found`, while `(len (list 1 2 3))` -> `3`. The `:help length` REPL command (Repl.cs:407 calls `BuiltInDocs.TryGet(name)`) would render documentation for a function that cannot be invoked — a doc surface that lies about callability. Not charitable-by-design: the failure is a hard 'Function not found' error, and the defect being hidden is a real one (the public docs/reference name a non-existent symbol). No wrong audio, no data loss, no determinism impact — purely composer-facing friction, hence low severity.
repro:
(length (list 1 2 3))
# -> error: Function 'length' not found
(len (list 1 2 3))
# -> 3
suggestedFix: Pick one of two corrections; option (a) is preferred per the project's ergonomics-first / charitable philosophy. (a) Register `length` as an alias for `len` in BuiltInFunctions.cs: alongside the existing `registry.Register("len", lenStrSignature, StdLib.LenString)` (line 164) add `registry.Register("length", new FunctionSignature("length", [StringType.Instance], ...), StdLib.LenString)`, and alongside `registry.Register("len", lenSignature, Collections.Len)` (line 581) add `registry.Register("length", new FunctionSignature("length", [new ArrayType(VoidType.Instance)], ...), Collections.Len)`. This makes the docs/CLAUDE.md truthful and welcomes composers from other languages who reach for `length`. (b) Alternatively, remove the `["length"]` entry at BuiltInDocs.cs:36 and change CLAUDE.md:371 from `length` to `len`. Either way the doc surface and the registry must agree. Adding the alias (a) is the lower-friction choice and is what the language's stated goals favor.

title: (if cond then else) evaluates BOTH branches unconditionally when branches are non-lazy expressions
line: 424-427 (IfStrict registration); root mechanism at flow-lang/Interpreter/ExpressionEvaluator.cs:306-313 (eager arg loop); self-documented at flow-lang/StandardLibrary/StdLib.cs:455-465 (IfStrict)
finding:
Calling (if false (print "THEN") (print "ELSE")) prints BOTH "THEN" and "ELSE". The lazy If overload [Bool, Lazy<Void>, Lazy<Void>] requires args to be wrapped in LazyExpression AST nodes, but the parser never auto-wraps them. At runtime, EvaluateFunctionCall eagerly evaluates all three args before dispatch: (print "THEN") and (print "ELSE") both fire, producing Void values. The OverloadResolver then picks IfStrict [Bool, Void, Void] (score 3000, all exact matches) over the lazy overload (score 0, Void does not match Lazy<Void>). IfStrict merely returns the already-computed selected branch — but both side effects have already fired. Return VALUE is correct; side effects are wrong. The same root cause makes (each arr (fn Int n => (if (gt n 0) (print "pos") (print "neg")))) print both branches on every element.
Minimal repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e '(if false (print "BUG-THEN") (print "ELSE"))'  -- prints both "BUG-THEN" and "ELSE".
rootCause: EvaluateFunctionCall (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:306-313) unconditionally evaluates ALL call arguments via Evaluate(call.Arguments[i]) in a single loop BEFORE overload resolution. The parser only ever produces a LazyExpression/Thunk for the explicit `lazy(...)` keyword (Parser.cs ParsePrimary:1382-1388) — it never auto-wraps the then/else branches of a builtin `(if ...)` call. So both branches are eagerly evaluated, yielding concrete (non-Thunk) values. The lazy If overload [Bool, Lazy<Void>, Lazy<Void>] (BuiltInFunctions.cs:416-419) cannot match concrete args, so the resolver selects the IfStrict overload [Bool, Void, Void] (BuiltInFunctions.cs:424-427), whose impl (StdLib.cs:461-465) merely returns the already-computed selected value: `return cond ? args[1] : args[2];`. The IfStrict doc-comment (StdLib.cs:455-459) explicitly acknowledges "Both branches are eagerly evaluated at the call site ... but only the selected value is returned" — but its claim to "Match the Lazy-if contract for concrete arguments" is false whenever a branch has a side effect OR can fail. Confirmed by repro: `(if false (print "THEN") (print "ELSE"))` prints BOTH; `(if true (print "THEN") (print "ELSE"))` ALSO prints both; the more severe guard case `(if (gt n 0) (idiv 10 n) (neg 1))` with n=0 throws "Integer division by zero" and `(if (empty (list)) "empty" (head (list)))` throws "Cannot get head of empty array" — i.e. `if` cannot guard against errors at all. The bug propagates into lambda bodies: `(each (list 1 (neg 1)) (fn Int n => (if (gt n 0) (print "pos") (print "neg"))))` prints pos AND neg per element. The lazy infrastructure itself works: `(if false lazy((print "THEN")) lazy((print "ELSE")))` correctly prints only "ELSE", proving the defect is solely the missing auto-wrap. The same systemic flaw also affects `and`/`or` (verified: `(and false (eq (print "RHS-FIRED") 1))` fires RHS-FIRED), since they use the identical lazy/strict dual-overload pattern — but the claim is scoped to `if`, which is conclusively confirmed.
repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e '(if false (print "THEN-BUG") (print "ELSE"))'
suggestedFix: Defer evaluation of the then/else branches so only the taken branch runs. Two viable approaches: (1) The claim's surgical parser fix — in Parser.cs where builtin calls are emitted, when the callee name is "if" (and "and"/"or" for the same class of bug), wrap argument expressions 2 and 3 (for if; 1 and 2 for and/or) in LazyExpression nodes so they arrive as Thunks and the existing lazy overload wins. This reuses the proven Thunk/Force path (StdLib.If at StdLib.cs:439-453). Value-producing branches still work because If calls Thunk.Force() and returns the inner value. (2) The more general interpreter fix — in EvaluateFunctionCall, when a resolved overload declares Lazy<T> parameter slots, defer those argument expressions by constructing Thunks (new Thunk(argExpr, this), per the LazyExpression path at ExpressionEvaluator.cs:1045) instead of eager Evaluate. Approach (2) fixes if/and/or and any future lazy-param builtin uniformly without parser name-coupling, but requires a two-pass (resolve-then-evaluate) restructure since resolution currently needs arg Types up front; the lazy slots can be typed as Lazy<Void> during resolution. Recommend (2) for robustness, or (1) as the minimal targeted patch. Either way, after fixing, the IfStrict overload (BuiltInFunctions.cs:424-427) becomes unnecessary for the side-effect/guard case and should be re-evaluated. Add a regression test: `(if false (print "T") (print "E"))` must print only "E", and `(if (empty (list)) "empty" (head (list)))` must return "empty" without error.

title: Symbol literal arms in pattern match (| #foo => ...) always fall through to wildcard
finding:
Pattern arm `| #kick => "bass drum"` never matches a #kick Symbol scrutinee — it always falls through to `| _ =>`. Root cause: at line 2048 the parser handles ALL TokenType.SymbolLiteral tokens in pattern position by creating a ConstructorPattern with IsArticulationSymbol=true and PreviousToken.Text as the name. PatternMatcher.MatchArticulation then tries Enum.TryParse<Articulation>(name) — for non-articulation symbols like #kick, #snare, #jazz, etc., this parse fails and the method returns false. The Symbol value is never compared for equality; the arm always misses. Only Articulation enum member names (#staccato, #legato, #accent, #marcato, #tenuto, #sforzando) can ever match in pattern position.
Minimal repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'Symbol s = #kick; String r = (match s | #kick => "matched" | _ => "missed"); (print r)' -- prints "missed" instead of "matched".
rootCause: Confirmed by re-reading the cited code and running the repro. In Parser.cs:2048-2065 the parser routes EVERY TokenType.SymbolLiteral in pattern position into a ConstructorPattern{IsArticulationSymbol=true}, with no branch that distinguishes articulation keywords from general symbols. PatternMatcher.PatternMatches (PatternMatcher.cs:117-118) then dispatches all such patterns to MatchArticulation (PatternMatcher.cs:184-193), which has two independent failure paths for a general Symbol scrutinee: (1) line 186 requires `scrutinee.Data is MusicalNoteData` — a Symbol value never is, so it returns false immediately; (2) line 189 `Enum.TryParse<Articulation>(name)` fails for non-enum names like kick/snare/jazz. Result: `| #kick => ...` against a #kick Symbol scrutinee always misses and falls through to `| _ =>`. There is NO Symbol-equality path anywhere in PatternMatcher.cs (the only Symbol-related token there is an unrelated specificity comment at line 296). Repro confirmed: `dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'Symbol s = #kick; String r = (match s | #kick => "matched" | _ => "missed"); (print r)'` prints "missed". Even `#staccato` as a Symbol value misses (the scrutinee is a Symbol, not a MusicalNote). Meanwhile `(equals s #kick)` returns true, proving the interning/equality machinery (Value.Symbol + ExecutionContext.SymbolInternTable, Value.cs:169-177) exists and works — it is simply not wired into pattern matching. This is not charitable-by-design: the composer gets a silent wrong-branch selection with no advisory, which is the "charity hides a real defect" case (wrong control flow), not "degenerate input -> sane default + advisory". Severity corrected to medium (not high): it is a genuine language-feature correctness defect / violated reasonable contract (every other literal type matches in patterns; Symbol is a first-class equality type per SYM-01), but it does not corrupt rendered audio or lose notes/voices in the render pipeline — it is incorrect-but-recoverable in a relatively niche construct (Symbol scrutinee in match).
repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'Symbol s = #kick; String r = (match s | #kick => "matched" | _ => "missed"); (print r)'
suggestedFix: In Parser.cs around line 2048, distinguish articulation keyword symbols from general symbols at parse time. Compute the articulation set once (Enum.GetNames<Articulation>(), case-insensitive) and check PreviousToken.Text against it: if it is an articulation name, keep the existing ConstructorPattern{IsArticulationSymbol=true}; otherwise emit a Symbol-equality pattern. Cleanest is a small new SymbolPattern record (Name = PreviousToken.Text) plus a MatchSymbol helper in PatternMatcher that returns `scrutinee.Type is SymbolType && string.Equals((string)scrutinee.Data, name, StringComparison.Ordinal)` — i.e. require the scrutinee to actually be a Symbol value and compare the interned name (matching Value.Symbol's SymbolInternTable semantics, Value.cs:169-177), so it cannot collide with articulation matching on note scrutinees. A lower-touch alternative reuses LiteralPattern with the interned Symbol Value and extends MatchLiteral to special-case SymbolType via interned-name/pointer equality. Also wire the new pattern into PatternMatcher.SpecificityOf and Interpreter.cs:912 structural pattern-equality, and add the literal-Symbol arm to the music-aware specificity gate so its score is distinct from articulation/wildcard. Add a tests/test_*.flow covering `(match #kick | #kick => ... | _ => ...)` reaching the non-wildcard arm.

title: (zip a b) documented and has BuiltInDocs entry but is never registered — Function not found at runtime
finding:
CLAUDE.md lists `zip` in the Collections builtin section. BuiltInDocs.cs line 65 has an entry: ["zip"] = new("Combines two arrays into an array of pairs, stopping at the shorter length.", ...). However, no FunctionSignature for "zip" is registered anywhere in BuiltInFunctions.cs or Collections.cs. Calling (zip a b) at runtime yields error: Function 'zip' not found.
Minimal repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'Int[] a = (list 1 2); Int[] b = (list 3 4); (print (str (zip a b)))'
rootCause: `zip` is advertised as a Collections builtin in CLAUDE.md (line 371) and carries a documentation entry in BuiltInDocs.cs (line 65: `["zip"] = new("Combines two arrays into an array of pairs, stopping at the shorter length.", ...)`), which feeds the REPL `:help zip` meta-command. However, no `FunctionSignature` for "zip" is ever registered. Exhaustive grep across flow-lang/StandardLibrary/ (BuiltInFunctions.cs, Collections.cs, Collections/DictFunctions.cs, InternalFunctionRegistry) and every `.flow` stdlib module (collections.flow, std.flow) shows the ONLY source reference to the zip function is the BuiltInDocs entry — there is no registration call and no `.flow` proc definition. So the symbol resolves at doc-time but not at call-time. The codebase itself flags this in examples/sweep/collections.flow as "BUG-3".
repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e "Int[] a = (list 1 2); Int[] b = (list 3 4); (print (str (zip a b)))"
suggestedFix: Implement and register `zip` in RegisterCollections (flow-lang/StandardLibrary/BuiltInFunctions.cs), mirroring the `map`/`filter` wildcard-array pattern at BuiltInFunctions.cs:1067. Use a two-array wildcard signature: `new FunctionSignature("zip", [new ArrayType(VoidType.Instance), new ArrayType(VoidType.Instance)], parameterNames: ["a", "b"])` and register `registry.Register("zip", zipSignature, args => Collections.Zip(args, context));`. Add `Collections.Zip` that iterates both arrays to `min(a.Length, b.Length)` and emits an Array of 2-tuples (TupleValue `<<a@i, b@i>>`), matching the doc text "stopping at the shorter length" and the CLAUDE.md Tuple semantics. Add a test exercising `(zip a b)` to lock it. (Alternatively, if zip is not actually wanted, remove the BuiltInDocs entry and the CLAUDE.md Collections-list mention to stop advertising a non-callable function — but implementing it is the ergonomics-first choice consistent with the docs.)

title: PhaseVocoder returns +frameSize extra frames in #vocoder mode
finding:
PhaseVocoder.Process allocates outFrames = (int)Math.Round(inFrames * factor) + frameSize (line 99), so stretch(buf, 1.5, #vocoder) on a 2.0s / 88200-frame source produces 134348 frames (3.046s) instead of the expected 132300 frames (3.000s). The extra frameSize=2048 frames (46.4ms at 44100Hz) are boundary OLA padding that is never trimmed. Psola.Process correctly uses outFrames = (int)Math.Round(inFrames * factor) without the +frameSize addition. StretchEngine.ProcessAuto (the #auto path) works around this inconsistency via Math.Min(vocResult.Frames, psoResult.Frames) at line 171, so #auto picks the correct PSOLA length. But stretch(#vocoder) alone exposes the extra frames to the composer. Confirmed repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'use "@audio"
Buffer src = (createSineTone 440Hz 2.0 0.5)
Buffer s = (stretch src 1.5 #vocoder)
(writeWav "/tmp/t.wav" s)' — output is 3.046s not 3.0s. Note: the existing test (StretchVocoderTests.cs:52) uses a 2*FrameSize upper bound which masks the bug.
rootCause: PhaseVocoder.Process sizes the RETURNED AudioBuffer as `(int)Math.Round(inFrames * factor) + frameSize` (line 99), so a #vocoder stretch returns frameSize (2048 samples = ~46ms at 44.1kHz) more than the factor implies. Psola.Process uses `(int)Math.Round(inFrames * factor)` with no +frameSize addend (Psola.cs:81), so the two modes disagree on output length for the same factor. Verified by running the repro: stretch(createSineTone 440Hz 2.0, 1.5, #vocoder) -> /tmp/voc.wav = 134348 frames (3.0464s) while #psola -> /tmp/pso.wav = 132300 frames (3.0000s); 134348 - 132300 = exactly 2048 = frameSize. The extra frames are NOT benign silence: the final analysis frame (t=88064, zero-padded since only 136 real input samples remain) writes its synthesis window from sample 132096..134144, overshooting the expected 132300 by ~1844 samples, and the tail measured RMS 0.084 with a near-full-scale spike at the very end. The +frameSize headroom is legitimately needed for the INTERNAL OLA accumulation buffer (ProcessChannel allocates `new float[outFrames + frameSize]` at line 162 for exactly this), but it should not leak into the returned buffer length. StretchEngine.ProcessAuto (line 171) already works around the inconsistency via `Math.Min(vocResult.Frames, psoResult.Frames)`, which is why only the direct mode=#vocoder (and mode=#psola, which is the shorter one) path exposes the mismatch to composers. The class XML doc (lines 58-59) claims "round(input.Frames*factor) plus a single-frame boundary slack" — code adds a full frameSize, contradicting its own documented contract. pitchShift is unaffected because PitchShiftEngine resamples back to a fixed input.Frames length.
repro:
use "@audio"
Buffer src = (createSineTone 440Hz 2.0 0.5)
Buffer s_voc = (stretch src 1.5 #vocoder)
Buffer s_pso = (stretch src 1.5 #psola)
(writeWav "/tmp/voc.wav" s_voc)
(writeWav "/tmp/pso.wav" s_pso)
Note: voc.wav is 3.046s, pso.wav is 3.000s — should match
suggestedFix: In PhaseVocoder.Process change line 99 from `int outFrames = (int)Math.Round(inFrames * factor) + frameSize;` to `int outFrames = (int)Math.Round(inFrames * factor);`. The internal OLA buffer in ProcessChannel already adds its own +frameSize headroom (`new float[outFrames + frameSize]`, line 162) so it still has room for the final synthesis windows; the re-interleave copy at line 117 (`Math.Min(channelOutput.Length, outFrames)`) then naturally trims the returned buffer to the correct length, matching Psola.Process. This drops ~46ms of final-window OLA fade-out tail (mostly the reconstruction of the zero-padded last analysis frame), which is acceptable and is exactly what PSOLA already does. Verified non-breaking against existing tests: PhaseVocoderColaLevelTests uses MidRms + two-run equality (no absolute frame-count assertion), and StretchVocoderTests:52 (`expected - FrameSize, expected + 2*FrameSize`) still passes with the trimmed length. Tighten that assertion's upper bound from `expected + 2 * FrameSize` to `expected + 1` to pin the contract going forward. Update the class XML doc (lines 58-59) which currently mismatches the code.

title: lowpass/highpass/bandpass throw on Nyquist-boundary cutoff instead of clamping
finding:
Filter.ValidateCutoff throws ArgumentException when cutoffHz >= sampleRate/2 (Nyquist). At 44100Hz sample rate this means any cutoff >= 22050Hz crashes the interpreter session with '0:0: error: Unexpected error: Cutoff frequency (22050 Hz) must be below Nyquist frequency (22050 Hz)'. This violates the project's charitable-interpretation policy: a composer passing (lowpass buf 22000Hz) gets a crash instead of a silently clamped filter. Repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'use "@audio"
Buffer src = (createSineTone 440Hz 1.0 0.5)
Buffer lp = (lowpass src 22050.0)
(print "done")' exits with code 1.
rootCause: Filter.ValidateCutoff (Filter.cs:95-104) throws ArgumentException whenever cutoffHz >= Nyquist (sampleRate/2). The composer-facing wrappers LowpassFilter (EffectsFunctions.cs:155-165) and HighpassFilter (EffectsFunctions.cs:170-180) pass the raw cutoff straight through with no clamp and no try/catch, so the exception propagates to the interpreter top level and is surfaced as a session-killing 'Unexpected error', exiting code 1. Bandpass has the identical throw for highHz >= nyquist (Filter.cs:62-64). Verified by running the exact repro: `dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'use "@audio"...Buffer lp = (lowpass src 22050.0)...'` -> stderr '0:0: error: Unexpected error: Cutoff frequency (22050 Hz) must be below Nyquist frequency (22050 Hz).', EXIT CODE 1. A valid cutoff (8000.0) succeeds. This violates the documented charitable-interpretation policy (degenerate input -> sane default + stderr advisory, never a hard error). The codebase already establishes this exact pattern: the bandpass Q-clamp at Filter.cs:71-84 uses RenderingDiagnostics.WarnOnce, and FormantSynthesizer.cs:53 explicitly pre-clamps highHz to `sampleRate/2f - 1f` precisely to dodge this throw — internal callers defend against it, composer-facing builtins do not.
repro:
use "@audio"
Buffer src = (createSineTone 440Hz 1.0 0.5)
Buffer lp = (lowpass src 22050.0)
(print "done")
Note: exits code 1 with 'Cutoff frequency (22050 Hz) must be below Nyquist frequency'
suggestedFix: Make ValidateCutoff charitable instead of throwing on the Nyquist boundary. Change its signature to `private static float ValidateCutoff(float cutoffHz, int sampleRate)` and return a clamped value; have Lowpass/Highpass use the returned value when computing coefficients. For cutoffHz <= 0 clamp to 20 Hz with a WarnOnce ('[filter] cutoff <= 0 — clamped to 20 Hz'); for cutoffHz >= nyquist clamp to nyquist - 1f (matching the FormantSynthesizer convention) with a WarnOnce ('[filter] cutoff >= Nyquist — clamped'). In Lowpass (Filter.cs:18-27) and Highpass (Filter.cs:36-45) assign `cutoffHz = ValidateCutoff(cutoffHz, input.SampleRate);` then pass the clamped value to ComputeLowpass/HighpassCoefficients. Apply the same clamp-and-warn to Bandpass at Filter.cs:56-64 (clamp highHz to nyquist-1 and warn; also handle lowHz <= 0 charitably to 20 Hz, and the highHz <= lowHz case by widening to a minimal band rather than throwing). Mirror the WarnOnce(sentinelKey, message) style already used for the Q clamp at Filter.cs:79-82, which is the house pattern. This keeps two-run determinism (deterministic clamp, deterministic sentinel-deduped advisory to stderr) and stops a benign musical edge from killing the interpreter session.

title: swing N { } context block is a no-op — no render path reads MusicalContext.Swing
finding: swing is a reserved keyword and documented headline feature ('swing 0.6', used in this very showcase and in CLAUDE.md). But MusicalContext.Swing is ONLY written (Interpreter.cs:278), cloned (MusicalContext.cs:194), defaulted/resolved (ExecutionContext.cs:918,960), and stringified (MusicalContext.cs:254). An exhaustive grep shows it is NEVER read by NoteStreamCompiler, SongRenderer, any synthesizer, or the MIDI export path. Repro proves it: rendering an 8th-note line inside `swing 0.62 { }` produces a WAV byte-identical to the same line with NO swing block (cmp = IDENTICAL). By contrast `(quantize line EIGHTH 1.0 0.66)` DOES change the render (cmp = DIFFER). So the swing-context block silently does nothing to audio or MIDI — a jazz composer who writes `swing 0.62 { ... }` gets straight eighths.
rootCause: MusicalContext.Swing is a dead field with respect to rendering. It is written by Interpreter.ExecuteMusicalContext (Interpreter.cs:278), cloned (MusicalContext.cs:194), stringified (MusicalContext.cs:254), validated (IsValidSwing), and propagated/defaulted inside ExecutionContext.GetMusicalContext (lines 918 ??=, 944 loop-break condition, 960 default 0.5). Those ExecutionContext lines are the ONLY reads of .Swing in the entire flow-lang C# tree, and they are purely internal to context resolution — they never feed a timing computation. No render-path consumer reads it: grep for '.Swing' across flow-lang/ shows zero hits in NoteStreamCompiler, SongRenderer, SequenceRenderer, BarRenderer, any synthesizer, or MidiExport.cs. The actual swing timing math exists only in the unrelated quantize builtin (TransformFunctions.cs:485-519, swingOffset = swing * subdivBeats/2 applied to odd subdivisions), which reads its swing strictly from args[3], never from MusicalContext.Swing. So the swing N { } context block is a verified no-op on both WAV and MIDI output. Empirically confirmed: an 8th-note line rendered inside `swing 0.62 { }` produced a WAV byte-identical (cmp = IDENTICAL) to the same line with no swing block, while `(quantize line EIGHTH 1.0 0.66)` produced a different WAV (cmp = DIFFER). swing is a reserved keyword documented in CLAUDE.md as one of the six musical-context blocks, and the interpreter even validates its range — but it silently produces straight rhythm with no advisory, so a composer who writes swing 0.62 { } gets straight eighths. Charity here hides a real defect (wrong/missing musical effect, silently). Severity downgraded from the claimed high to medium: notes are correct and not lost/corrupted, output is recoverable via the documented quantize workaround, and there is no crash or data loss — it is a violated documented contract producing an incorrect-but-recoverable render (the rubric's medium band). requiresHardware=false: reproduced with offline writeWav on this Linux box, no audio device or hardware needed.
repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'use "@audio"\ntempo 120 { timesig 4/4 { swing 0.62 { section a { Sequence p = | C4e D4e E4e F4e G4e A4e B4e C5e | } Song s=[a] (writeWav "/tmp/on.wav" (renderSong s "piano")) } } }'  then the same without the swing block -> /tmp/off.wav ; cmp /tmp/on.wav /tmp/off.wav -> IDENTICAL
suggestedFix: Wire MusicalContext.Swing into the render path. Cleanest location is where note onsets are placed from the active context — SequenceRenderer/BarRenderer (or NoteStreamCompiler), reusing the existing quantize swing math from TransformFunctions.QuantizeBar: shift every odd subdivision by swingOffset = swing * (subdivBeats / 2). CRITICAL convention bridge: the context value is [0.0, 1.0] with 0.5 = straight (default resolved to 0.5 at ExecutionContext.cs:960), whereas the transform math uses [-1.0, 1.0] with 0 = straight. Map before applying, e.g. transformSwing = (contextSwing - 0.5) * 2, and short-circuit when transformSwing == 0 to preserve the byte-identical / two-run cmp-clean determinism contract (mirror the Pitfall 9 strength==0 && swing==0 identity guard in TransformFunctions.cs:150). Apply on the eighth-note subdivision grid against the active timesig so it composes with tempo/timesig blocks. If full wiring is deferred to v1.6, at minimum emit a one-shot stderr advisory from Interpreter.ExecuteMusicalContext when a swing block is entered (e.g. '[swing] swing-context block has no render effect yet — use quantize(seq, EIGHTH, strength, swing)') so the feature is not silently dead, and soften the CLAUDE.md presentation of swing 0.6 { } as functional.

title: Articulation on a chord bracket silently corrupts: [C4 E4 G4]q.stacc -> dotted chord + phantom rest, no articulation
line: 256-259 (main note-stream path); same gap at 792-795 (voice-block path)
finding: The chord-bracket parse path parses durSuffix, isDotted (Match(Dot)) and isTied but NEVER calls TryParseArticulation() — unlike NoteElement (line 361), RomanNumeral (636) and VariableReference (765). Consequences: (a) `[C4 E4 G4]q>` is a HARD parse error ('Unexpected token GreaterThan'); (b) `[C4 E4 G4]q.stacc` does NOT error and does NOT staccato — the `.` is consumed as isDotted=true (so the chord becomes a DOTTED quarter, i.e. WRONG DURATION), and `stacc` is then parsed as a separate lowercase variable reference, resolves to undefined, and is replaced by a REST (NoteStreamCompiler.cs:1021). So a single token of intended articulation silently produces: lost articulation + wrong chord duration + a spurious extra rest, surfaced only by a misleading 'undefined variable stacc' advisory. This is exactly the friction that forced this showcase to split its piano voicing onto single notes.
rootCause: The chord-bracket parse branch parses durSuffix, isDotted (Match(Dot)), and isTied but never calls TryParseArticulation() — unlike NoteElement, which calls it at all three of its parse sites (line 361 main path, 636 tuplet children, 765 voice block). The ChordElement record (Ast/Expressions/NoteStreamExpression.cs:41-47) has no Articulation field, so even if parsed it could not be carried. Consequences confirmed by live repro: (a) `[C4 E4 G4]q>` -> hard parse error 'Unexpected token GreaterThan' (the trailing > is not a valid note-stream-element start after a chord); (b) `[C4 E4 G4]q.stacc` -> no error and no staccato: the `.` is swallowed as isDotted=true at line 257 (chord silently becomes a DOTTED quarter = wrong duration), then `stacc` is parsed as a lowercase VariableReferenceElement (line 383-394), resolves to undefined, and NoteStreamCompiler.cs:1021 replaces it with a REST. Net result from valid-looking input: lost articulation + wrong chord duration + a phantom extra rest, surfaced only by a misleading 'undefined variable stacc' stderr advisory. This is charity hiding a real defect (wrong audio + lost notes), not charitable-by-design. Note: the claim mislabels lines 636/765 as 'RomanNumeral' and 'VariableReference' — they are actually NoteElement-in-tuplet and NoteElement-in-voice-block — but the asymmetry it asserts (NoteElement parses articulation, chord bracket does not) is fully correct and applies to both chord-bracket parse sites.
repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'tempo 120 { timesig 4/4 { Sequence s = | [C4 E4 G4]q.stacc D4q E4q F4q | (print "ok") } }'  -> prints "Warning: undefined variable 'stacc' in note stream, inserting rest" and "ok" (no error). Also: ...[C4 E4 G4]q>... -> 'Unexpected token GreaterThan'.
suggestedFix: Add an `Articulation? Articulation = null` field to the ChordElement record (NoteStreamExpression.cs:41-47). In BOTH chord-bracket parse branches — main path (after isTied at Parser.NoteStream.cs:258) and the voice-block path (after isTied at 794) — call `Articulation? artic = TryParseArticulation();` and pass it into the ChordElement constructor, mirroring NoteElement (line 361-363). Thread the articulation into CompileChordElement (NoteStreamCompiler.cs:831) so each emitted MusicalNoteData carries it, exactly as the per-note path does. This makes `[C4 E4 G4]q>` and `[C4 E4 G4]q.stacc` parse and render correctly (dotted-staccato chord). At absolute minimum, recognize a trailing articulation token so it is not silently re-interpreted as a dotted-duration + stray variable reference.

title: Rest-with-duration-suffix _q / _w lexes as an identifier -> bar rejected as 'Empty note stream'
finding: Notes attach their duration directly (C4q), so a composer naturally writes `_q` for a quarter rest. But SimpleLexer.cs:201 only emits TokenType.Underscore when `_` is NOT followed by a letter/digit/underscore — so `_q`/`_w`/`_h`/`_e`/`_s` lex as the identifier `_q` etc. In ParseNoteStream the identifier `_q` is not a duration (line 380) and char.IsLower('_') is false (line 383), so it is neither a duration nor a variable reference -> the loop breaks -> the bar yields zero elements -> 'Empty note stream' (line 412). Result: `| _w |` (a whole-bar rest — totally valid music, how an instrument lays out) and `| _q _q _q _q |` both fail to parse with a confusing error. Already acknowledged in-repo as a 'known parser bug' (examples/sweep/transforms_voices.flow:33-36). Workaround used here: bare `_` (duration inferred from bar) and ppp ghost bars for a laying-out instrument.
rootCause: The `_` case in SimpleLexer (line 197-203) only emits TokenType.Underscore when `_` is at end-of-input OR not followed by a letter/digit/underscore. So `_q`/`_w`/`_h`/`_e`/`_s` fall through to identifier scanning (line 230-232 -> ScanIdentifierOrKeyword) and lex as a single identifier token `_q`. In ParseNoteStream (Parser.NoteStream.cs), the rest path at line 90 requires TokenType.Underscore (never produced here); the identifier branch rejects `_q` because it is not a duration suffix (line 380 set is w/h/q/e/s/t) and `char.IsLower('_')` is false (line 383), so the variable-reference path is also skipped. The loop hits the unconditional `break` at line 401 with currentBarElements empty; for a bar whose only content was the rest, no NoteStreamBar is saved (line 405) and bars.Count==0 triggers `ReportError("Empty note stream", ...)` at line 412. Confirmed by repro: `| _w | C4w |` and `| _q _q _q _q |` both report "Empty note stream", while bare `| _ | C4w |` works. The defect is independently acknowledged in-repo as a "known parser bug" at examples/sweep/transforms_voices.flow:33-36. This is the same root cause as the transforms-voiceblocks `_q` finding (SimpleLexer underscore branch); both should be fixed by the same lexer change.
repro: dotnet run --no-build --project flow-interpreter -- -e 'tempo 120 { timesig 4/4 { Sequence s = | _w | C4w | (print "ok") } }'  -> '<eval>:1:40: error: Empty note stream'. With bare `_`: `| _ | C4w |` works.
suggestedFix: Symmetric with note literals (`C4q`), rests should accept a duration suffix (`_q`). Two clean options: (1) Lexer fix at SimpleLexer.cs:197-203 — when `_` is followed by exactly one duration letter (w/h/q/e/s/t) that is itself NOT followed by a word char (so `__enableXModule` and multi-letter idents like `_qux` are excluded), emit TokenType.Underscore WITHOUT consuming the duration letter, leaving `q`/`w`/etc. as the next token so the existing RestElement path (Parser.NoteStream.cs:90-96, which calls TryParseDurationSuffix at line 93) picks it up. (2) Cleaner/lower-risk: keep the lexer as-is and handle it in Parser.NoteStream.cs's identifier branch — before the break at line 401, detect an identifier of form `_` + single duration letter, and emit `new RestElement(elemLoc, durLetter, isDotted)` (also honoring a trailing Dot/Tilde), preserving the `__`-prefixed internal-marker carve-out. Either way, add a note-stream test covering `| _w |`, `| _q _q _q _q |`, dotted `| _q. |`, and confirm `__enableSfzModule` still lexes as one identifier. Update the now-stale workaround comment at examples/sweep/transforms_voices.flow:33-36.

title: No 'bass' GM prefix — a sequence named bass* exports to MIDI as piano (program 0)
finding: ResolveGmProgram has prefixes for piano/brass/sax/flute/string/organ/bell/drum and many Phase 33 orchestral names, but NO 'bass' (or 'acousticbass'/'upright') entry. A walking-bass sequence named `bass`/`bassWalk` falls through to the default (0,0) = GM 0 Acoustic Grand Piano. Verified: a section sequence named `bass` emits 'c0 00' (Program Change ch0, prog 0) in the .mid — it plays as PIANO, not a bass. There is no advisory. The closest workaround (used in this showcase) is to name the bass `stringBass*` so it hits the `string*` -> GM 48 prefix, but GM 48 is String Ensemble 1, not Acoustic/Upright Bass (GM 32). So a jazz composer cannot get a bass MIDI program by the obvious name, and the natural name silently exports the wrong instrument.
rootCause: ResolveGmProgram (flow-lang/StandardLibrary/Notation/InstrumentRouting.cs:45-83) has no prefix entry for "bass" (nor acousticbass/upright/electricbass/synthbass/doublebass). Phase 33 adds "contrabass"->43 (line 58) and "bassoon"->70 (line 61), but a plain "bass*" sequence matches none of the 24 prefixes and hits the line 82 fallthrough `return (0, 0)` = GM 0 Acoustic Grand Piano. This table is the single source of truth consumed by writeMidi (MidiExport.cs:458), real-time MIDI out (MidiFunctions.cs:498), and the Phase 39 MusicXML/LilyPond emit paths, so a walking-bass line named `bass`/`bassWalk` exports across ALL notation surfaces as a piano.
